      2: ====================
      3: 
      4: Ibex is a production-quality open source 32-bit RISC-V CPU core written in SystemVerilog.

sections.label: Verification Overview
sections.snippet:
>     1: Verification Overview
      2: =====================
      3: 
      4: Ibex is verified using a :ref:`UVM based testbench<verification>` that employs a :ref:`co-simulation methodology<cosim>` to cross-check Ibex execution against an ISS reference model (`Spike <https://github.com/lowRISC/riscv-isa-sim>`_).
      5: The testbench runs binaries built from source produced by the `RISC-DV <https://github.com/chipsalliance/riscv-dv>`_ random instruction generator.

sections.label: Verification Status
sections.snippet:
5: The testbench runs binaries built from source produced by the `RISC-DV <https://github.com/chipsalliance/riscv-dv>`_ random instruction generator.
      6: Additional stimulus is provided in the form of randomized memory timings, memory errors, interrupts and debug requests by the testbench.
      7: A comprehensive :ref:`testplan<testplan>` and :ref:`coverage plan<coverage-plan>` are implemented.
      8: 
>     9: Verification Status
     10: -------------------
     11: 
     12: Ibex has a large number of parameters resulting in a large number of possible configurations.
     13: The configuration space is too large to fully verify the design for all possible parameter sets.

>    10: Register File
     11: -------------
     12: 
     13: Ibex comes with three different register file implementations that can be selected using the enumerated parameter ``RegFile`` defined in :file:`rtl/ibex_pkg.sv`.
     14: Depending on the target technology, either the flip-flop-based ("ibex_pkg::RegFileFF", default), the latch-based ("ibex_pkg::RegFileLatch") or an FPGA-targeted ("ibex_pkg::RegFileFPGA") implementation should be selected.

sections.label: Trap Handling
sections.snippet:
103: If any errors occur during the step they can be accessed via ``get_errors`` which returns a vector of error messages.
    104: For the DPI interface errors are accessed using ``riscv_cosim_get_num_errors`` and ``riscv_cosim_get_error``.
    105: When errors have been checked they can be cleared with ``clear_errors``.
    106: 
>   107: Trap Handling
    108: ^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    109: 
    110: Traps are separated into two categories, synchronous and asynchronous.
    111: Synchronous traps are caused by a particular instruction's execution (e.g. an illegal instruction).

sections.label: Interrupts and Debug Requests
sections.snippet:
122: 
    123: While a debug request is not strictly an asynchronous trap (it doesn't use the same exception handling mechanism), they work identically to asynchronous traps for the co-simulation system.
    124: When a debug request is pending when ``step`` is called the co-simulation will expect the instruction checked by ``step`` to be the first instruction of the debug handler.
    125: 
>   126: Interrupts and Debug Requests
    127: ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
    128: 
    129: The DV environment must observe any incoming interrupts and debug requests generated by the testbench and notify the co-simulation system of them using ``set_mip``, ``set_debug_req`` and ``set_nmi``.
    130: An interrupt or debug request will take immediate effect at the next ``step`` (if architecturally required to do so).

128: Note that Ibex cannot generated an 'instruction address misaligned' exception as all configurations implement the 'C' extension.
    129: Under the RISC-V architecture it is simply not possible to branch or otherwise start executing from a PC that isn't 16-bit aligned.
    130: So with 'C' implemented all possible PCs are appropriately aligned.
    131:

>     9: Outputs
     10: -------
     11: 
     12: Ibex has three alert outputs for signalling security issues.
     13: The internal major alert (**alert_major_internal_o**) indicates a critical security issue from which the core cannot recover which was detected internally in `ibex_top`.

sections.label: Data Independent Timing
sections.snippet:
13: The internal major alert (**alert_major_internal_o**) indicates a critical security issue from which the core cannot recover which was detected internally in `ibex_top`.
     14: The bus major alert (**alert_major_bus_o**) indicates a critical security issue from which the core cannot recover which was detected on incoming bus data.
     15: The minor alert (**alert_minor_o**) indicates potential security issues which can be monitored over time by a system.
     16: 
>    17: Data Independent Timing
     18: -----------------------
     19: 
     20: When enabled (via the **data_ind_timing** control bit in the **cpuctrl** register), execution times and power consumption of all instructions shall be independent of input data.
     21: This makes it more difficult for an external observer to infer secret data by observing power lines or exploiting timing side-channels.

>    41: Dummy Instruction Insertion
     42: ---------------------------
     43: 
     44: When enabled (via the **dummy_instr_en** control bit in the **cpuctrl** register), dummy instructions will be inserted at random intervals into the execution pipeline.
     45: The dummy instructions have no functional impact on processor state, but add some difficult-to-predict timing and power disruption to executed code.

>    48: #### Core Agent
     49: 
     50: The core agent emulates a core making requests of the cache.
     51: This is an active master with a standard UVM structure (sequencer, driver, monitor).
     52: Code implementing the agent can be found in [`dv/uvm/icache/dv/ibex_icache_core_agent`](https://github.com/lowRISC/ibex/tree/master/dv/uvm/icache/dv/ibex_icache_core_agent).

sections.label: Memory Agent
sections.snippet:
65: This means that the cache doesn't need to avoid multi-way hits with inconsistent data.
     66: In order that the testbench can guarantee this doesn't happen, the core agent must be in charge of deciding when to update the contents of memory with a new seed (see the Memory Agent, below).
     67: A new seed is picked on every invalidation (since this gives the maximum test sensitivity) and is picked occasionally when the cache is fetching when disabled.
     68: 
>    69: #### Memory Agent
     70: 
     71: The memory agent emulates the instruction bus, supplying data to the cache.
     72: This must be deterministic (in order for the scoreboard to tell whether the cache fetched the right data), but must also be able to change with time (in order to check invalidation works correctly).
     73: To support this, the memory contents are modelled with a 32-bit seed value.

1: # Primitive Component: PRESENT Scrambler
      2: 
>     3: # Overview
      4: 
      5: `prim_present` is an (unhardened) implementation of the encryption pass of the [64bit PRESENT block cipher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PRESENT).
      6: It is a fully unrolled combinational implementation that supports both key lengths specified in the paper (80bit and 128bit).
      7: Further, the number of rounds is fully configurable, and the primitive supports a 32bit block cipher flavor which is not specified in the original paper.

      9: It should be noted, however, that reduced-round and/or 32bit versions **are not secure** and must not be used in a setting where cryptographic cipher strength is required.

      5: `prim_prince` is an (unhardened) implementation of the [64bit PRINCE block cipher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_(cipher)).

sections.label: Overview
sections.snippet:
1: # Primitive Component: SRAM Scrambler
      2: 
>     3: # Overview
      4: 
      5: The scrambling primitive `prim_ram_1p_scr` employs a reduced-round (5 or 7 instead of 11) PRINCE block cipher in CTR mode to scramble the data.
      6: The PRINCE lightweight block cipher has been selected due to its low latency and low area characteristics, see also [prim_prince](./prim_prince.md) for more information on PRINCE.
      7: In the default configuration, the number of rounds is reduced to 7 in order to ease timing pressure and ensure single cycle operation (the number of rounds can always be increased via the `NumPrinceRoundsHalf` parameter if it turns out that there is enough timing slack).

     26: Note that since this optional data diffusion can affect end-to-end bus and memory integrity schemes, it is disabled by default.

>     6: # Context
      7: 
      8: Hardware companies often invest in engineering resources to build and maintain custom tooling to manage EDA tool flows.
      9: It enables them to deploy and scale EDA workloads efficiently across their projects onto their compute infrastructure, monitor their execution, assess success and generate and publish queryable report to track the overall health and progress of their projects.
     10: These are often proprietary in nature, which makes them unsuitable for the development of open source projects such as OpenTitan.

>   115: ### EDA tool flow steps
    116: 
    117: The simulation tool flow progresses through the following *steps*:
    118: - **build** (build the design / testbench database)
    119: - **run** (run the test as a simulation)

sections.label: Flow-specific Makefile
sections.snippet:
123: All other EDA tools flows stop at the **build** step, because they build the design and run the flow on the same invocation, unlike simulations where the EDA tool is invoked separately for the build and run steps.
    124: Each of these steps is executed as a single job that is launched to a compute machine.
    125: They are hence, also referred to as "jobs".
    126: 
>   127: ### Flow-specific Makefile
    128: 
    129: Each of these steps may contain sub-steps, which are sequenced by a **flow-specific Makefile** ([example](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/dv/tools/dvsim/sim.mk)).
    130: This Makefile is very lean, and has targets for each of the flow-specific steps.
    131: It is a project-specific source, not maintained within the DVSim codebase, which allows a greater degree of flexibility for adoption.

sections.label: DUT configuration
sections.snippet:
134: The Makefile also sequences housekeeping actions, such as constructing the paths for the output artifacts, dumping the environment variables for ease of debug, etc.
    135: When the job is launched, a make command is executed, with the Make variables set to the values required to correctly run the job, using the flow-specific Makefile.
    136: Thus, all Make variables must be defined in the DUT configuration file and differentiated as needed for the jobs.
    137: 
>   138: ### DUT configuration
    139: 
    140: The **DUT configuration** is expressed in Hjson, split into a tree of files.
    141: The root DUT configuration file indicates the [flow](./glossary.md#eda-tool-flow) and the EDA tool used to execute the flow, among several other things.
    142: It may recursively import auxiliary Hjson files containing additional EDA tool flow configuration data, such as test specifications that are common to multiple DUTs.

>     1: # OpenTitan Continuous Integration
      2: 
      3: All changes to the OpenTitan source code are tested thoroughly in a continuous integration system.
      4: Tests run automatically when changes are proposed for inclusion by submitting a pull request, and on the `master` branch after changes are merged.
      5: This ensures that the OpenTitan source code meets certain quality criteria at all points in time, as defined by the tests which are executed.

>    99: #### Mitigating issues

>     1: # Security Countermeasure Verification Framework
      2:

>     3: ## Purpose
      4: In a security chip, there are many hardening security countermeasures implemented in security blocks.

1: # RACL: Register Access Control List
      2: 
>     3: ## Introduction
      4: A System-on-Chip (SOC) must provide differentiated security on access to registers in the SOC and the CPU.
      5: RACL is a lightweight, fine-grained access control mechanism to restrict CSR access to specific originators, which fulfils this need.
      6: 
      7: ### Definitions

sections.label: Definitions
sections.snippet:
3: ## Introduction
      4: A System-on-Chip (SOC) must provide differentiated security on access to registers in the SOC and the CPU.
      5: RACL is a lightweight, fine-grained access control mechanism to restrict CSR access to specific originators, which fulfils this need.
      6: 
>     7: ### Definitions
      8: Each processing element in the SOC, i.e. each component that can actively generate a register read and/or write request, is a _subject_.
      9: A subject may have one or more _roles_ associated with it and the subject may be allowed to switch between the roles.
     10: For example, a CPU processing element may switch between multiple roles based on the mode of execution.
     11: The set of roles that can be assumed by a subject may also change temporally.

sections.label: Overview
sections.snippet:
19: The implementation shall provide an abstraction to allow different implementers defining their role assignments based on their needs.
     20: The role is transmitted across the fabric as part of a transaction so that a given policy can be enforced at the target based on this role.
     21: For the TLUL fabric used within OpenTitan, the [top-level RACL configuration](#top-level-racl-configuration) defines which bits of the `a_user` field are used to carry this information.
     22: 
>    23: ### Overview
     24: ![RACL structure](racl.svg)
     25: 
     26: The figure above shows how the role of a source processing element is sent across the fabric along with the transaction.
     27: In this example, the source processing element can pick between 3 roles - `RoleID0`, `RoleID1`, and `RoleID2`.

sections.label: RACL Policies
sections.snippet:
28: The RoleSelector - selects the current role - muxes out the ID corresponding to the current role onto the fabric.
     29: At the target, the role and the attributes of the transaction (Read/Write, address, and size) are used to determine if the access is allowed or denied.
     30: If the access is denied then the error is logged into an Error-Log register.
     31: 
>    32: ### RACL Policies
     33: Each policy register takes the form of a pair of permission bitmaps, `ReadPerm` and `WritePerm`, where each bit corresponds to a role.
     34: E.g., if 16 different roles are defined, the register looks as follows, where the bit position of each role is defined by the role encoding that is specified via the `role_id` in the [configuration file](#top-level-racl-configuration).
     35: 
     36: |                 | Role 0 | Role 1 | ... | Role 14 | Role 15 |

sections.label: RACL Controller
sections.snippet:
64: The read and write permissions are used from this policy as defined in the configuration file at design time.
     65: For all policy registers, the configuration specified in the configuration file is the reset default value.
     66: However, depending on the permissions defined for the `rot_private`-designated policy, the policy registers may also be updated at runtime.
     67: 
>    68: ### RACL Controller
     69: 
     70: For a top-level that uses RACL, there is an associated RACL Controller (`racl_ctrl`), which acts as the interface between the TileLink bus and the RACL matching logic.
     71: For example, see the documentation for the [Darjeeling racl_ctrl](../../../../hw/top_darjeeling/ip_autogen/racl_ctrl/README.md).
     72: The RACL Controller implements the policy registers, distributes them to subscribing IPs and collects error logs from them through its hardware interface.

     72: The RACL Controller implements the policy registers, distributes them to subscribing IPs and collects error logs from them through its hardware interface.
     73: 
>    74: ### RACL Controller Groups
     75: A RACL controller group is defined by a name and a set of policies.
     76: Each group must also have one instance of a RACL controller associated with this group.
     77: Currently, only a single group is supported, but this is expected to change in the future.
     78: Any RACL-enabled IP subscribing to a specific RACL controller group is automatically connected to the associated RACL controller to get the appropriate policies and to collect the error logs from that specific group.

>    80: ## RACL Rules
     81: 1. Each instantiation of a RACL-enabled IP must state which [RACL Controller Group](#racl-controller-groups) it subscribes to.

     83: 3. For each bus interface where RACL is enabled, each of its registers and windows must be mapped to a RACL policy that exists within the RACL Controller Group which is used for this IP.

>   105: ## Processing Element (Subject) Requirements
    106: 1. Processing elements must not allow the role encodings for a transaction to be mutable under firmware control to a role that is not defined for that processing element.
    107: 2. The processing element may obtain the encodings for each role through a set of straps from the SOC.
    108:    Alternatively, the processing element may support a configurable register that allows configuring encodings for each role.
    109:    If such a configurable register exists that register must be access controlled such that it can be only updated by the ROT role.

>   112: ## Pass-through processing elements
    113: Some processing elements pass-through transactions received upstream to fabric downstream.
    114: Examples of such processing elements include I/O bridges.
    115: Such bridges must pass through the role verbatim from the upstream to downstream and must not substitute their own role for the downstream transaction.

      4: In both cases, we need to import and use code from external repositories in our OpenTitan code base.
      5: Read on for step-by-step instructions for common tasks, and for background information on the topic.
      6: 
>     7: ## Summary
      8: 
      9: Code in subdirectories of `hw/vendor` is imported (copied in) from external repositories (which may be provided by lowRISC or other sources).
     10: The external repository is called "upstream".
     11: Any development on imported in `hw/vendor` code should happen upstream when possible.

sections.label: Background
sections.snippet:
25: Pushing changes upstream first isn't always possible or desirable: upstream might not accept changes, or be slow to respond.
     26: In some cases, code changes are needed which are irrelevant for upstream and need to be maintained by us.
     27: Our vendoring infrastructure is able to handle such cases, read on for more information on how to do it.
     28: 
>    29: ## Background
     30: 
     31: OpenTitan is developed in a "monorepo", a single repository containing all its source code.
     32: This approach is beneficial for many reasons, ranging from an easier workflow to better reproducibility of the results, and that's why large companies like [Google](https://ai.google/research/pubs/pub45424) and Facebook are using monorepos.
     33: Monorepos are even more compelling for hardware development, which cannot make use of a standardized language-specific package manager like npm or pip.

108: Do not use `volatile` for hardening purposes.

    110: See `hardened.h` for the hardening primitives we have.
    111: 
>   112: ### `const` and Non-`const` Variables Initialized Outside the Lifetime of a Program
    113: 
    114: There are several cases in OpenTitan silicon creator code where a variable with static storage duration is initialized either partially or completely in a way that isn’t visible to the C source code overriding the static initializer of the C object.
    115: A `const` example to this case is the definition of `kManifest` in `sw/device/silicon_creator/lib/manifest_def.c`.
    116: `kManifest` is an aggregate object of type `manifest_t` that resides in flash memory whose actual value at runtime is different from the initializer in source code because the binary is modified by the build system before it is loaded into flash memory.

sections.label: Pointers Created Out of Thin Air
sections.snippet:
121:     *   _Rationale: Even if the object resides in read-only memory, it must not be declared as a `const`-qualified type. If `const` is used, the compiler is not required to allocate space for the object and may replace reads with the value specified in the initializer. If needed, `const` related compiler diagnostics must be enabled by providing a getter that returns a `const` pointer to the actual object instead of exposing the non-`const` declaration._
    122: *   non-`volatile`.
    123:     *   _Rationale: The `volatile` qualifier prevents various optimizations and the use of `memcpy`, `memset`, and many other standard functions. The specification states that "All objects with static storage duration shall be initialized (set to their initial values) before program startup. The manner and timing of such initialization are otherwise unspecified." (C11, section 5.1.2, paragraph 1). By not using `volatile` we’re no longer informing the compiler that the value of the object "may be modified in ways unknown to the implementation" (C11, section 6.7.3, paragraph 7). In principle, this could be problematic in situations where the implementation is allowed to assume that the object contains its initial value, e.g. when the object is `const` or when performing LTO and the compiler assumes that it has visibility into the whole program (using the `-fwhole-program` flag in gcc)_[^2]_. Since neither of these are true in this case, it seems safe to conclude that the compiler has to be conservative and cannot assume that the object has not been modified since the program startup._
    124: 
>   125: ### Pointers Created Out of Thin Air
    126: 
    127: OpenTitan secure boot consists of at least three stages: `rom`, `rom_ext`, and the first owner boot stage.
    128: All boot stages except `rom` are stored in flash and all in-flash boot stages are required to start with a "manifest" so that their integrity and authenticity can be verified.
    129: Since OpenTitan uses a fixed flash layout, `rom` and `rom_ext` exactly know the next stage's manifest's location in flash.

sections.label: Rule 2: Use volatile in Tests For Correctness
sections.snippet:
130: Since this address is not part of their images, `rom` and `rom_ext` create pointers essentially out of thin air using functions like `_const manifest_t *boot_policy_manifest_a_get(void)_`.
    131: If the pointers in question do not point to something already known by the compiler, an optimizing compiler cannot optimize away the first access.
    132: Thus, there is no need to declare such pointers as `volatile`.
    133: 
>   134: ## Rule 2: Use `volatile` in Tests For Correctness
    135: 
    136: `rom` and `rom_ext` do not enable interrupts and their handlers shut down the chip instead of returning.
    137: Tests, however, can define their custom interrupt/exception handlers for their own purposes.
    138: In cases where a variable is shared between a handler and the rest of the program, it must be declared as `volatile` to ensure correctness.

32: DIFs **must not** depend on DIFs for other IP blocks, or other external libraries.
     33: 
     34: This decision is motivated by the requirement that DIFs must be extremely flexible in their possible execution environments, including being hosted in bare metal, or being called from other languages such as Rust through Foreign Function Interface.
     35: 
>    36: #### Runtime Independence
     37: 
     38: DIFs **must not** depend on runtime services provided by an operating system.
     39: If functions must be called in response to system stimulus such as interrupts then the DIF must make these requirements explicit in their documentation.
     40: This decision makes DIFs appropriate for execution environments without OS support such as DV.

sections.label: Architecture Independence
sections.snippet:
38: DIFs **must not** depend on runtime services provided by an operating system.
     39: If functions must be called in response to system stimulus such as interrupts then the DIF must make these requirements explicit in their documentation.
     40: This decision makes DIFs appropriate for execution environments without OS support such as DV.
     41: 
>    42: ### Architecture Independence
     43: 
     44: DIFs **should not** depend on architecture-specific constructs such as inline assembly or platform-defined registers, except where a peripheral is integrated into the core in a way making them unavoidable.
     45: As a concrete example: a SPI DIF must not depend on a pinmux or clock control DIF in order to be operated.
     46: This highlights a clear separation of concern: making a pin on the package driven from the SPI block involves multiple systems.

sections.label: Coverage Requirements
sections.snippet:
45: As a concrete example: a SPI DIF must not depend on a pinmux or clock control DIF in order to be operated.
     46: This highlights a clear separation of concern: making a pin on the package driven from the SPI block involves multiple systems.
     47: By design, a DIF cannot coordinate cross-functional control.
     48: 
>    49: #### Coverage Requirements
     50: 
     51: DIFs *must* actuate all of the specification-required functionality of the hardware that they are written for, and no more.
     52: A DIF cannot be declared complete until it provides an API for accessing all of the functionality that is expected of the hardware.
     53: This is distinct from mandating that a DIF be required to cover all of the functionality of a given piece of hardware.

5: This document aims to enable a contributor to get started with a design verification (DV) effort within the OpenTitan project.
      6: While most of the focus is on development of a testbench from scratch, it should also be useful to understand how to contribute to an existing effort.
      7: Please refer to the [DV methodology](../contributing/dv/methodology/README.md) document for information on how design verification is done in OpenTitan.

>     9: ## Stages of DV
     10: 
     11: The life stages of a design / DV effort within the OpenTitan are described in the [Hardware Development Stages](../project_governance/development_stages.md) document.
     12: It separates the life of DV into three broad stages: Initial Work, Under Test and Testing Complete.
     13: This document attempts to give guidance on how to get going with the first stage and have a smooth transition into the Under Test stage.

      3: The following Communications Policy addresses OpenTitan-related communications by the OpenTitan Partners or their employees or affiliates, where those individual employees or affiliates may know, or reasonably have the appearance of knowing, non-public information about the OpenTitan Project.
      4: It also discusses the responsible use of G Suite accounts by OpenTitan Committers and Authorized Contributors, as well as the heightened responsibilities of OpenTitan Committee Members.

1: # OpenTitan Hardware Development Stages
      2: 
>     3: ## Document Goals
      4: 
      5: This document describes development stages for hardware within the OpenTitan program.
      6: This includes design and verification stages meant to give a high-level view of the status of a design.
      7: OpenTitan being an open-source program aimed at a high quality silicon release, the intent is to find a balance between the rigor of a heavy tapeout process and the more fluid workings of an open source development.

sections.label: Introduction
sections.snippet:
1: # OpenTitan RFC Process
      2: 
>     3: ## Introduction
      4: 
      5: The OpenTitan RFC process is the mechanism by which technical proposals can be reviewed and voted upon by the Technical Committee (TC).
      6: More generally, the RFC process ensures changes are appropriately reviewed, gives the contributor community opportunity to give feedback, and helps ensure alternative implementation options are also evaluated.
      7: Many other open source projects implement such a process with varying degrees of formality, e.g. Python Enhancement Proposals, RFCs in the LLVM community, and more.

sections.label: RFC lifetime
sections.snippet:
10: E.g. "Implement IP block X" is not a useful RFC unless either the proposer is willing to do that work or someone else is interested in pursuing it.
     11: 
     12: This document outlines the basic structure of the RFC process, with the expectation that it will evolve over time based on the experience of active contributors.
     13: 
>    14: ## RFC lifetime
     15: 
     16: * [Optional: Seek feedback on whether an RFC is desired.
     17:   This is recommended for a lengthy "out of the blue" proposal, to ensure time isn't wasted writing up a detailed proposal for something that is out of scope or that can't be decided upon at this stage.]
     18: * An author (or set of authors) writes an RFC.

sections.label: Potential future RFC process refinements
sections.snippet:
42: 
     43: RFCs should be created at least for any major new piece of code (e.g. IP block), or cross-cutting changes that need careful consideration.
     44: Generally speaking, an RFC should be created when there is demand for one (especially when that request comes from a Committer).
     45: 
>    46: ## Potential future RFC process refinements
     47: 
     48: The process has been kept as simple as possible to start with, closely mimicking the informal consensus approach being used in the early stages of the OpenTitan project.
     49: However, there are a range of potential improvements that it may make sense for the Technical Committee and wider contributor community to explore:

>    52: #### Specialized status codes
     53: 
     54: The cryptolib status code `otcrypto_status_t` is bit-compatible with `status_t`, but the error values are always the same.
     55: Typically, `status_t` would display the module ID and line number to help debugging, but since this information could theoretically help an attacker we do not want to expose it.

1: # Reset vs. Non-Reset Flops
      2: 
>     3: ## Overview
      4: 
      5: Various components inside OpenTitan operate on sensitive assets such as identities and key material.
      6: This includes both the main processor core (executing cryptographic algorithms, configuring cryptographic hardware accelerators) and peripherals such as the key manager (key derivation, sideloading) and cryptographic accelerators themselves.
      7: In most cases, such sensitive assets are locally registered in the hardware block and it is of high importance that they do not get exposed to potential adversaries even with physical access to the chip.

     18: 
>    19: ## Flip-Flop Types
     20: 
     21: At register-transfer level (RTL), OpenTitan considers two different flip-flop (flop) types for implementing registers: Reset Flops[^1] and Non-Reset Flops.
     22: The main difference between the two is the behavior upon reset: The former puts the storage element into a well-defined state, whereas in the latter the value inside the storage element is not altered.
     23: From a security perspective, both behaviors need consideration.

sections.label: Reset flops
sections.snippet:
21: At register-transfer level (RTL), OpenTitan considers two different flip-flop (flop) types for implementing registers: Reset Flops[^1] and Non-Reset Flops.
     22: The main difference between the two is the behavior upon reset: The former puts the storage element into a well-defined state, whereas in the latter the value inside the storage element is not altered.
     23: From a security perspective, both behaviors need consideration.
     24: 
>    25: ### Reset flops
     26: 
     27: Putting the storage element into a well-defined state upon reset automatically wipes any content from the storage element, but directly exposes the Hamming distance between the content (a potential secret) and the reset value in side-channel analysis (SCA).
     28: 
     29: This means that after a reset, there is no need to worry about sensitive data from before the reset being somehow extracted.

sections.label: Non-reset flops
sections.snippet:
41:   To protect such critical cores, designers resort to different countermeasures for security hardening and this suggests that the susceptibility to reset glitch attacks should be viewed in the context of these measures (see below).
     42: - Sidenote: Relying on glitch detectors for detecting localized glitches and initiating a complete system reset or alternatively a wipe with random data on top of the asynchronous reset is probably not sufficient as even a minimal delay of a couple of cycles between the glitch and the wipe can suffice to capture the Hamming distance.
     43:   In OpenTitan, already the alert handler triggering the system reset has a delay of multiple cycles.
     44: 
>    45: ### Non-reset flops
     46: 
     47: Not altering the value inside the storage element upon a reset has the advantage of completely avoiding the Hamming distance leakage during reset which makes the design much more robust against reset glitch attacks.
     48: 
     49: However, leaving the value of the storage element untouched upon a reset requires special care to avoid that sensitive assets get into the wrong hands after a reset.

>    65: ## Scan Mode
     66: 
     67: Theoretically, scan mode could be misused to simply scan sensitive assets out of registers.
     68: The obvious approach of taking all registers potentially holding sensitive data off the scan chain is not a viable solution.
     69: This may affect many registers (e.g. ~1400 flops for unhardened AES) and have a very big impact on design for testability (DFT).

>    80: ## Interplay with other Countermeasures and Security Hardening
     81: 
     82: In many cases, the weak spot of sensitive assets is not their storage in a peripheral register and transition from one block into another (e.g. over a bus), but the usage of the asset such as in heavy, predictable data processing potentially happening on just a subset of the asset with a small-sized hypothesis space (e.g. a single byte-sized S-Box in AES).
     83: Such functionality is typically protected against SCA by additional countermeasures implemented later during the design process in a security hardening phase.
     84: Obviously the implemented countermeasures have a big impact on the susceptibility to various attack types and therefore must be known when weighing up the risks of non-reset vs. reset flops for the considered OpenTitan hardware block.

>    93: ## Conclusion

>     8: ## Logical Entities
      9: 
     10: At a high level, the OpenTitan logical security model is composed of 4 entities - Silicon Creator, Silicon Owner, Application Provider and the End User.
     11: This document focuses on the first 3 entities.
     12: These entities are directly involved in creating a fully trademark compliant OpenTitan.

>    16: ### Silicon Creator

     18: The Silicon Creator is the **logical entity**, or **logical collection of entities** that manufactures, packages, tests and provisions the chip with its first identity.

>    73: # Silicon Creator Keys
     74:

     21: 
     22: - Register interface to dual ADC analog block

sections.label: Initialization

1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
>     3: ## Initialization
      4: 
      5: The controller should be initialized with the properties of the ADC and scan times.
      6: * The ADC power up delay must be set in [`adc_pd_ctl.pwrup_time`](registers.md#adc_pd_ctl).
      7: * The time to delay between samples in a slow scan should be set in [`adc_pd_ctl.wakeup_time`](registers.md#adc_pd_ctl).

sections.label: Running in normal mode
sections.snippet:
12: * All ones should be written to [`adc_intr_status`](registers.md#adc_intr_status) and  [`filter_status`](registers.md#filter_status) to ensure there are no spurious pending triggers.
     13: * Optionally, the low-power mode should be set in [`adc_pd_ctl.lp_mode`](registers.md#adc_pd_ctl) if the system is going to the low-power mode.
     14: * The state machine will only start running when [`adc_en_ctl`](registers.md#adc_en_ctl) is set.
     15: 
>    16: ## Running in normal mode
     17: 
     18: If fast sampling is always required then the [`adc_pd_ctl.lp_mode`](registers.md#adc_pd_ctl) bit should be clear.
     19: In this case the values in the [`adc_lp_sample_ctl`](registers.md#adc_lp_sample_ctl) are not used.
     20: The ADC will always be enabled and consuming power.

sections.label: Running with the rest of the chip in sleep
sections.snippet:
21: 
     22: If power saving is required then the controller can be set to operate in low power mode by setting [`adc_pd_ctl.lp_mode`](registers.md#adc_pd_ctl).
     23: The [`adc_lp_sample_ctl`](registers.md#adc_lp_sample_ctl) must be programmed prior to setting this bit.
     24: 
>    25: ## Running with the rest of the chip in sleep
     26: 
     27: Once programmed the controller and ADC can run when the rest of the chip is in low power state and the main clocks are stopped.
     28: This allows the chip to be woken when appropriate values are detected on the two ADC channels.
     29: The fast sampling mode can be used but will usually consume more power than desired when the chip is in sleep.

sections.label: Use Case
sections.snippet:
30: So it is expected that [`adc_lp_sample_ctl`](registers.md#adc_lp_sample_ctl) is configured and low power mode enabled by setting [`adc_pd_ctl.lp_mode`](registers.md#adc_pd_ctl) prior to the sleep being initiated.
     31: 
     32: If the ADC wakeup is not required then the controller and ADC should both be disabled by clearing [`adc_en_ctl`](registers.md#adc_en_ctl) prior to the sleep being initiated.
     33: 
>    34: ## Use Case
     35: 
     36: While the ADC controller is meant to be used generically, it can be configured to satisfy more complex use cases.
     37: As an illustrative example, the programmers guide uses the [Chrome OS Hardware Debug](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromiumos/third_party/hdctools/+/HEAD/docs/ccd.md) as an example of how the ADC controller can be used.
     38:

>    12: # Overview
     13: 
     14: This document specifies the AES hardware IP functionality.
     15: [Advanced Encryption Standard (AES)](https://www.nist.gov/publications/advanced-encryption-standard-aes) is the primary symmetric encryption and decryption mechanism used in OpenTitan protocols.
     16: The AES unit is a cryptographic accelerator that accepts requests from the processor to encrypt or decrypt 16 byte blocks of data.

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
16: The AES unit is a cryptographic accelerator that accepts requests from the processor to encrypt or decrypt 16 byte blocks of data.
     17: It is attached to the chip interconnect bus as a peripheral module and conforms to the [Comportable guideline for peripheral functionality.](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md)
     18: 
     19: 
>    20: ## Features
     21: 
     22: The AES unit supports the following features:
     23: 
     24: - Encryption/Decryption using AES-128/192/256 in the following cipher block modes:

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
45: Cipher modes other than ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and GCM are beyond this version of the AES unit but might be supported in future versions.
     46: If hardware support for GCM is disabled, it can be implemented by leveraging [Ibex](../../top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/rv_core_ibex/README.md) for the GHASH operation as demonstrated in the [OpenTitan Cryptography Library](../../../doc/security/cryptolib/README.md).
     47: 
     48: 
>    49: ## Description
     50: 
     51: The AES unit is a cryptographic accelerator that accepts requests from the processor to encrypt or decrypt 16B blocks of data.
     52: It supports AES-128/192/256 in Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode, Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode, Cipher Feedback (CFB) mode (fixed data segment size of 128 bits, i.e., CFB-128), Output Feedback (OFB) mode, Counter (CTR) mode and Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) (fixed IV length of 96 bits, fixed tag length of 128 bits).
     53: For more information on these cipher modes, refer to [Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38a.pdf).

The content of the Control Register is not modified (See Control Register). The AES unit can be recovered from such a condition by restarting the AES operation, i.e., by re-writing the Control Register. This should be monitored by the system.                                                                                                                                                     |
     26: | fatal_fault           | This fatal alert is triggered upon detecting a fatal fault inside the AES unit. Examples for such faults include i) storage errors in the shadowed Control Register, ii) any internal FSM entering an invalid state, iii) any sparsely encoded signal taking on an invalid value, iv) errors in the internal round counter, v) escalations triggered by the life cycle controller, and vi) fatal integrity failures on the TL-UL bus. The AES unit cannot recover from such an error and needs to be reset. |

sections.label: Clear upon Reset
sections.snippet:
2: 
      3: This section discusses how software can interface with the AES unit.
      4: 
      5: 
>     6: ## Clear upon Reset
      7: 
      8: Upon reset, the AES unit will first reseed the internal PRNGs for register clearing and masking via EDN, and then clear all key, IV and data registers with pseudo-random data.
      9: Only after this sequence has finished, the unit becomes idle (indicated in [`STATUS.IDLE`](registers.md#status)).
     10: The AES unit is then ready for software initialization.

sections.label: Initialization
sections.snippet:
10: The AES unit is then ready for software initialization.
     11: Note that at this point, the key, IV and data registers' values can no longer be expected to match the reset values.
     12: 
     13: 
>    14: ## Initialization
     15: 
     16: Before initialization, software must ensure that the AES unit is idle by checking [`STATUS.IDLE`](registers.md#status).
     17: If the AES unit is not idle, write operations to [`CTRL_SHADOWED`](registers.md#ctrl_shadowed), the Initial Key registers [`KEY_SHARE0_0`](registers.md#key_share0) - [`KEY_SHARE1_7`](registers.md#key_share1) and initialization vector (IV) registers [`IV_0`](registers.md#iv) - [`IV_3`](registers.md#iv) are ignored.
     18:

sections.label: Block Operation
sections.snippet:
38: The order in which these registers are written does not matter.
     39: Note that the AES unit automatically updates the IV registers when running in CBC, CFB, OFB or CTR mode (after having consumed the current IV value).
     40: To start the encryption/decryption of a new message, software must wait for the AES unit to become idle and then provide new values to the IV registers.
     41: 
>    42: ## Block Operation
     43: 
     44: For block operation, software must initialize the AES unit as described in the previous section.
     45: In particular, the AES unit must be configured to run in normal/automatic mode.
     46: This is indicated by the MANUAL_OPERATION bit in [`CTRL_SHADOWED`](registers.md#ctrl_shadowed) reading as `0`.

>   134: ## Galois/Counter Mode (GCM)
    135: 
    136: GCM is a mode of Authenticated Encryption with Additional Data (AEAD) specified in [NIST 800-38D](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf) and widely adopted in industry.
    137: At a high level, GCM builds on top of the ECB and CTR block cipher modes of operation as well as a Galois Field GF(2^128) multiplication for the integrity tag computation (GHASH).
    138: The AES unit follows a hybrid implementation approach where software cycles the AES hardware unit through the different phases of GCM.

sections.label: GCM Encryption
sections.snippet:
143: - This implementation uses a fixed IV length of 96 bits, thereby following the recommendation of [NIST 800-38D (Section 5.2.1.1)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38d.pdf).
    144: - This implementation uses a fixed tag length of 128 bits.
    145:   Software is free to discard unused bits.
    146: 
>   147: ### GCM Encryption
    148: 
    149: To perform an GCM encryption, software performs the following steps:
    150: 
    151: 1. Software configures the AES unit in GCM mode by setting the [`CTRL_SHADOWED.MODE`](registers.md#ctrl_shadowed) field to `AES_GCM` and the `OPERATION` field to `AES_ENC`.

sections.label: GCM Decryption
sections.snippet:
189:    This configures the module internally to forward any input provided via the Input Data registers [`DATA_IN_0`](registers.md#data_in) - [`DATA_IN_3`](registers.md#data_in) to the GHASH module but NOT to the AES cipher core.
    190:    Software then provides a single data block of 128 bits containing the length of the AAD as well as the length of the ciphertext.
    191:    This causes the GHASH module to produce the final authentication tag which is then written to the Output Data registers [`DATA_OUT_0`](registers.md#data_out) - [`DATA_OUT_3`](registers.md#data_out).
    192: 
>   193: ### GCM Decryption
    194: 
    195: To perform an GCM decryption, software performs the following steps:
    196: 
    197: 1. Software configures the AES unit in GCM mode by setting the [`CTRL_SHADOWED.MODE`](registers.md#ctrl_shadowed) field to `AES_GCM` and the `OPERATION` field to `AES_DEC`.

>   221: ### GCM Context Restoring
    222: 
    223: To restore a context, software must perform the following steps:
    224: 
    225: 1. Software configures the AES unit in GCM mode by setting the [`CTRL_SHADOWED.MODE`](registers.md#ctrl_shadowed) field to `AES_GCM` and the `OPERATION` field to `AES_ENC`/`AES_DEC`.

sections.label: Padding
sections.snippet:
247: 1. Software configures [`CTRL_GCM_SHADOWED.PHASE`](registers.md#ctrl_gcm_shadowed) to `GCM_AAD` or `GCM_TEXT` and the `NUM_VALID_BYTES` field to `16` to continue processing where it left off previously.
    248: 
    249: Note that since both the masked hash subkey `H` and the masked encrypted initial counter block `S` are recomputed by the AES cipher core as part of the context restoring, the context switching feature can be leveraged to effectively refresh their sharing thereby injecting fresh entropy into the GHASH module.
    250: 
>   251: ## Padding
    252: 
    253: For the AES unit to automatically start encryption/decryption of the next data block, software is required to always update all four Input Data registers [`DATA_IN_0`](registers.md#data_in) - [`DATA_IN_3`](registers.md#data_in) and read all four Output Data registers [`DATA_OUT_0`](registers.md#data_out) - [`DATA_OUT_3`](registers.md#data_out).
    254: This is also true if the AES unit is operated in OFB or CTR mode, i.e., if the plaintext/ciphertext not necessarily needs to be a multiple of the block size (for more details refer to Appendix A of [Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/SP/nistspecialpublication800-38a.pdf)).
    255: The same also holds for the last AAD or plaintext/ciphertext block in GCM.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: The AES unit supports both encryption and decryption for AES-128/192/256 in ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR modes as well as GCM using a single, shared data path.
      4: That is, it can either do encryption or decryption but not both at the same time.

>    82: ### Datapath Architecture and Operation
     83: 
     84: The AES unit implements the Equivalent Inverse Cipher described in the [AES specification](https://csrc.nist.gov/csrc/media/publications/fips/197/final/documents/fips-197.pdf).
     85: This allows for more efficient cipher data path sharing between encryption/decryption as the operations are applied in the same order (less muxes, simpler control), but requires the round key during decryption to be transformed using an inverse MixColumns in all rounds except for the first and the last one.
     86:

>   182: ### SubBytes / S-Box
    183: 
    184: The SubBytes operation is a non-linear byte substitution that operates independently on each byte of the state using a substitution table (S-Box).
    185: It is both used for the cipher data path and the key expand data path.
    186: In total, the AES unit instantiates 20 S-Boxes in parallel (16 for SubBytes, 4 for KeyExpand), each having 8-bit input and output.

198: The DOM S-Box has a latency of 5 clock cycles.

    201: 
>   202: ### ShiftRows
    203: 
    204: The ShiftRows operation simply performs a cyclic shift of Rows 1, 2 and 3 of the state matrix.
    205: Consequently, it can be implemented using 3\*4 32-bit 2-input muxes (encryption/decryption).

sections.label: MixColumns
sections.snippet:
204: The ShiftRows operation simply performs a cyclic shift of Rows 1, 2 and 3 of the state matrix.
    205: Consequently, it can be implemented using 3\*4 32-bit 2-input muxes (encryption/decryption).
    206: 
    207: 
>   208: ### MixColumns
    209: 
    210: Each of the four columns of the state are considered as polynomials over GF(2^8) and individually multiplied with another fixed polynomial.
    211: The whole operation can be implemented using 36 2-input XORs and 16 4-input XORs (all 8-bit), 8 2-input muxes (8-bit), as well as 78 2-input and 24 3-input XOR gates.
    212:

sections.label: KeyExpand
sections.snippet:
210: Each of the four columns of the state are considered as polynomials over GF(2^8) and individually multiplied with another fixed polynomial.
    211: The whole operation can be implemented using 36 2-input XORs and 16 4-input XORs (all 8-bit), 8 2-input muxes (8-bit), as well as 78 2-input and 24 3-input XOR gates.
    212: 
    213: 
>   214: ### KeyExpand
    215: 
    216: The key expand module (KEM) integrated in the AES unit is responsible for generating the various round keys from the initial key for both encryption and decryption.
    217: The KEM generates the next 128/192/256-bit full key in parallel to the actual encryption/decryption based on the current full key or the initial key (for the first encryption round).
    218: The actual 128-bit round key is then extracted from this full key.

>    11: ## Overview
     12: 
     13: The Always-On ("AON") Timer contains two upcounting timers, designed to run in the always-on domain.

>    27: ## Wakeup timer
     28: 
     29: The wakeup timer (WKUP) is a 64-bit timer.

     31: Once the timer is enabled, it increments on every tick of the AON clock, divided by a pre-scaler.

>    15: ## Wakeup count and threshold access
     16: 
     17: The wakeup counter and threshold are both 64-bit values accessed via two 32-bit hi and lo registers.
     18: It is not possible to read or modify the 64-bit values in a single atomic access.
     19: Care must be taken to avoid issues due to race conditions caused by this.

     19: Care must be taken to avoid issues due to race conditions caused by this.
     20: Below are some recommendations on how to access the counter and threshold to avoid problems.
     21: 
>    22: ### Reading the counter
     23: 
     24: The counter might increment between the read of [`WKUP_COUNT_HI`](registers.md#wkup_count_hi) and the read of [`WKUP_COUNT_LO`](registers.md#wkup_count_lo).
     25: If the [`WKUP_COUNT_LO`](registers.md#wkup_count_lo) value overflows between the two register reads the combined 64-bit value may be incorrect.
     26: Consider the scenario where the 64-bit counter value is `0x1_ffff_ffff`.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: AON Timer interacts with the CPU core and the power manager and reset manager to generate interrupts as well as wakeup and  reset events.
      4: Each timer increases its count as long as its enable signal (`wdog_ctrl.enable` for WDOG and `wkup_ctrl.enable` for WKUP) is set.
      5: Both timers halt the counting if the signal `lc_escalate_en_i` is set, which tells the alert handler is the system is in a "killed" state.

>    18: ## Design Details
     19: 
     20: The always-on timer will run on a ~200KHz clock.

     22: This gives a maximum timeout window of roughly ~6 hours for the watchdog and almost 3 million years for the wakeup timer.

sections.label: Overview
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Overview
      2: 
      3: This document specifies the [Ascon](https://ascon.iaik.tugraz.at/) hardware IP functionality.
      4: Ascon is a sponge-based, single pass, online Authenticated Encryption Scheme (that can also be used for hashing).
      5: It was selected by [NIST as the winner](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2023/02/nist-selects-lightweight-cryptography-algorithms-protect-small-devices) of the NIST lightweight cryptography competition and is soon to be standardized.

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
4: Ascon is a sponge-based, single pass, online Authenticated Encryption Scheme (that can also be used for hashing).
      5: It was selected by [NIST as the winner](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2023/02/nist-selects-lightweight-cryptography-algorithms-protect-small-devices) of the NIST lightweight cryptography competition and is soon to be standardized.
      6: 
      7: 
>     8: ## Features
      9: 
     10: The Ascon units supports the following features:
     11: 
     12: * Authenticated encryption/decryption using either Ascon-128 (64 bit block size, 6 rounds per block update) or Ascon-128a (128 bit block size, 8 rounds per block update), whichever variant is standardized by NIST[^1], with a key and tag size of 128 bit, which leads to 128 bit security, and a state size of 320 bits.

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
26: This Ascon unit targets medium performance (~1 clock cycle per round for the unmasked implementation).
     27: High-speed, multiple rounds per clock cycles for high-bandwidth data streaming is not required.
     28: 
     29: 
>    30: ## Description
     31: 
     32: The Ascon unit is a cryptographic accelerator that accepts requests from the processor to encrypt or decrypt pairs of associated data A and messages M. A and M are divided into blocks, where each block is 64/128 bits, except the last block that can be potentially smaller.
     33: Empty strings are allowed, where either A, M or both are empty.
     34: The unit also takes a unique nonce N per each pair (A,M).

4: It describes the basic principles of Sponge and Ascon.

      6: 
      7: 
>     8: #### Duplex Sponge
      9: 
     10: A cryptographic public permutation is a cryptographic primitive that efficiently applies a permutation over b-bit blocks.
     11: The description of the permutation itself is fully public (unlike block ciphers that take a secret input) and the security stems from how the permutation is used.
     12: The duplex sponge construction[^2] is a popular method for implementing keyed primitives, such as Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD)[^3] from public permutations.

26: ![alt_text](duplex.svg "Simplified view of the duplex construction.")

     28: 
     29: 
>    30: ## Ascon AEAD
     31: 
     32: Ascon AEAD, depicted in Figure 2, is inspired by the duplex construction using Ascon-p, where the state size is 320 bits, with a few changes.
     33: First, two similar permutations are used instead of 1, where P12 is used for the initialization and finalization (first and last calls)
     34: and is expected to be significantly stronger than Pr, which is used for all other calls.

     10: 
>    11: # Overview
     12: 
     13: This document specifies the Cryptographically Secure Random Number Generator (CSRNG) hardware IP functionality.
     14: Due to the importance of secure random number generation (RNG), it is a topic which is extensively covered in security standards.
     15: This IP targets compliance with both [BSI's AIS31 recommendations for Common Criteria (CC)](https://www.bsi.bund.de/SharedDocs/Downloads/DE/BSI/Zertifizierung/Interpretationen/AIS_31_Functionality_classes_for_random_number_generators_e.pdf), as well as [NIST's SP 800-90A](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-90Ar1.pdf) and [NIST's SP 800-90C (Second Draft)](https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Publications/sp/800-90c/draft/documents/sp800_90c_second_draft.pdf), both of which are referenced in [FIPS 140-3](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/fips/140/3/final).

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
24: This IP block is attached to the chip interconnect bus as a peripheral module conforming to the [comportability definition and specification](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md), but also has direct hardware links to other IPs for secure and software-inaccessible transmission of random numbers.
     25: The bus connections to peripheral modules are done using the CSRNG application interface.
     26: This interface allows peripherals to manage CSRNG instances, and request the CSRNG module to return obfuscated entropy.
     27: 
>    28: ## Features
     29: - Provides support for both deterministic (DRNG) and true random number generation (TRNG), when combined with a secure entropy source (i.e. one constructed and implemented in compliance with SP 800-90A,B,C and AIS31).
     30:   The TRNG mode is provided directly by the entropy source.
     31: - Compliant with NIST and BSI recommendations for random number generation.
     32: - Hardware peripherals and software applications issue commands to dedicated RNG instances through a common application interface.

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
51:     - Implementation follows the NRBG "Oversampling Construction" approved by SP 800-90C, to meet both [Common Criteria (CC, ISO/IEC 15408)](https://www.iso.org/standard/50341.html) and FIPS TRNG constructions.
     52: - In addition to the approved DRNG mode, any instance can also operate in "Fully Deterministic mode", meaning the seed depends entirely on application inputs or personalization strings.
     53:     - This provides an approved means of seed construction in FIPS 140-2 as described in the [FIPS 140-2 Implementation Guidance](https://csrc.nist.gov/csrc/media/projects/cryptographic-module-validation-program/documents/fips140-2/fips1402ig.pdf), section 7.14, resolution point 2(a).
     54: 
>    55: ## Description
     56: 
     57: Though the recommendations in AIS31 are based around broad functional requirements, the recommendations in SP 800-90 are very prescriptive in nature, outlining the exact constructs needed for approval.
     58: Thus the interface and implementation are largely driven by these explicit constructs, particularly the CTR_DRBG construct.
     59:

>    77: ## Note on the term "Entropy"
     78: 
     79: Every DRNG requires some initial seed material, and the requirements for the generation of that seed material varies greatly between standards, and potentially between Common Criteria security targets.
     80: In all standards considered, DRNGs require some "entropy" from an external source to create the initial seed.
     81: However, the rules for obtaining said entropy differ.

sections.label: Module enable and disable
sections.snippet:
1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
      3: This section discusses how software can interface with CSRNG.
      4: 
>     5: ## Module enable and disable
      6: 
      7: CSRNG may only be disabled if all EDNs are disabled.
      8: 
      9: The recommended enable sequence for the entropy complex is to first enable ENTROPY_SRC, then CSRNG, and finally the EDNs.

sections.label: Running CSRNG with ENTROPY SRC disabled
sections.snippet:
7: CSRNG may only be disabled if all EDNs are disabled.
      8: 
      9: The recommended enable sequence for the entropy complex is to first enable ENTROPY_SRC, then CSRNG, and finally the EDNs.
     10: 
>    11: ## Running CSRNG with ENTROPY_SRC disabled
     12: 
     13: Once the entropy complex has been enabled and all configured CSRNG instances have been seeded with entropy, software can again disable ENTROPY_SRC (and the PTRNG noise source to e.g. save power) while CSRNG and the EDNs remain running to keep serving entropy to consumers.
     14: 
     15: Depending on the mode in which the CSRNG instance is running, software can use a different mechanism to efficiently operate the entropy complex without having the ENTROPY_SRC continuously running:

sections.label: Regular, non-deterministic mode
sections.snippet:
13: Once the entropy complex has been enabled and all configured CSRNG instances have been seeded with entropy, software can again disable ENTROPY_SRC (and the PTRNG noise source to e.g. save power) while CSRNG and the EDNs remain running to keep serving entropy to consumers.
     14: 
     15: Depending on the mode in which the CSRNG instance is running, software can use a different mechanism to efficiently operate the entropy complex without having the ENTROPY_SRC continuously running:
     16: 
>    17: ### Regular, non-deterministic mode
     18: 
     19: If a CSRNG instance is running in regular, non-deterministic mode (`flag0` being false, see [Generated Bits (`genbits`) Interface](theory_of_operation.md#generated-bits-genbits-interface) for details), the `cs_entropy_req` interrupt will assert whenever the instance requests entropy from ENTROPY_SRC.
     20: Once software observes the interrupt, it has to enable ENTROPY_SRC.
     21: The ENTROPY_SRC block will then perform the startup health testing and eventually deliver a new seed to the CSRNG instance.

sections.label: Fully deterministic mode
sections.snippet:
21: The ENTROPY_SRC block will then perform the startup health testing and eventually deliver a new seed to the CSRNG instance.
     22: Note that the startup health testing may take a non-negligible time (see [Startup Health Testing](../../entropy_src/doc/theory_of_operation.md#startup-health-testing) during which the CSRNG instance is blocked.
     23: Thus, it is recommended that software tracks the age of the seed currently in use via the corresponding [`RESEED_COUNTER`](registers.md#reseed_counter) register to re-enable ENTROPY_SRC ahead of the `cs_entropy_req` interrupt firing.
     24: 
>    25: ### Fully deterministic mode
     26: 
     27: For CSRNG instances running in fully deterministic mode (`flag0` being true, see [Generated Bits (`genbits`) Interface](theory_of_operation.md#generated-bits-genbits-interface) for details), software has to provide entropy for instantiation and reseeding via the additional data field of the <tt>instantiate</tt> and <tt>reseed</tt> command, respectively.
     28: If no additional data is provided, CSRNG will use an all-zero seed.
     29: Additional entropy can be provided via the additional data field of every <tt>generate</tt> command.

sections.label: Endianness and Known-Answer Tests
sections.snippet:
29: Additional entropy can be provided via the additional data field of every <tt>generate</tt> command.
     30: The entropy to be provided to these commands can for example be generated by running the ENTROPY_SRC block in a dedicated mode, see [Reading Entropy Output](../../entropy_src/doc/programmers_guide.md#reading-entropy-output) for details.
     31: Software is recommended to manage a buffer of seeds which is filled whenever it enables ENTROPY_SRC in this mode to reduce the duty cycle of ENTROPY_SRC (and the PTRNG noise source) thereby improving power efficiency and latency.
     32: 
>    33: ## Endianness and Known-Answer Tests
     34: 
     35: All CSRNG registers are little-endian.
     36: 
     37: When providing additional data for an <tt>instantiate</tt>, <tt>reseed</tt> or <tt>update</tt> command the data words have to be written to [`CMD_REQ`](registers.md#cmd_req) in the correct order.

>    42: #### Non-blocking Commands
     43: Regarding command processing, all commands process immediately except for the generate command.

>   111: ### Application Interface
    112: 
    113: This section describes the application interface, which is required for performing any operations using a CSRNG instance (i.e. instantiation, reseeding, RNG generation, or uninstantiation).
    114: Each CSRNG instance corresponds to a unique application interface port, which implements the application interface described here.
    115: Any hardware peripherals which require complete control of an instance may connect directly to a dedicated interface port.

129: In general, users of the application interface are either firmware or some hardware module entity.
    130: For hardware, a module can either directly control the application interface, or it can connect to an EDN module.
    131: Attaching to an EDN module allows for a simpler interface connection to a more layout-friendly distributed-chip network.
    132: 
>   133: #### General Command Format
    134: 
    135: The general format for the application interface is a 32-bit command header, optionally followed by additional data, such as a personalization string, typically twelve 32-bit words in length.
    136: Depending on the command, these strings are typically required to be 384-bits in length, to match the size of the seed-length when operating with 256-bit security-strength.
    137: The exact function of the additional data field depends in the command.

sections.label: DMA Controller dma
sections.snippet:
>     1: # DMA Controller (dma)
      2: 
      3: The Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller is a peripheral within the OpenTitan system-on-chip (SoC).
      4: It is designed to provide processor-independent data transfer capabilities between different locations in the system memory map and/or peripherals.
      5: Its primary purpose is to free the main processor (the Ibex core) from the overhead of large or slow data copy operations, thereby freeing up the CPU for other computational tasks.

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
6: 
      7: The DMA controller is a single-channel device that processes one data transaction at a time. It acts as a master on the system's **TileLink Uncached Lightweight (TL-UL)** bus, allowing it to autonomously read from and write to any memory-mapped peripheral or memory region.
      8: The DMA enforces a hardware-based isolation mechanism to restrict the access to the OpenTitan internal memory.
      9:

40: ## Use Cases

     42: This section describes possible use cases of the DMA controller.

>    44: ### Bulk Data Transfer
     45: 
     46: The services of an integrated OpenTitan require the movement of bulk data from SoC / system memory to the OpenTitan (OT) private memory and vice-versa.
     47: The DMA controller provides OpenTitan with the ability to move data blobs securely in and out of the OpenTitan memory while offloading the Ibex core to focus on security critical tasks.
     48: The DMA provides a hardware isolation layer between OpenTitan and the rest of the SoC.

     58: 
     59: Additional efficiency benefits are derived by supporting inline operations within the DMA controller such as on-the-fly hashing.
     60: 
>    61: ### IO Data Transfer
     62: 
     63: The DMA controller features a hardware-handshake mode that enables automatic data transfers with a peripheral's I/O FIFO.
     64: This mode offloads the main processor by allowing the DMA to read or write multiple data frames without software intervention, which is ideal for long-running I/O operations.

sections.label: Initiate a Memory transfer
sections.snippet:
10: 1.  **Define the Memory Range:** First, software must write the base address to the [`ENABLED_MEMORY_RANGE_BASE`](registers.md#enabled_memory_range_base) register and the upper limit of the accessible range to the [`ENABLED_MEMORY_RANGE_LIMIT`](registers.md#enabled_memory_range_limit) register.
     11: 2.  **Validate the Range:** Next, to indicate that the configured range contains valid data, software must write to the [`RANGE_VALID`](registers.md#range_valid) register.
     12: 3.  **Optional Range Locking:** Optionally, software can write to the [`RANGE_REGWEN`](registers.md#range_regwEN) register to lock the configured memory range. Once locked, the range configuration cannot be modified until the next reset of the DMA.

sections.label: Aborting a Transfer
sections.snippet:
37: 
     38: The current status of the DMA, including pending interrupts, can be read from the [`STATUS`](registers.md#status) register.
     39: Since interrupts are implemented as status bits, they are cleared by writing a '1' to the corresponding bit in the `STATUS` register.
     40: 
>    41: ### Aborting a Transfer
     42: 
     43: Software can terminate an ongoing DMA transfer at any point by writing to the `abort` bit in the [`CONTROL`](registers.md#control) register.
     44: Aborting an operation happens immediately after writing the `abort` bit and does not require any further scheduling or waiting.
     45: The [`STATUS`](registers.md#status) indicates via the `aborted` bit that the DMA operation was aborted and the DMA stopped its operation.

sections.label: Chunked Data Transfers
sections.snippet:
43: Software can terminate an ongoing DMA transfer at any point by writing to the `abort` bit in the [`CONTROL`](registers.md#control) register.
     44: Aborting an operation happens immediately after writing the `abort` bit and does not require any further scheduling or waiting.
     45: The [`STATUS`](registers.md#status) indicates via the `aborted` bit that the DMA operation was aborted and the DMA stopped its operation.
     46: 
>    47: ## Chunked Data Transfers
     48: 
     49: The DMA performs memory transfers in discrete units called chunks.
     50: Each chunk consists of a contiguous block of data with a size defined by the [`CHUNK_DATA_SIZE`](registers.md#chunk_data_size) register.
     51: After transferring a chunk, the DMA can optionally generate an interrupt.

sections.label: Hardware Handshaking Mode

54: A potential use case for chunked memory-to-memory transfers is memory initialization, where a small chunk of data (e.g., a block of zeros) can be repeatedly transferred to a larger memory region.
     55: For chunked data transfers the first transfer needs to assert the `initial_transfer` bit in the [`CONTROL`](registers.md#control) register.
     56: Initiating the transfer of subsequent chunks must not assert the `initial_transfer` bit.
     57: 
>    58: ## Hardware Handshaking Mode
     59: 
     60: The DMA supports a hardware handshaking mode that enables seamless data transfers between IO peripherals and memory.
     61: This mode leverages the chunked data transfer mechanism and interrupts from the IO peripheral.

>    83: ## Inline Hashing
     84: 
     85: The DMA incorporates an inline hashing capability for SHA-2 algorithms (SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512).

>   100: ## Error Condition
    101: 
    102: For security reasons, the DMA controller performs extensive checking of the configuration registers before starting a transfer.
    103: If any part of the configuration is invalid, the controller reports all detected errors in the [`ERROR_CODE`](registers.md#error_code) register.
    104: An error may also be reported during a transfer if either the source device or the destination device detects an error condition.

>    17: ## Features
     18: 
     19: The Entropy Distribution Network (EDN) block provides both hardware and software interfaces to the [CSRNG IP](../csrng/README.md) module.
     20: A primary objective of the EDN block is to provide a simpler hardware interface for the peripheral blocks to use, in which case they do not have to directly interface with the CSRNG module.
     21: - The EDN block provides a set of registers for firmware to manage a CSRNG application interface port.

     31:   - A recoverable alert to report recoverable error. A list of fatal errors are listed in the [`RECOV_ALERT_STS`](data/edn.hjson#recov_alert_sts) register.
     32: 
>    33: ## Description
     34: 
     35: This IP block acts as a gasket between peripheral hardware blocks and the CSRNG block.
     36: One function this IP block performs is to translate data transfer size.
     37: For example, CSRNG will return 128 bits on the `genbits` bus.

sections.snippet:
1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
      3: This section discusses how firmware can interface with EDN.
      4: 
>     5: ## Module enable and disable
      6: 
      7: EDN may only be enabled if CSRNG is enabled.
      8: Once disabled, EDN may only be re-enabled after CSRNG has been disabled and re-enabled.
      9: The only exception to this is when firmware takes care of properly uninstantiating the associated CSRNG instance before disabling EDN.

sections.label: Uninstantiating CSRNG through EDN
sections.snippet:
11: For details, refer to [Uninstantiating CSRNG instance through EDN](#uninstantiating-csrng-through-edn).
     12: 
     13: The recommended enable sequence for the entropy complex is to first enable ENTROPY_SRC, then CSRNG, and finally EDN.
     14: 
>    15: ## Uninstantiating CSRNG through EDN
     16: 
     17: To disable and re-enable EDN without disabling and re-enabling CSRNG, firmware must ensure the associated CSRNG instance is properly uninstantiated.
     18: Otherwise, EDN and the associated CSRNG application interface may get out of sync at which point both EDN and CSRNG have to be disabled and re-enabled.
     19: This means unrelated CSRNG instances and EDNs also get disabled and then need to be re-configured.

sections.label: Running EDN in Auto Request Mode with ENTROPY SRC disabled
sections.snippet:
46:     Once all entropy is consumed, the program doesn't finish anymore and the [`STATUS` register](../../otbn/doc/registers.md#status) remains at `BUSY_EXECUTE`.
     47: 
     48:   Future versions of EDN will likely support an automated way for consuming any remaining entropy, see also [Issue #22850](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/issues/22850).
     49: 
>    50: ## Running EDN in Auto Request Mode with ENTROPY_SRC disabled
     51: 
     52: Once the entropy complex has been enabled and all configured CSRNG instances have been seeded with entropy, firmware can again disable ENTROPY_SRC (and the PTRNG noise source to e.g. save power) while CSRNG and EDN remain running to keep serving entropy to consumers.
     53: 
     54: Depending on the mode in which EDN and the associated CSRNG instance are running, firmware can use a different mechanism to efficiently operate the entropy complex without having the ENTROPY_SRC continuously running:

sections.label: Fully deterministic mode
sections.snippet:
56: ### Regular, non-deterministic mode
     57: 
     58: The same guidance applies as for [CSRNG](../../csrng/doc/programmers_guide.md#regular-non-deterministic-mode).
     59: 
>    60: ### Fully deterministic mode
     61: 
     62: The same guidance applies as for [CSRNG](../../csrng/doc/programmers_guide.md#fully-deterministic-mode).
     63: However, the `generate` and `reseed` commands including the additional data fields can only be configured before starting **[Auto Request Mode](./theory_of_operation.md#auto-request-mode)** via the [`GENERATE_CMD`](registers.md#generate_cmd) and [`RESEED_CMD`](registers.md#reseed_cmd) FIFOs.
     64: To inject fresh entropy, firmware thus has to [uninstantiate the CSRNG instance through EDN](#uninstantiating-csrng-through-edn), disable EDN, configure the FIFOs and then re-enable EDN in Auto Request Mode, and finally trigger the `instantiate` command.
