sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: The EDN is for distributing random number streams to hardware blocks, via peripheral ports on the EDN.
      4: Each block connected to a peripheral port is referred to as an endpoint.
      5:

sections.label: Interaction with CSRNG Application Interface Ports
sections.snippet:
4: Each block connected to a peripheral port is referred to as an endpoint.
      5: 
      6: To enable the EDN block, set the `EDN_ENABLE` field in the [`CTRL`](registers.md#ctrl) register..
      7: 
>     8: ## Interaction with CSRNG Application Interface Ports
      9: 
     10: The CSRNG application interface implements the "function envelopes" recommended by [NIST SP 800-90A](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-90Ar1.pdf) for random number generation, and these function envelopes establish certain requirements for the order of operations.
     11: For instance, the application interface port must receive an explicit `instantiate` command before receiving any `generate` commands.
     12: The sequences of commands generated by a particular EDN are either controlled by the EDN state machine or by commands forwarded from firmware through the [`SW_CMD_REQ`](registers.md#sw_cmd_req) register.

sections.label: Boot-time Request Mode
sections.snippet:
24: CSRNG command format details can be found in [CSRNG](../../csrng/README.md).
     25: 
     26: There are two broad modes for state machine control: auto request mode and boot-time request mode.
     27: 
>    28: ### Boot-time Request Mode
     29: 
     30: Random values are needed by peripherals almost immediately after reset, so to simplify interactions with the boot ROM, boot-time request mode is the default mode.
     31: 
     32: In boot-time request mode, the command sequence is fully hardware-controlled and no command customization is possible.

sections.label: Note on Security Considerations when Using Boot-time Request Mode
sections.snippet:
50: There is a limit to how much entropy can be requested in the boot-time request mode BOOT_GEN_CMD command (GLEN = 4K).
     51: It is the responsibility of firmware to switch to the software port operation.
     52: If the BOOT_GEN_CMD command ends while an endpoint is requesting, EDN will never ack and the endpoint bus will hang.
     53: 
>    54: #### Note on Security Considerations when Using Boot-time Request Mode
     55: 
     56: Boot-time request mode is not intended for normal operation, as it tolerates the potential use of preliminary seeds for the attached CSRNG instance.
     57: These preliminary seeds are described as "pre-FIPS" since they are released from the `entropy_src` before the complete start-up health-checks recommended by FIPS have been completed.
     58: Thus pre-FIPS seeds have weaker guarantees on the amount of physical entropy included in their creation.

sections.label: Multiple EDNs in Boot-time Request Mode
sections.snippet:
60: All following seeds from the `entropy_src` are passed through the full FIPS-approved health checks.
     61: Therefore at most one EDN can receive a pre-FIPS seed after reset.
     62: Since boot-time request mode EDN streams may be FIPS non-compliant, firmware must at some point disable boot-time request mode and reinitialize the EDN for either firmware-driven operation or auto request mode.
     63: 
>    64: #### Multiple EDNs in Boot-time Request Mode
     65: 
     66: If many endpoints require boot-time entropy, multiple boot-time EDNs may be required, as the EDN has a fixed maximum number of peripheral ports.
     67: Since physical entropy generation takes time, there exists a mechanism to prioritize the EDNs, to match the boot priority of each group of attached endpoints.
     68: To establish an order to the instantiation of each EDN, enable them one at a time.

sections.label: Auto Request Mode
sections.snippet:
75: The `entropy_src` only creates one pre-FIPS seed, so any other EDNs must wait for their seeds to pass the full FIPS-recommended health checks.
     76: This means that for [Top Earlgrey](../../../top_earlgrey/README.md), each subsequent EDN must wait an additional 5ms before it can start distributing data.
     77: For instance, if there are three boot-time request mode EDN's in the system, the first will start distributing data 2ms after reset, the second will start distributing data 7ms after reset, and the third will start distributing data 12ms after reset.
     78: 
>    79: ### Auto Request Mode
     80: 
     81: Before enabling auto request mode, firmware must configure the EDN's `generate` and `reseed` commands.
     82: These can be loaded into their respective command replay FIFOs through the [`GENERATE_CMD`](registers.md#generate_cmd) and [`RESEED_CMD`](registers.md#reseed_cmd) registers.
     83: These `generate` commands will be issued as necessary to meet the bandwidth requirements of the endpoints.

sections.label: Note on State Machine Shutdown Delays
sections.snippet:
99: 
    100: It should be noted that when in auto request mode, no status will be updated that is used for the software port operation once the `instantiate` command has completed.
    101: If some hang condition were to occur when in this mode, the main state machine debug register should be read to determine if a hang condition is present.
    102: 
>   103: ### Note on State Machine Shutdown Delays
    104: 
    105: When leaving boot-time request mode or auto request mode, the EDN state machine waits for completion of the last command, before sending a shutdown acknowledgement to firmware.
    106: The longest possible commands are the `instantiate` or `reseed` requests, which typically take about 5ms in [Top Earlgrey](../../../top_earlgrey/README.md), due to the time required to gather the necessary physical entropy.
    107: By contrast, the largest possible `generate` command allowed by [NIST SP 800-90A](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-90Ar1.pdf) is for 2<sup>19</sup> bits (or 4096 AES codewords).

sections.label: Note on Sharing of CSRNG Instance State Variables
sections.snippet:
106: The longest possible commands are the `instantiate` or `reseed` requests, which typically take about 5ms in [Top Earlgrey](../../../top_earlgrey/README.md), due to the time required to gather the necessary physical entropy.
    107: By contrast, the largest possible `generate` command allowed by [NIST SP 800-90A](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-90Ar1.pdf) is for 2<sup>19</sup> bits (or 4096 AES codewords).
    108: Assuming an AES encryption delay of 16 clocks, a 100 MHz clock frequency, and that entropy consumers are able to immediately consume the distributed entropy, the longest allowable `generate` command would take only 0.7 ms to complete.
    109: 
>   110: ### Note on Sharing of CSRNG Instance State Variables
    111: 
    112: Once an application interface port has received an `instantiate` command, that application interface port then has access to a unique CSRNG instance, which is shared by all endpoints on the same EDN.
    113: Therefore from a security perspective, an attack to that particular CSRNG instance is an attack on all the endpoints that share the same EDN.
    114: Meanwhile, seeds and other state variables specific to a particular CSRNG instance are not shared between endpoints on *separate* EDN instances, or with any hardware devices with direct connections to dedicated CSRNG application interface ports.

    113: Therefore from a security perspective, an attack to that particular CSRNG instance is an attack on all the endpoints that share the same EDN.
    114: Meanwhile, seeds and other state variables specific to a particular CSRNG instance are not shared between endpoints on *separate* EDN instances, or with any hardware devices with direct connections to dedicated CSRNG application interface ports.
    115: 
>   116: ## Interactions with Peripheral Devices
    117: 
    118: Peripheral ports distribute data to the endpoints using four signals: `req`, `ack`, `bus`, and `fips`.
    119: 
    120: Fresh (i.e. previously unseen) random values are distributed to the endpoints via the 32 bit `bus` signal, in response to a `req` signal.

125: 
    126: The `fips` signal is used to identify whether the values received on the `bus` have been prepared with complete adherence to the recommendations in NIST SP 800-90.
    127: If the `fips` signal is deasserted, it means the associated CSRNG instance has been instantiated with a pre-FIPS seed.

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
12: 
     13: This document specifies ENTROPY_SRC hardware IP functionality.
     14: This module conforms to the [Comportable guideline for peripheral functionality.](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md)
     15: 
>    16: ## Features
     17: 
     18: - This revision provides an interface to an external physical random noise generator (also referred to as a physical true random number generator or PTRNG).
     19: The PTRNG external source is a physical true random noise source.
     20: A noise source and its relation to an entropy source are defined by [SP 800-90B.](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-90b/final)

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
29: - Two additional hardware health checks are performed by this revision: Bucket and Markov tests.
     30: - Firmware-defined (mailbox-based) and vendor-defined health checks are also supported.
     31: - A health check failure alert is supported by this revision.
     32: 
>    33: ## Description
     34: 
     35: This IP block provides an entropy source that is capable of using a PTRNG (Physical True Random Number Generator) noise source to generate random values in a manner that is compliant both with FIPS (though NIST SP 800-90B) and CC (AIS31) recommendations.
     36: 
     37: At a high-level, the ENTROPY_SRC block, when enabled, will continuously collect entropy bits from the PTRNG noise source, perform health tests on the collected entropy bits, pack them, send them through a conditioning unit, and finally store them into a FIFO.

sections.label: Compatibility
sections.snippet:
85: When this firmware conditioning feature is activated, data read directly out of the noise source can be re-inserted into the entropy pipeline via a TL-UL register after it has been processed by firmware.
     86: It should be noted that this firmware algorithm must be vetted by NIST to satisfy the requirements for a full-entropy source.
     87: This feature can also be disabled for security purposes, either by locking the feature via the [`REGWEN`](./doc/registers.md#regwen) register at boot, or by a write to one-time programmable (OTP) memory.
     88: 
>    89: ## Compatibility
     90: This IP block does not have any direct hardware compatibility requirements.
     91: However, the general design of this block follows the overall NIST recommendations, as described by SP 800-90B.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: The ENTROPY_SRC hardware block collects entropy bits from the PTRNG (Physical True Random Number Generator) noise source, performs health tests on the collected entropy bits, packs them, sends them through a conditioning unit, and finally stores them into the `esfinal` FIFO for consumption by firmware or hardware.
      4: 
      5: It operates in a manner compliant with both FIPS (though NIST SP 800-90B) and CC (AIS31) recommendations.

sections.label: Initialization and Enabling
sections.snippet:
4: 
      5: It operates in a manner compliant with both FIPS (though NIST SP 800-90B) and CC (AIS31) recommendations.
      6: This revision supports only an external interface for a PTRNG noise source implementation.
      7: 
>     8: ### Initialization and Enabling
      9: 
     10: After power-up, the ENTROPY_SRC block is disabled.
     11: The first step is initialization and enabling.
     12:

sections.label: Boot-Time / Bypass Mode
sections.snippet:
15: 
     16: Once the ENTROPY_SRC block is enabled, also the PTRNG noise source starts up.
     17: The ENTROPY_SRC block will then start to collect entropy bits indefinitely until disabled.
     18: 
>    19: ### Boot-Time / Bypass Mode
     20: 
     21: After a reset, the ENTROPY_SRC block will start up in boot-time / bypass mode by default.
     22: This feature is designed to provide an initial seed's worth of entropy with lower latency than the normal FIPS/CC compliant health check process.
     23: Health testing will still be performed on boot-time mode entropy, but the window of checking is, by default, 384 bits instead of 2048 bits.

sections.label: FIPS/CC Compliant Mode
sections.snippet:
21: After a reset, the ENTROPY_SRC block will start up in boot-time / bypass mode by default.
     22: This feature is designed to provide an initial seed's worth of entropy with lower latency than the normal FIPS/CC compliant health check process.
     23: Health testing will still be performed on boot-time mode entropy, but the window of checking is, by default, 384 bits instead of 2048 bits.
     24: 
>    25: ### FIPS/CC Compliant Mode
     26: 
     27: Once the initial boot-time mode phase has completed, the ENTROPY_SRC block can be switched to FIPS/CC compliant mode (for simplicity referred to as FIPS mode) by setting the `FIPS_ENABLE` field in the [`CONF`](registers.md#conf) register to `kMultiBitBool4True`.
     28: In this mode, once the raw entropy has been health checked, it will be passed into a conditioner block.
     29: This block will compress the bits such that the entropy bits/physical bits, or min-entropy value, should be improved over the raw data source min-entropy value.

sections.label: Startup Health Testing
sections.snippet:
37: When entropy is delivered to the downstream hardware block, a signal will indicate what type of entropy it is - FIPS/CC compliant or not.
     38: This signal is determined by the `FIPS_FLAG` field in the [`CONF`](registers.md#conf) register.
     39: When `RNG_FIPS` field in the [`CONF`](registers.md#conf) register is set to `kMultiBitBool4True`, the ENTROPY_SRC block will request higher quality entropy from the noise source by asserting the `rng_fips` output signal.
     40: 
>    41: ### Startup Health Testing
     42: 
     43: Note that after enabling the ENTROPY_SRC block, the health tests need to pass for two subsequent windows of [`HEALTH_TEST_WINDOWS.FIPS_WINDOW`](registers.md#health_test_windows--fips_window) tested symbols (startup health testing).
     44: By default, 1024 tested symbols of RngBusWidth bits (1024 1-bit symbols when running in single-channel mode) are used for producing the startup seed.
     45: If a health test fails, the startup health testing starts over and the conditioner block continues absorbing the next window.

sections.label: Firmware Override Mode
sections.snippet:
45: If a health test fails, the startup health testing starts over and the conditioner block continues absorbing the next window.
     46: If the health tests don't pass for two subsequent windows, the ENTROPY_SRC block stops operating and signals a recoverable alert.
     47: Firmware then needs to disable/re-enable the block to restart operation including the startup health testing.
     48: 
>    49: ### Firmware Override Mode
     50: 
     51: The hardware conditioning can also be bypassed and replaced in normal operation with a firmware-defined conditioning algorithm.
     52: This firmware conditioning algorithm can be disabled on boot for security purposes.
     53:

sections.label: Health Tests
sections.snippet:
72: The normal SHA3 processing will continue and finally push the conditioned entropy through the module.
     73: 
     74: For more details, refer to the [programmer's guide](programmers_guide.md/#firmware-override--bypass-modes).
     75: 
>    76: ### Health Tests
     77: 
     78: Health checks are performed on the input raw data from the PTRNG noise source when in that mode.
     79: There are four health tests that will be performed: Repetition Count Test, Adaptive Proportion Test, bucket test, and Markov test.
     80: By default, all tests are enabled, but can be turned off by setting the thresholds to the maximum value.

sections.label: Health Test Failure Alert
sections.snippet:
89: It should be noted that for all error counter registers, they are sized for 16 bits, which prevents any case where counters might wrap.
     90: 
     91: Additional, vendor-specific tests are supported through an [external health test interface (xht)](#external-health-tests).
     92: 
>    93: ### Health Test Failure Alert
     94: 
     95: The [`ALERT_THRESHOLD`](registers.md#alert_threshold) register determines during how many subsequent health test windows one or more health test failures can occur before a recoverable alert is raised and the ENTROPY_SRC block stops operating.
     96: In case this threshold is reached, firmware needs to disable/re-enable the block to restart operation including the startup health testing.
     97: By default, the threshold is set to two, such that the occurrence of two failing test cycles back-to-back would provide a very low α value.

sections.label: Routing Entropy to Firmware
sections.snippet:
104: The [`ALERT_FAIL_COUNTS`](registers.md#alert_fail_counts) reports the number of health test failures since the last passing health test window on a per-test basis.
    105: If multiple health tests fail for a certain window, the value in [`ALERT_SUMMARY_FAIL_COUNTS`](registers.md#alert_summary_fail_counts) is incremented by just one whereas multiple fields in [`ALERT_FAIL_COUNTS`](registers.md#alert_fail_counts) may get incremented.
    106: The same holds for [`EXTHT_FAIL_COUNTS`](registers.md#extht_fail_counts) which reports the number of external health test failures since the last passing health test window on a per-test basis.
    107: 
>   108: ### Routing Entropy to Firmware
    109: 
    110: Firmware has a path to read entropy from the ENTROPY_SRC block.
    111: The [`ES_ROUTE`](registers.md#entropy_control--es_route) field in the [`ENTROPY_CONTROL`](registers.md#entropy_control) register allows firmware to set the internal multiplexers to steer entropy data to the [`ENTROPY_DATA`](registers.md#entropy_data) register.
    112: When enabled, no entropy is being passed to the block hardware interface.

sections.label: Disabling
sections.snippet:
113: The control field [`ES_TYPE`](registers.md#entropy_control--es_type) sets whether the entropy will come from the conditioning block or be sourced through the bypass path.
    114: A status bit will be set that can either be polled or generate an interrupt when the entropy bits are available to be read from the [`ENTROPY_DATA`](registers.md#entropy_data) register.
    115: The firmware needs to read the [`ENTROPY_DATA`](registers.md#entropy_data) register twelve times in order to cleanly evacuate the 384-bit seed from the hardware path (12 * 32 bits = 384 bits in total).
    116: 
>   117: ### Disabling
    118: 
    119: At any time, the [`MODULE_ENABLE`](registers.md#module_enable) field can be cleared to halt the entropy generation and health testing.
    120: See the [programmer's guide section](programmers_guide.md/#entropy-source-module-disable) for more details on the ENTROPY_SRC block disable sequence.
    121:

     27:

     29: 
     30: The HMAC module is a [SHA-2][sha256-spec] hash-based authentication code generator to check the integrity of an incoming message and a signature signed with the same secret key.

>     1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
      3: This chapter shows how to use the HMAC/SHA-2 IP by showing some snippets such as initialization, initiating SHA-2 or HMAC process and processing the interrupts.
      4: This code is not compilable but serves to demonstrate the IO required.
      5: A more detailed SW implementation can be found in software under `sw/` in [cryptolib code](../../../../sw/device/lib/crypto/drivers/hmac.c) which is the recommended reference implementation for further SW development.

sections.label: Initialization
sections.snippet:
5: A more detailed SW implementation can be found in software under `sw/` in [cryptolib code](../../../../sw/device/lib/crypto/drivers/hmac.c) which is the recommended reference implementation for further SW development.
      6: HMAC/SHA-2 IP is also used in [ROM code](../../../../sw/device/silicon_creator/lib/drivers/hmac.c) but this is a constrained implementation for specific ROM code purposes. Therefore, it is not a recommended software implementation reference.
      7: Code in [HMAC DIF](../../../../sw/device/lib/dif/dif_hmac.c) is intended for testing development purposes, but remains limited to configuring HMAC only in SHA-2 256 with 256-bit key, with plans to update it in the near future.
      8: 
>     9: ## Initialization
     10: 
     11: This section of the code describes initializing the HMAC with SHA-2 256 digest using a 256-bit key: setting up the interrupts, endianness, and HMAC/SHA-2 mode.
     12: [`CFG.endian_swap`](registers.md#cfg) reverses the byte-order of input words when software writes into the message FIFO.
     13: [`CFG.digest_swap`](registers.md#cfg) reverses the byte-order in the final HMAC or SHA hash.

     40: The following code shows how to send a message to the HMAC, the procedure is the same whether a full HMAC or just a SHA-2 computation is required (choose between them using [`CFG.hmac_en`](registers.md#cfg)).

78: The [`KEY`](registers.md#key) register ignores any attempt to access the secret key in the middle of the process.
     79: If the software tries to update the KEY, the IP reports an error through the [`ERR_CODE`](registers.md#err_code) register.
     80: The error code is `SwUpdateSecretKeyInProcess`, `0x0003`.
     81: 
>    82: ## Saving and restoring the context
     83: 
     84: Software can let the HMAC IP process multiple message streams in a time-interleaved fashion by saving and restoring the context (i.e., parts of the hardware-internal state).
     85: 
     86: Such context switches are possible only at the boundary of complete message blocks (512-bit for SHA-2 256 or 1024-bit for SHA-2 384/512).

sections.label: Errors
sections.snippet:
110: 1. Write an arbitrary number of message blocks to HMAC's `MSG_FIFO`.
    111: 1. Continue this with as many message blocks and parallel message streams as needed.
    112: The final hash for any message stream can be obtained at any time (no need for complete blocks) by setting `CMD.hash_process` and waiting for the `hmac_done` interrupt / status bit (or polling on the `STATUS.hmac_idle` bit) to indicate the ongoing operation has completed, and finally reading the digest from the `DIGEST` registers.
    113: 
>   114: ## Errors
    115: 
    116: When HMAC errors are triggered, the IP reports the error via [`INTR_STATE.hmac_err`](registers.md#intr_state).
    117: The details of the error type is stored in [`ERR_CODE`](registers.md#err_code).
    118:

    128: `SwInvalidConfig`            | `0x6` | The error is reported when HMAC has been configured incorrectly by SW, i.e. invalid digest size for SHA-2/HMAC modes or invalid key length for HMAC mode.

    131: 
    132: If the SW is slow and the SHA2 engine pops the data fast enough, the Message FIFO's depth may remain **0**.
    133: The Message FIFO's `fifo_empty` status bit, however, is lowered for a cycle.

      7: The HMAC block diagram above shows that the HMAC core converts the secret key registers into an inner padded key and an outer padded key which are fed to the SHA-2 hash engine (which is a SHA-2 engine primitive instantiated with the multi-mode feature enabled) when appropriate.

sections.snippet:
24: With the 1024-bit block (for SHA-2 384/512), the compression function runs 80 rounds instead.
     25: SHA-2 384 is a truncated version of SHA-2 512 where the last 128 bits of the final digest output are truncated to reduce the digest size to 384 bits.
     26: 
     27: 
>    28: ## Design Details
     29: 
     30: ### SHA-2 message feed and pad
     31: 
     32: A message is fed via a memory-mapped message FIFO.

sections.label: SHA-2 message feed and pad
sections.snippet:
26: 
     27: 
     28: ## Design Details
     29: 
>    30: ### SHA-2 message feed and pad
     31: 
     32: A message is fed via a memory-mapped message FIFO.
     33: Any write access to the memory-mapped window [`MSG_FIFO`](registers.md#msg_fifo) updates the message FIFO.
     34: If the FIFO is full, the HMAC block will block any writes leading to back-pressure on the interconnect (as opposed to dropping those writes or overwriting existing FIFO contents).

sections.label: SHA-2 computation
sections.snippet:
75: If incomplete words are written, the packet logic appends `0x80` in the proper byte
     76: location, such as `0xXX800000` for the message length % 4B == 1 case.
     77: This similarly occurs for SHA-2 384/512 but with a 128-bit message length and block size of 1024 bits.
     78: 
>    79: ### SHA-2 computation
     80: 
     81: For SHA-2 256, the SHA-2 engine receives 16 32-bit words from the message FIFO or the HMAC core, which get padded into 16 64-bit words for the SHA-2 engine (upper 32 bits of each data word are all-zero padded), and then begin 64 rounds of the hash computation which is also called *compression*.
     82: Alternatively for SHA-2 384/512, the SHA-2 engine receives 32 32-bit words from message FIFO, which get packed into 16 64-bit words for the SHA-2 engine, and then begin the 80 compression rounds.
     83: In each round, the compression function fetches a 64-bit word from the buffer and computes the internal variables.

sections.label: HMAC computation
sections.snippet:
93: The digest, again, is used as initial hash values for the next block compression.
     94: During the compression rounds, it doesn't fetch data from the message FIFO.
     95: The software can push up to 16 (or 32 for SHA-2 384/512) entries to the FIFO for the next hash computation.
     96: 
>    97: ### HMAC computation
     98: 
     99: ![Two steps of HMAC](../doc/hmac_dataflow.svg)
    100: 
    101: HMAC can be used with any hash algorithm but this version of HMAC IP uses SHA-2 256/384/512.

sections.label: Performance in SHA-2 mode and HMAC mode
sections.snippet:
127: It is also up to the software to shrink the key to the supported key length (up to 512-bit for SHA-2 256 and up to 1024-bit for SHA-2 384/512) using a hash function when setting up the HMAC.
    128: For example, common key sizes may be 2048-bit or 4096-bit.
    129: Software is expected to hash these into the supported key length and write the hashed result as the configured key to the HMAC IP.
    130: 
>   131: ### Performance in SHA-2 mode and HMAC mode
    132: 
    133: The SHA-2 256 hash algorithm computes 512 bits of data at a time.
    134: The first 16 rounds need the actual 16 x 32-bit message and the following 48 rounds need some value derived from the message.
    135:

sections.label: MSG FIFO
sections.snippet:
148: If HMAC mode is turned on, it introduces extra latency due to the second round of computing the final hash of the outer key and the result of the first round using the inner key.
    149: This adds an extra 240 cycles (80 for the inner key, 80 for the outer key, and 80 for the result of the first round) to complete a HMAC SHA-2 256 digest of a message.
    150: For instance, if an empty message is given then it takes 360 cycles (80 for msg itself and 240 for the extra) to get the HMAC authentication token.
    151: 
>   152: ### MSG_FIFO
    153: 
    154: The MSG_FIFO in the HMAC IP has a wide address range not just one 4 byte address.
    155: Any writes to the address range go into the single entry point of the `prim_packer`.
    156: Then `prim_packer` compacts the data into the word-size if not a word-write then writes to the MSG_FIFO.

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
13: This document specifies I2C hardware IP functionality.
     14: This module conforms to the [Comportable guideline for peripheral functionality.](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md)
     15: See that document for integration overview within the broader top level system.
     16: 
>    17: ## Features
     18: 
     19: - Two-pin clock-data parallel bidirectional external interface: SCL (serial clock line) and SDA (serial data line)
     20: - Support for I2C Controller ("I2C Master"<sup>1</sup>) and I2C Target ("I2C Slave"<sup>1</sup>) device modes
     21: - Support for Standard-mode (100 kbaud), Fast-mode (400 kbaud) and Fast-mode Plus (1 Mbaud)

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
47: <sup>2</sup> The target is only compatible with controllers that support clock stretching.
     48: For controllers that do not support clock stretching, it is expected that there must be an additional protocol to guarantee there is always sufficient space and data.
     49: These protocols are not in scope of this document.
     50: 
>    51: ## Description
     52: 
     53: This IP block implements the [I2C specification (rev. 6)](https://web.archive.org/web/20210813122132/https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/user-guide/UM10204.pdf), though with some variation in nomenclature.
     54: For the purposes of this document, an "I2C Controller" meets the specifications put forth for a "Master" device.
     55: Furthermore, a device which meets the specifications put forward for an "I2C Slave" device is here referred to as an "I2C Target" or "I2C Target Device".

sections.label: Compatibility
sections.snippet:
84: 
     85: This protocol is generally quite flexible with respect to timing constraints, and slow enough to be managed by a software microcontroller, however such an implementation requires frequent activity on the part of the microcontroller.
     86: This IP presents a simple register interface and state-machine to manage the corresponding I/O pins directly using a byte-formatted programming model.
     87: 
>    88: ## Compatibility
     89: 
     90: This IP block should be compatible with any target device covered by the [I2C specification (rev. 6)](https://web.archive.org/web/20210813122132/https://www.nxp.com/docs/en/user-guide/UM10204.pdf), operating at speeds up to 1 Mbaud.
     91: This IP in the controller mode issues addresses in 7-bit encoding, and in the target mode, receives addresses in 7-bit encoding.
     92: (It remains the obligation of system designers to ensure that devices remain in a 7-bit address space.)

179: If enabled, this function allows software to confirm the data in the TX FIFO should be released for the current read.
    180: This may be useful for cases where the TX FIFO has data that does not apply to the current transfer.

>   183: ### CTRL . MULTI_CONTROLLER_MONITOR_EN
    184: Enable the bus monitor in multi-controller mode.
    185: 
    186: If a 0->1 transition happens while [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](#ctrl) and [`CTRL.ENABLETARGET`](#ctrl) are both 0, the bus monitor will enable and begin in the "bus busy" state.
    187: To transition to a bus free state, [`HOST_TIMEOUT_CTRL`](#host_timeout_ctrl) must be nonzero, so the bus monitor may count out idle cycles to confirm the freedom to transmit.

>     7: ## Functional Description
      8: 
      9: The I2C IP is a controller-target combo that can function as an I<sup>2</sup>C controller and/or an I<sup>2</sup>C target.
     10: These functional modules are enabled at runtime by setting the register fields [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl) and [`CTRL.ENABLETARGET`](registers.md#ctrl).
     11: If the Controller Module is to be used in a multi-controller environment, [`CTRL.MULTI_CONTROLLER_MONITOR_EN`](registers.md#ctrl) would also need to be set.

sections.label: Bus Monitor
sections.snippet:
20: `InputDelayCycles` can exclude the rise time that would be captured by [`TIMING1.T_R`](registers.md#timing1).
     21: The reference point for `InputDelayCycles` is the clock edge after the launch clock edge.
     22: In other words, a value of 0 means that the IP's 2-flop synchronizer would sample the IP's own outputs within one clock cycle (if the external pad driver could switch instantaneously).
     23: 
>    24: ### Bus Monitor
     25: 
     26: The Bus Monitor block examines the SCL and SDA inputs and any transmitted outputs from the Controller Module and Target Module.
     27: It detects START and STOP conditions and forwards the events.
     28: In addition, it tracks whether a bus transaction is currently active and informs the Controller Module when the bus is free for it to transmit a new transaction.

sections.label: Controller Module
sections.snippet:
36: 
     37: At initial attachment in a multi-controller environment, typically the controller needs to wait until it determines the bus is free, and the initial state should be assumed to be busy.
     38: To make this happen, [`HOST_TIMEOUT_CTRL`](registers.md#host_timeout_ctrl) should be programmed before enabling the bus monitor in [`CTRL`](registers.md#ctrl), and [`CTRL.MULTI_CONTROLLER_MONITOR_EN`](registers.md#ctrl) should be set either before or at the same time as enabling the Controller Module with [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`](registers.md#ctrl).
     39: 
>    40: ### Controller Module
     41: 
     42: The Controller Module implements all mandatory controller features of the I<sup>2</sup>C protocol for multi-controller configurations, including clock synchronization and bus arbitration.
     43: It also implements support for handling clock stretching.
     44:

sections.label: Controller NACK Handling
sections.snippet:
84: 
     85: Note that a full RX FIFO does not stop command processing.
     86: Ensure the RX FIFO has enough space, else overflows can occur.
     87: 
>    88: #### Controller NACK Handling
     89: 
     90: If the Controller Module transmits a byte and the 9th bit is a NACK from the Target/Bus, the `controller_halt` interrupt is usually asserted (modulo the effect of [`FDATA.NAKOK`](registers.md#fdata)).
     91: If the `controller_halt` interrupt is asserted, the Controller FSM will halt until the interrupt condition has been cleared in the [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS.NACK`](registers.md#controller_events) register.
     92: Software will likely want to do one of two things in handling this irq:

sections.label: Bus Arbitration
sections.snippet:
108: The Controller Module stops immediately following the (N)ACK bit's hold time after the SCL falling edge, and SCL remains asserted low.
    109: If a NACK handling timeout occurs or [`CTRL.ENABLEHOST`] is cleared, then the FSM will halt again after the STOP condition is sent.
    110: The STOP condition terminates the transaction, leaving the FSM halted in the "bus idle" state, with SDA and SCL released.
    111: 
>   112: #### Bus Arbitration
    113: 
    114: In a multi-controller configuration, the Controller Module may begin transmitting at the same time as another controller.
    115: The Bus Monitor will detect when the Controller Module loses arbitration, such as when it attempts to transmit a logic high, but another device is pulling SDA low.
    116: The monitor will inform the Controller Module, and the Controller Module will abort its command and halt.

sections.label: Target Module
sections.snippet:
120: The FMT FIFO will have the entries that remained, but typically, this event will result in software retrying the full transaction.
    121: In that case, software would clear the FMT FIFO (and possibly the RX FIFO), then load the FMT FIFO with the original commands, starting from the beginning of the transaction.
    122: All bits in [`CONTROLLER_EVENTS`](registers.md#controller_events) must be cleared for the Controller Module to release from the halted state.
    123: 
>   124: ### Target Module
    125: 
    126: The Target Module implements all mandatory features for targets in multi-controller configurations, as enumerated in the I<sup>2</sup>C specification.
    127: It also supports clock stretching from that same specification.
    128:

sections.label: Target Address Registers
sections.snippet:
130: Address bytes may be configured to be always ACK'd, and the Target ACK Control feature may be used to stretch the clock until software can decide whether to ACK the incoming byte.
    131: The Target Module can also be configured to observe SMBus's maximum cumulative target clock extension time.
    132: There is no hardware support for calculating or checking the Packet Error Code, however; these values would need to be handled in software.
    133: 
>   134: #### Target Address Registers
    135: 
    136: Every transfer involving the I2C Target Module begins with an address.
    137: The I2C Target Module supports up to two 7-bit address and 7-bit mask pairs.
    138: The Target Module accepts a transaction if the result of the bitwise AND operation performed on the transaction address sent by the controller and a mask matches the assigned address corresponding to the mask.

sections.label: Target Transfers
sections.snippet:
145: If the user wishes to have the target respond to *all* addresses, then this can be achieved by setting mask0 and mask1 to 0x01 and setting address0 to 0x00 and address1 to 0x01.
    146: 
    147: The assigned address and mask pairs are set in registers [`TARGET_ID.ADDRESS0`](registers.md#target_id), [`TARGET_ID.MASK0`](registers.md#target_id), [`TARGET_ID.ADDRESS1`](registers.md#target_id), and [`TARGET_ID.MASK1`](registers.md#target_id).
    148: 
>   149: #### Target Transfers
    150: 
    151: When the Target Module accepts a transfer, it acquires the transfer address, read/write bit, and START signal sent by the controller and inserts them into ACQ FIFO, where they can be accessed by software.
    152: [`ACQDATA`](registers.md#acqdata) represents the ACQ FIFO output.
    153: See the register description for more information about the representation.

11: # Overview
     12: 
     13: This document specifies the functionality of the OpenTitan key manager.
     14: 
>    15: ## Features
     16: 
     17: - One-way key and identity (working) state hidden from software.
     18: - Version controlled identity and key generation.
     19: - Key generation for both software consumption and hardware sideload.

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
19: - Key generation for both software consumption and hardware sideload.
     20: - Support for DICE open profile.
     21: 
     22: 
>    23: ## Description
     24: 
     25: The key manager implements the hardware component of the [identities and root keys](../../../doc/security/specs/identities_and_root_keys/) strategy of OpenTitan.
     26: 
     27: It enables the system to shield critical assets from software directly and provides a simple model for software to use derived key and identity outputs.

1: # Programmer's Guide
      2:

>     5: ## Advance or Generate
      6: Software selects a command and triggers a "start".
      7: If the command is valid and successful, key manager indicates done and no errors.
      8: If the command is invalid or unsuccessful, key manager indicates done with error.
      9: Regardless of the validity of the command, the hardware sequences are triggered to avoid leaking timing information.

sections.label: Caveats
sections.snippet:
13: When issuing the `generate-output-hw` command, software must select a destination primitive (AES, KMAC or OTBN).
     14: At the conclusion of the command, key and valid signals are forwarded by the key manager to the selected destination primitive.
     15: The key and valid signals remain asserted to the selected destination until software explicitly disables the output via another command, or issues another `generate-output-hw` command with a different destination primitive.
     16: 
>    17: ## Caveats
     18: The keymgr [`WORKING_STATE`](registers.md#working_state) register allows software to discover the current state of `keymgr`.
     19: However, since these values are not hardened, they can be attacked.
     20: As such, software should be careful to not make critical system decisions based on these registers.
     21: They are meant generally for informational or debug purposes.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: Key manager behavior can be summarized by the functional model below.
      4: 
      5: ![Key Manager Functional Model](../doc/keymgr_functional_model.svg)

sections.label: Key Manager State
sections.snippet:
25: 
     26: For clarity, all commands issued to the key manager by software are referred to as operations.
     27: Transactions refer to the interaction between key manager and KMAC if a valid operation is issued.
     28: 
>    29: ## Key Manager State
     30: 
     31: The key manager working state (red boxes in the functional model) represents both the current state of the key manager as well as its related internal key.
     32: Each valid state (`Initialized` / `CreatorRootKey` / `OwnerIntermediateKey` / `OwnerRootKey`), supplies its secret material as the "key" input to a KMAC operation.
     33: Invalid states, such as `Reset / Disabled` on the other hand, either do not honor operation requests, or supplies random data when invoked.

sections.label: Reset
sections.snippet:
33: Invalid states, such as `Reset / Disabled` on the other hand, either do not honor operation requests, or supplies random data when invoked.
     34: 
     35: The data input is dependent on each state, see below.
     36: 
>    37: ### Reset
     38: To begin operation, the state must first transition to Initialize.
     39: The advancement from `Reset` to `Initialized` is irreversible during the current power cycle.
     40: Until the initialize command is invoked, the key manager rejects all other software commands.
     41:

sections.label: Initialized
sections.snippet:
38: To begin operation, the state must first transition to Initialize.
     39: The advancement from `Reset` to `Initialized` is irreversible during the current power cycle.
     40: Until the initialize command is invoked, the key manager rejects all other software commands.
     41: 
>    42: ### Initialized
     43: 
     44: When transitioning from `Reset` to `Initialized`, random values obtained from the entropy source are used to populate the internal key first.
     45: Then the root key stored in OTP, if valid, is loaded into the internal key.
     46: This ensures that the hamming delta from the previous value to the next value is non-deterministic.

sections.label: CreatorRootKey
sections.snippet:
45: Then the root key stored in OTP, if valid, is loaded into the internal key.
     46: This ensures that the hamming delta from the previous value to the next value is non-deterministic.
     47: The advancement from `Initialized` to `CreatorRootKey` is irreversible during the current power cycle.
     48: 
>    49: ### CreatorRootKey
     50: 
     51: `CreatorRootKey` is the first operational state of the key manager.
     52: When transitioning from `Initialized` to this state, a KMAC operation is invoked using the `RootKey` as the key (from OTP), and the remaining inputs as data.
     53: The output of the KMAC operation replaces the previous value of the internal key, and the new value becomes the `CreatorRootKey`.

sections.label: OwnerIntermediateKey
sections.snippet:
71: The advancement from `CreatorRootKey` to the `OwnerIntermediateKey` is irreversible during the current power cycle.
     72: 
     73: Keymgr reads the root key from OTP in a single clock cycle. It assumes that when keymgr's internal FSM reaches to this clock cycle, OTP root key is already available (`valid` is set to 1). Otherwise, keymgr skips loading the root key.
     74: 
>    75: ### OwnerIntermediateKey
     76: 
     77: This is the second operational state of the key manager.
     78: This state is reached through another invocation of the KMAC operation using the previous internal key, and other inputs as data.
     79: The output of the KMAC operation replaces the previous value of the internal key, and the new value becomes the `OwnerIntermediateKey`.

sections.label: OwnerRootKey
sections.snippet:
86: The key used for all 3 functions is the `OwnerIntermediateKey`.
     87: 
     88: The advancement from `OwnerIntermediateKey` to the `OwnerRootKey` is irreversible during the current power cycle.
     89: 
>    90: ### OwnerRootKey
     91: 
     92: This is the last operational state of the key manager.
     93: This state is reached through another invocation of the KMAC operation using the previous internal key, and other inputs as data.
     94: The output of the KMAC operation replaces the previous value of the internal key, and the new value becomes the `OwnerRootKey`.

sections.label: Disabled
sections.snippet:
102: 
    103: The generate output and generate identity functions use `OwnerRootKey` as the KMAC key.
    104: The advancement from `OwnerRootKey` to the `Disabled` is irreversible during the current power cycle.
    105: 
>   106: ### Disabled
    107: `Disabled` is a state where the key manager is no longer operational.
    108: Upon `Disabled` entry, the internal key is updated with KMAC computed random values; however, previously generated sideload key slots and software key slots are preserved.
    109: This allows the software to keep the last valid keys while preventing the system from further advancing the valid key.
    110:

sections.label: Invalid
sections.snippet:
112: Key manager enters disabled state based on direct invocation by software:
    113: * Advance from `OwnerRootKey`
    114: * Disable operation
    115: 
>   116: ### Invalid
    117: `Invalid` state is entered whenever key manager is deactivated through the [life cycle connection](#life-cycle-connection) or when an operation encounters a [fault](#faults-and-operational-faults) .
    118: Upon `Invalid` entry, the internal key, the sideload key slots and the software keys are all wiped with entropy directly.
    119: 
    120: #### Invalid Entry Wiping

sections.label: Invalid Entry Wiping
sections.snippet:
116: ### Invalid
    117: `Invalid` state is entered whenever key manager is deactivated through the [life cycle connection](#life-cycle-connection) or when an operation encounters a [fault](#faults-and-operational-faults) .
    118: Upon `Invalid` entry, the internal key, the sideload key slots and the software keys are all wiped with entropy directly.
    119: 
>   120: #### Invalid Entry Wiping
    121: Since the life cycle controller can deactivate the key manager at any time, the key manager attempts to gracefully handle the wiping process.
    122: When deactivated, the key manager immediately begins wiping all keys (internal key, hardware sideload key, software key) with entropy.
    123: However, if an operation was already ongoing, the key manager waits for the operation to complete gracefully before transitioning to invalid state.
    124:

sections.label: Programmer's Guide
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
      3: Before initiating any of the following key generation operations, it is recommended (but not mandatory) to check that keymgr_dpe is ready to handle them.
      4: Except for the first advance call that initializes keymgr_dpe, this means keymgr_dpe is idle (as reported in `OP_STATUS`) and FSM is in `Available` state (reported in `WORKING_STATE`).
      5:

sections.label: Initialize first advance call
sections.snippet:
5: 
      6: Similarly, at the end of the operation (when `OP_STATUS` is not `WIP` anymore), it is recommended to check that the operation was successful by reading `ERR_CODE`.
      7: SW can also read the reported FSM state through `WORKING_STATE` to confirm that keymgr_dpe reaches the expected state.
      8:

>     1: # Theory of Operation

sections.label: Key Manager Slots
sections.snippet:
25: A keymgr slot refers to the storage unit for DPE contexts, and the actual DPE context it stores is dynamically controlled by SW commands.
     26: In order to address the relationships among keymgr_dpe slots and their stored DPE contexts more clearly, we use the terms _parent slot_ and _child slot_ to mean that their stored DPE contexts follow parent-child relationship in DICE hierarchy.
     27: `a || b` is used to denote the concatenation of two bit strings `a` and `b` (noticeably, not the logical OR operation).
     28: 
>    29: ## Key Manager Slots
     30: 
     31: Keymgr_dpe consists of `DpeNumSlots` slots, which is a generic parameter.
     32: Each of these key manager slots can store a DPE context, i.e. all DICE-related information for a particular boot stage. That includes a secret key along with additional context information described below.
     33: The secret key size is fixed to 256-bit.

sections.label: Key Manager State
sections.snippet:
59: Otherwise all advance requests are rejected that specify this slot as its source.
     60: *  If `retain_parent` is set to `true`/`1`, then the parent slot remains valid after an advance call.
     61: Otherwise, after the derivation of a child slot, the DPE context of the parent slot is removed automatically.
     62: 
>    63: ## Key Manager State
     64: 
     65: The key manager working state represents the current working state of the key manager and it is decoupled from the DICE hierarchy.
     66: From SW point of view, keymgr_dpe's FSM can only be in the following states: {`Reset`, `Available`, `Disabled`, `Invalid`}.
     67: After reset, keymgr_dpe remains in `Reset` state until the first advance call that latches the OTP creator root key, which is also referred to as Unique Device Secret (UDS).

sections.label: Reset
sections.snippet:
68: After this advance call, the FSM remains in `Available` state, and it can serve the advance/generate/erase requests.
     69: Unless keymgr_dpe encounters a fault or is explicitly disabled, the FSM remains in `Available` state.
     70: Invalid states such as {`Reset`, `Invalid`}, on the other hand, are used to denote out-of-operation states.
     71: 
>    72: ### Reset
     73: The advancement from `Reset` to `Available` internally goes through few FSM states, but from the SW point of view, this only requires a single advance call.
     74: During these FSM transitions, the OTP creator root key is latched into a destination slot specified by SW.
     75: The latching of the root key can only happen once until the keymgr_DPE is reset.
     76: Until the initial advance is invoked and keymgr_DPE reaches to `Available` state, the key manager rejects key generation requests.

sections.label: Available
sections.snippet:
74: During these FSM transitions, the OTP creator root key is latched into a destination slot specified by SW.
     75: The latching of the root key can only happen once until the keymgr_DPE is reset.
     76: Until the initial advance is invoked and keymgr_DPE reaches to `Available` state, the key manager rejects key generation requests.
     77: 
>    78: ### Available
     79: 
     80: During `Available`, keymgr_DPE accepts further advance and key generation requests.
     81: When transitioning from `Reset` to `Available`, as a SCA counter-measure, random values obtained from the entropy source are used to populate the key slot first in a manner that both shares have the same random mask.
     82: Then the root key is XORed on top of this randomness, in order to have fresh randomness for UDS at every power cycle.

sections.label: Disabled
sections.snippet:
81: When transitioning from `Reset` to `Available`, as a SCA counter-measure, random values obtained from the entropy source are used to populate the key slot first in a manner that both shares have the same random mask.
     82: Then the root key is XORed on top of this randomness, in order to have fresh randomness for UDS at every power cycle.
     83: During these transitions, keymgr_DPE's working state will be reported as `Reset`, until the latching is done and keymgr_DPE is ready to accept further commands.
     84: 
>    85: ### Disabled
     86: `Disabled` is reached through an explicit disable command invocation.
     87: In this state, keymgr_DPE is no longer operational and advance/generate/erase/disable commands return error.
     88: Upon `Disabled` entry, the internal key slots are wiped.
     89: However, previously generated sideload key slots and the software key stored in registers are preserved.

sections.label: Invalid
sections.snippet:
88: Upon `Disabled` entry, the internal key slots are wiped.
     89: However, previously generated sideload key slots and the software key stored in registers are preserved.
     90: This allows the software to keep the last valid keys while preventing keymgr_DPE to compute further versioned keys.
     91: 
>    92: ### Invalid
     93: `Invalid` state is entered whenever key manager is deactivated through the [life cycle connection](#life-cycle-connection) or when an operation encounters a [fault](#faults-and-operational-faults).
     94: Upon `Invalid` entry, the internal key, the sideload key slots and the software key are all wiped.
     95: 
     96: ### Invalid and Disabled State

sections.label: Invalid and Disabled State
sections.snippet:
92: ### Invalid
     93: `Invalid` state is entered whenever key manager is deactivated through the [life cycle connection](#life-cycle-connection) or when an operation encounters a [fault](#faults-and-operational-faults).
     94: Upon `Invalid` entry, the internal key, the sideload key slots and the software key are all wiped.
     95: 
>    96: ### Invalid and Disabled State
     97: 
     98: `Invalid` and `Disabled` states are functionally very similar.
     99: The main difference between the two is how the states are reached and the entry behavior.
    100:

104: If after entering `Disabled` life cycle is deactivated or a fault is encountered, the same [invalid entry procedure](#Invalid) is followed to bring the system to a terminal `Invalid` state.
    105: 
    106: If multiple conditions happen to collide (a fault is detected at the same clock cycle SW issues disable command), the `Invalid` entry path always takes precedence.

    109: During each state, there are 4 valid commands software can issue:

    111: * Key generation (a.k.a versioned key generation)
    112: * Erase slot

14: This document specifies the Keccak Message Authentication Code (KMAC) and Secure Hashing Algorithm 3 (SHA3) hardware IP functionality.

     16: See that document for integration overview within the broader OpenTitan top level system.
     17: 
>    18: ## Features
     19: 
     20: - Support for SHA3-224, 256, 384, 512, SHAKE[128, 256] and cSHAKE[128, 256]

>    32: ## Description

>    10: ## Software Initiated KMAC/SHA3 process
     11: 
     12: This section describes the expected software process to run the KMAC/SHA3 HWIP.
     13: At first, the software configures [`CFG_SHADOWED.kmac_en`](registers.md#cfg_shadowed) for KMAC operation.
     14: If KMAC is enabled, the software should configure [`CFG_SHADOWED.mode`](registers.md#cfg_shadowed) to cSHAKE and [`CFG_SHADOWED.kstrength`](registers.md#cfg_shadowed) to 128 or 256 bit security strength.

sections.label: Endianness
sections.snippet:
44: Done command clears the Keccak state, FSM in SHA3 and KMAC, and a few internal variables.
     45: Secret key and other software programmed values won't be reset.
     46: 
     47: 
>    48: ## Endianness
     49: 
     50: This KMAC HWIP operates in little-endian.
     51: Internal SHA3 hashing engine receives in 64-bit granularity.
     52: The data written to SHA3 is assumed to be little endian.

sections.label: EDN Entropy Mode

     64:

>    66: ## EDN Entropy Mode
     67: 
     68: For regular operation, [`CFG_SHADOWED.entropy_mode`](registers.md#cfg_shadowed--entropy_mode) should be set to EDN mode.
     69: In this mode, the module automatically reseeds the internal PRNG with fresh entropy from EDN after every [`ENTROPY_REFRESH_THRESHOLD_SHADOWED`](registers.md#entropy_refresh_threshold_shadowed) key absorption phases in KMAC mode.
     70: Alternatively, software can manually initiate reseeding operations using the [`CMD.entropy_req`](registers.md#cmd--entropy_req) bit while the module is idle.

sections.label: Preventing potential deadlocks in EDN mode
sections.snippet:
69: In this mode, the module automatically reseeds the internal PRNG with fresh entropy from EDN after every [`ENTROPY_REFRESH_THRESHOLD_SHADOWED`](registers.md#entropy_refresh_threshold_shadowed) key absorption phases in KMAC mode.
     70: Alternatively, software can manually initiate reseeding operations using the [`CMD.entropy_req`](registers.md#cmd--entropy_req) bit while the module is idle.
     71: 
     72: 
>    73: ### Preventing potential deadlocks in EDN mode
     74: 
     75: Under normal operating conditions, the SHA3 engine will process data a lot faster than software can push it to the Message FIFO.
     76: However, the Message FIFO may run full while the SHA3 engine is busy.
     77: In particular, this might happen because KMAC is waiting for fresh entropy from EDN.

sections.label: Design Details
sections.snippet:
33: By default, 1600 bits of internal state are used and stored in two shares (1st order masking).
     34: The masked Keccak core takes 4 clock cycles per round if sufficient entropy is available.
     35: If desired, the masking can be disabled and the internal state width can be reduced to 25, 50, or 100 bits at compile time.
     36: 
>    37: ## Design Details
     38: 
     39: ### Keccak Round
     40: 
     41: A Keccak round implements the Keccak_f function described in the SHA3 specification.

sections.label: Keccak Round
sections.snippet:
35: If desired, the masking can be disabled and the internal state width can be reduced to 25, 50, or 100 bits at compile time.
     36: 
     37: ## Design Details
     38: 
>    39: ### Keccak Round
     40: 
     41: A Keccak round implements the Keccak_f function described in the SHA3 specification.
     42: Keccak round logic in KMAC/SHA3 HWIP not only supports 1600 bit internal states but also all possible values {50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600} based on a parameter `Width`.
     43: If masking is disabled via compile-time Verilog parameter `EnMasking`, also 25 can be selected as state width.

sections.label: Padding for Keccak
sections.snippet:
71: If the masking compile time option is enabled, Keccak round logic requires an additional 3200 flip flops to store the intermediate half state inside the 800 DOM multipliers.
     72: In addition to that Keccak round logic needs two sets of the same Theta, Rho, and Pi functions.
     73: As a result, the masked Keccak round logic takes more than twice as much as area than the unmasked version of it.
     74: 
>    75: ### Padding for Keccak
     76: 
     77: Padding logic supports SHA3/SHAKE/cSHAKE algorithms.
     78: cSHAKE needs the extra inputs for the Function-name `N` and the Customization string `S`.
     79: Other than that, SHA3, SHAKE, and cSHAKE share similar datapath inside the padding module except the last part added next to the end of the message.

sections.label: Padding for KMAC
sections.snippet:
111: 
    112: The software completes the operation by issuing Done command after reading the digest.
    113: The padding logic clears internal variables and goes back to Idle state.
    114: 
>   115: ### Padding for KMAC
    116: 
    117: ![](../doc/kmac-padding.svg)
    118: 
    119: KMAC core prepends and appends additional bitstream on top of Keccak padding logic in SHA3 core.

sections.label: Message FIFO
sections.snippet:
125: The KMAC padding logic prepends a block containing the encoded secret key to the output message.
    126: The KMAC first sends the block of secret key then accepts the incoming message bitstream.
    127: At the end of the message, the software writes `right_encode(output_length)` to MSG_FIFO prior to issue Process command.
    128: 
>   129: ### Message FIFO
    130: 
    131: The KMAC HWIP has a compile-time configurable depth message FIFO inside.
    132: The message FIFO receives incoming message bitstream regardless of its byte position in a word.
    133: Then it packs the partial message bytes into the internal 64 bit data width.

sections.label: FIFO Depth calculation
sections.snippet:
132: The message FIFO receives incoming message bitstream regardless of its byte position in a word.
    133: Then it packs the partial message bytes into the internal 64 bit data width.
    134: After packing the data, the logic stores the data into the FIFO until the internal KMAC/SHA3 engine consumes the data.
    135: 
>   136: #### FIFO Depth calculation
    137: 
    138: The depth of the message FIFO is chosen to cover the throughput of the software or other producers such as DMA engine.
    139: The size of the message FIFO is enough to hold the incoming data while the SHA3 engine is processing the previous block.
    140: Details are in `kmac_pkg::MsgFifoDepth` parameter.

sections.label: Empty and Full status
sections.snippet:
142: 
    143: - `kmac_pkg::RegLatency`: The register write takes 5 cycles.
    144: - `kmac_pkg::Sha3Latency`: Keccak round latency takes 96 cycles, which is the masked version of the Keccak round.
    145: 
>   146: #### Empty and Full status
    147: 
    148: Under normal operating conditions, the SHA3 engine will process data a lot faster than software can push it to the Message FIFO.
    149: The Message FIFO depth observable from [`STATUS.fifo_depth`](registers.md#status--fifo_depth) will remain **0** while the [`STATUS.fifo_empty`](registers.md#status--fifo_empty) status bit is lowered for one clock cycle whenever software provides new data.

sections.label: Masking
sections.snippet:
166: The entropy not getting delivered in time can in particular happen if the entropy complex or parts of it are disabled, e.g., [to save power](../../csrng/doc/programmers_guide.md#running-csrng-with-entropy_src-disabled).
    167: Refer to [Preventing potential deadlocks in EDN mode](programmers_guide.md#preventing-potential-deadlocks-in-edn-mode) for guidance on how to safely avoid this scenario.
    168: 
    169: 
>   170: #### Masking
    171: 
    172: The message FIFO does not generate the masked message data.
    173: Incoming message bitstream is not sensitive to the leakage.
    174: If the `EnMasking` parameter is set and [`CFG_SHADOWED.msg_mask`](registers.md#cfg_shadowed) is enabled, the message is masked upon loading into the Keccak core using the internal entropy generator.

8: This IP has been taped out in Earl Grey 1.0.0. The corresponding documentation and regression results can be found [here](https://opentitan.org/earlgrey_1.0.0/book/hw/ip/lc_ctrl/index.html).
      9:

     11: 
>    12: # Overview
     13: 
     14: This document specifies the functionality of the life cycle controller.
     15: The life cycle controller is a module that is a peripheral on the chip interconnect bus, and thus follows the [Comportability Specification](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md).
     16: For the high-level description of the life cycle architecture of OpenTitan, please refer to the [Device Life Cycle Architecture](../../../doc/security/specs/device_life_cycle/README.md).

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
23: - The reset / power controller
     24: - The debug infrastructure, specifically TAP isolation
     25: - Any other peripheral where life cycle information may alter its behavior
     26: 
>    27: ## Features
     28: 
     29: The life cycle controller provides the following features:
     30: - Dedicated OTP interface to read and update the redundantly encoded device life cycle state.
     31: - A CSR and a JTAG interface for initiating life cycle transitions.

sections.label: Prelude - Why Not Software?
sections.snippet:
32: - Dedicated concurrent decoding of the redundant life cycle state and broadcasting of redundantly encoded life cycle qualification signals (e.g., to enable DFT features or the main processor).
     33: - A token hashing and matching mechanism to guard important life cycle transitions.
     34: - An escalation receiver for the alert subsystem, which allows to invalidate the life cycle state as part of an escalation sequence (see also alert handler subsystem).
     35: 
>    36: ## Prelude - Why Not Software?
     37: 
     38: There are many ways to implement life cycle functions in a design.
     39: This document opts for a more hardware driven approach, although there is still significant software hand holding required.
     40:

>   143: #### Power Manager Interface
    144: 
    145: The power manager interface is comprised of three signals overall: an initialization request (`pwr_lc_i.lc_init`), an initialization done response (`pwr_lc_o.lc_done`) and an idle indicator (`pwr_lc_o.lc_idle`).

    166: 
>   167: #### Control Signal Propagation
    168: 
    169: For better security, all the [life cycle control signals](theory_of_operation.md#life-cycle-decoded-outputs-and-controls) are broadcast in multi-bit form.
    170: The active ON state for every signal is broadcast as `4'b1010`, while the inactive OFF state is encoded as `4'b0101`.
    171: For all life cycle signals except the escalation signal ESCALATE_EN, all values different from ON must be interpreted as OFF in RTL.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: The following sections give an overview of the life cycle function.
      4: It begins with life cycle sensing at power up, progresses through how life cycle transitions are made, and then focuses specifically on how life cycle impacts various functionality of the design.
      5:

sections.label: Power Up Sequence
sections.snippet:
2: 
      3: The following sections give an overview of the life cycle function.
      4: It begins with life cycle sensing at power up, progresses through how life cycle transitions are made, and then focuses specifically on how life cycle impacts various functionality of the design.
      5: 
>     6: ## Power Up Sequence
      7: 
      8: Upon power up, the life cycle controller will default to "RAW" state and wait for the OTP controller to initialize and sense the contents of the life cycle partition (for example, see earlgrey's [life cycle partition doc](../../../top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/otp_ctrl/doc/theory_of_operation.md#partition-listing-and-description)).
      9: When the OTP is ready, the life cycle controller reads the contents of the life cycle partition, decodes the life cycle state and updates its internal state to match.
     10: This implies that unlike the life cycle definition diagram, there is a one-time "RAW to any state" logical transition that is implicit within the implementation.

sections.label: Normal Operation
sections.snippet:
20: Note the sequence is not designed into one specific module, but rather a result of coordination between the OTP controller, life cycle controller and the reset / power controllers.
     21: 
     22: ![LC Power Up Sequence](../doc/lc_ctrl_power_up.svg)
     23: 
>    24: ## Normal Operation
     25: 
     26: Once the life cycle system is powered up and stable, its outputs remain static unless specifically requested to change or affected by security escalation.
     27: The life cycle controller can accept [change requests](#life-cycle-request-interface) from software as well as external entities.
     28:

sections.label: Unconditional Transitions
sections.snippet:
25: 
     26: Once the life cycle system is powered up and stable, its outputs remain static unless specifically requested to change or affected by security escalation.
     27: The life cycle controller can accept [change requests](#life-cycle-request-interface) from software as well as external entities.
     28: 
>    29: ### Unconditional Transitions
     30: 
     31: For unconditional transitions, the life cycle controller advances the state by requesting an OTP update to the OTP controller.
     32: Once the programming is confirmed, the life cycle controller reports a success to the requesting agent and waits for the device to reboot.
     33:

sections.label: Conditional Transitions
sections.snippet:
30: 
     31: For unconditional transitions, the life cycle controller advances the state by requesting an OTP update to the OTP controller.
     32: Once the programming is confirmed, the life cycle controller reports a success to the requesting agent and waits for the device to reboot.
     33: 
>    34: ### Conditional Transitions
     35: 
     36: For conditional transitions, such as those that require a token (RAW_UNLOCK, TEST_UNLOCK, TEST_EXIT, RMA_UNLOCK), the life cycle controller advances the state via OTP programming only after it is supplied with the valid token.
     37: [Some tokens](../../../../doc/security/specs/device_life_cycle/README.md#manufacturing-states) are hardcoded design constants, while others are stored in OTP.
     38: Note that conditional transitions will only be allowed if the OTP partition holding the corresponding token has been provisioned and locked.

sections.label: Transition Counter Limits
sections.snippet:
45: It is the only token among those listed that is a global constant and stored in gates.
     46: 
     47: All others CAN be device unique and are stored in OTP.
     48: 
>    49: ### Transition Counter Limits
     50: 
     51: For conditional transitions, there is a limit to how many times they can be attempted.
     52: This is to prevent an attacker from brute-forcing any specific token, as this also helps to reduce the overall required token size.
     53:

sections.label: Token Hashing Mechanism
sections.snippet:
56: 
     57: The token counters are maintained in the OTP.
     58: To ensure the security of token limits cannot be bypassed, each request for a conditional transition **FIRST** increments the token count, and **THEN** checks for the validity of the token.
     59: 
>    60: ### Token Hashing Mechanism
     61: 
     62: All 128bit lock and unlock tokens are passed through a cryptographic one way function in hardware before the life cycle controller compares them to the provisioned values in OTP or to the netlist constant in case of RAW_UNLOCK.
     63: 
     64: This mechanism is used to guard against reverse engineering and brute-forcing attempts.

sections.label: Post Transition Handling
sections.snippet:
65: An attacker able to extract the hashed token values from the scrambled OTP partitions or from the netlist would first have to find a hash collision in order to perform a life cycle transition, since the values supplied to the life cycle controller must be valid hash pre-images.
     66: 
     67: The employed one way function is a 128bit cSHAKE hash with the function name "" (empty string) and customization string "LC_CTRL", see also [kmac documentation](../../kmac/README.md) and AppCfgLcCtrl in [`kmac_pkg.sv`](https://github.com/lowRISC/opentitan/blob/master/hw/ip/kmac/rtl/kmac_pkg.sv).
     68: 
>    69: ### Post Transition Handling
     70: 
     71: After a transition request, whether it was unconditional or conditional, the life cycle controller always disables all of its decoded outputs and puts the system in an inert state.
     72: The device is then expected to reboot before returning to a functional state.
     73:

sections.label: Security Escalation
sections.snippet:
73: 
     74: Note this happens for either successful or unsuccessful transitions.
     75: This general policy places a time-bound on how quickly life cycle states can change and also forces the device to behave more predictably.
     76: 
>    77: ## Security Escalation
     78: 
     79: The life cycle controller contains two escalation paths that are connected to escalation severities 1 and 2 of the alert handler.
     80: 
     81: The two escalation paths are redundant, and both trigger the same mechanism.

     86: 
     87: Whether to escalate to the life cycle controller or not is a software decision, please see the alert handler for more details.

sections.label: Overview
sections.snippet:
1: # Mailbox Technical Specification
      2: 
>     3: ## Overview
      4: 
      5: The mailbox IP block in the OpenTitan Integrated design implements a request-response channel that the host System-on-Chip (SoC) may use to request security services of the Root Of Trust (RoT).
      6: Communication is via message-passing with neither party requiring direct access to the memory address space or bus fabric of the other party.
      7:

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
4: 
      5: The mailbox IP block in the OpenTitan Integrated design implements a request-response channel that the host System-on-Chip (SoC) may use to request security services of the Root Of Trust (RoT).
      6: Communication is via message-passing with neither party requiring direct access to the memory address space or bus fabric of the other party.
      7: 
>     8: ## Features
      9: 
     10: The IP block has the following features:
     11: 
     12: - Interrupt-based signaling to the RoT when the full request message has been received from the SoC.

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
18: - Software-controlled abort mechanisms that either party may use to reset and re-establish communications.
     19: 
     20: The [Theory of Operation](doc/theory_of_operation.md) covers the detailed design and implementation of the IP block.
     21: 
>    22: ## Description
     23: 
     24: The mailbox IP block provides a sequenced request-response communication from the SoC host to the RoT and back.
     25: 
     26: Once the mailbox IP block has been configured from the RoT side with a description of the address ranges to be used for the Inbox and the Outbox, communication is initiated from the SoC side by it writing a request into the Inbox.

sections.label: Compatibility
sections.snippet:
31: Once the SoC has retrieved the full response message from the RoT, the request-response sequence is regarded as complete and the mailbox resets for a subsequent request.
     32: 
     33: For further details on how to use the mailbox IP block from software, please consult the [Programmer's Guide](doc/programmers_guide.md).
     34: 
>    35: ## Compatibility
     36: 
     37: The mailbox implementation adopts the [PCIe specification defined Data Object Exchange (DOE)](https://members.pcisig.com/wg/PCI-SIG/document/18363) mailbox protocol.
