sections.label: Programmer's Guide
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
      3: In a typical use case there are two software agents involved in the mailbox communication:
      4: 
      5: - RoT firmware configures the mailbox IP block and awaits requests from the SoC side.

sections.label: Initialization
sections.snippet:
9: 
     10: Each of the request and the response is composed of 'DWORD's which are 32 bits in size, so all messages sent and received by the mailbox must be a multiple of 4 bytes in length.
     11: An additional constraint of at most 1024 DWORDs (4 KiB) applies to the size of any response from the RoT (Outbox message).
     12: 
>    13: ## Initialization
     14: 
     15: Since the mailbox logic acts as a host on the TileLink fabric, before requests may be received from the SoC side the firmware of the RoT must configure the address ranges that may be accessed by the Inbox (SoC->RoT) and Outbox (RoT->SoC) logic.
     16: 
     17: To configure the mailbox for use, four registers - two for each side (Inbox and Outbox) - must be written:

sections.label: Request message from SoC to RoT
sections.snippet:
23: 
     24: Having supplied the address ranges, the RoT firmware shall declare the ranges valid by writing a value of 1 to the [`address_range_valid`](registers.md#address_range_valid) register, and may optionally lock the address range by writing MuBi4False to register [`address_range_regwen`](registers.md#address_range_regwen).
     25: Clearing the 'write enable' register in this manner prevents any further changes to the address range configuration until the mailbox IP block is reset, protecting against accidental or malicious changes.
     26: 
>    27: ## Request message from SoC to RoT
     28: 
     29: A software/hardware agent on the SoC side is required to check that the BUSY bit is clear before starting to send a request to the RoT.
     30: The BUSY bit indicates that the mailbox is already part-way through a request-response operation, so another request cannot be accepted.
     31:

sections.label: Collection of RoT response message by SoC
sections.snippet:
39: 
     40: The RoT firmware shall consult the [`inbound_write_ptr`](registers.md#inbound_write_ptr) register to ascertain the length of the transferred request message.
     41: The address in this register is advanced whenever a DWORD of the request message is written to the Inbox, so upon receipt of the complete request it holds the 4-byte aligned address _beyond_ the final DWORD of the request. The register [`inbound_write_ptr`](registers.md#inbound_write_ptr) is a read only register to the RoT firmware and its value is automatically reset to that of [`inbound_base_address`](registers.md#inbound_base_address) at the start of each request message.
     42: 
>    43: ## Collection of RoT response message by SoC
     44: 
     45: When the RoT firmware has performed the requested operation it is required to produce a response for the SoC side to collect.
     46: The firmware shall write the response message into the Outbox memory starting at the address specified in [`outbound_base_address`](registers.md#outbound_base_address), and shall then specify the number of DWORDs of message data by writing a non-zero value to the [`outbound_object_size`](registers.md#outbound_object_size) register.
     47: This register permits the sending of responses that are up to 1024 DWORDs in length for a maximum size of 4 KiB.

sections.label: Abort mechanism
sections.snippet:
45: When the RoT firmware has performed the requested operation it is required to produce a response for the SoC side to collect.
     46: The firmware shall write the response message into the Outbox memory starting at the address specified in [`outbound_base_address`](registers.md#outbound_base_address), and shall then specify the number of DWORDs of message data by writing a non-zero value to the [`outbound_object_size`](registers.md#outbound_object_size) register.
     47: This register permits the sending of responses that are up to 1024 DWORDs in length for a maximum size of 4 KiB.
     48: 
>    49: ## Abort mechanism
     50: 
     51: If the SoC side needs to cancel an in-progress service request, it may use the Abort mechanism of the DOE mailbox control register.
     52: Setting the `abort` bit of the [`soc_control`](registers.md#soc_control) register will raise the `mbx_abort` interrupt to the RoT firmware, instructing it that any in-progress operation shall be aborted.
     53:

sections.label: Firmware-initiated reset
sections.snippet:
52: Setting the `abort` bit of the [`soc_control`](registers.md#soc_control) register will raise the `mbx_abort` interrupt to the RoT firmware, instructing it that any in-progress operation shall be aborted.
     53: 
     54: The RoT firmware should then clear the `abort` indicator via its [`control`](registers.md#control) register on the RoT side and initiate any recovery procedures.
     55: 
>    56: ## Firmware-initiated reset
     57: 
     58: In addition to the SoC-side Abort mechanism specified for DOE mailboxes, the RoT firmware has the ability to perform a complete reset of the mailbox logic to recover from any error condition or synchronization issue that may have been detected.
     59: 
     60: This is achieved by writing 1 to the `abort` bit of the [`control`](registers.md#control) register. In addition to clearing any pending Abort condition from the SoC side this action has the effect of resetting all of the internal mailbox logic as a fallback recovery mechanism.

>    16: # Overview
     17: 
     18: This document specifies functionality of the OpenTitan Big Number Accelerator, or OTBN.
     19: OTBN is a coprocessor for asymmetric cryptographic operations like RSA or Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC).
     20:

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
20: 
     21: This module conforms to the [Comportable guideline for peripheral functionality](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md).
     22: See that document for integration overview within the broader top level system.
     23: 
>    24: ## Features
     25: 
     26: * Processor optimized for wide integer arithmetic
     27: * 32b wide control path with 32 32b wide registers
     28: * 256b wide data path with 32 256b wide registers

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
29: * Full control-flow support with conditional branch and unconditional jump instructions, hardware loops, and hardware-managed call/return stacks.
     30: * Reduced, security-focused instruction set architecture for easier verification and the prevention of data leaks.
     31: * Built-in access to random numbers.
     32: 
>    33: ## Description
     34: 
     35: OTBN is a processor, specialized for the execution of security-sensitive asymmetric (public-key) cryptography code, such as RSA or ECC.
     36: Such algorithms are dominated by wide integer arithmetic, which are supported by OTBN's 256b wide data path, registers, and instructions which operate these wide data words.
     37: On the other hand, the control flow is clearly separated from the data, and reduced to a minimum to avoid data leakage.

sections.label: Compatibility
sections.snippet:
41: For example, no interrupts or exceptions are included in the design, and all instructions are designed to be executable within a single cycle.
     42: 
     43: OTBN is designed as a self-contained co-processor with its own instruction and data memory, which is accessible as a bus device.
     44: 
>    45: ## Compatibility
     46: 
     47: OTBN is not designed to be compatible with other cryptographic accelerators.
     48: It received some inspiration from assembly code available from the [Chromium EC project](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromiumos/platform/ec/),
     49: which has been formally verified within the [Fiat Crypto project](http://adam.chlipala.net/papers/FiatCryptoSP19/FiatCryptoSP19.pdf).

>    65: ### General Purpose Registers (GPRs)
     66: 
     67: OTBN has 32 General Purpose Registers (GPRs), each of which is 32b wide.
     68: The GPRs are defined in line with RV32I and are mainly used for control flow.

sections.label: Call Stack
sections.snippet:
92: If a calling convention is needed at some point, it is expected to be aligned with the RISC-V standard calling conventions, and the roles assigned to registers in that convention.
     93: Even without a agreed-on calling convention, software authors are encouraged to follow the RISC-V calling convention where it makes sense.
     94: For example, good choices for temporary registers are `x6`, `x7`, `x28`, `x29`, `x30`, and `x31`.
     95: 
>    96: ### Call Stack
     97: 
     98: OTBN has an in-built call stack which is accessed through the `x1` GPR.
     99: This is intended to be used as a return address stack, containing return addresses for the current stack of function calls.
    100: See the documentation for {{#otbn-insn-ref JAL}} and {{#otbn-insn-ref JALR}} for a description of how to use it for this purpose.

107: A single instruction can both read and write to the stack.
    108: In this case, the read is ordered before the write.
    109: Providing the stack has at least one element, this is allowed, even if the stack is full.
    110: 
>   111: ### Control and Status Registers (CSRs)
    112: 
    113: Control and Status Registers (CSRs) are 32b wide registers used for "special" purposes, as detailed in their description;
    114: they are not related to the GPRs.
    115: CSRs can be accessed through dedicated instructions, {{#otbn-insn-ref CSRRS}} and {{#otbn-insn-ref CSRRW}}.

>   102: ### Life Cycle Controller (LC_CTRL)
    103: 
    104: OTBN has three LC_CTRL connections: one for triggering life cycle escalation requests (`lc_escalate_en`) and two for handling RMA entry (`lc_rma_req/ack`).

sections.label: Introduction to OTBN
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Introduction to OTBN
      2: 
      3: OTBN (the **O**pen**T**itan **B**ig **N**umber accelerator) is a specialized coprocessor designed for cryptography.
      4: It runs as part of OpenTitan in addition to the main processor, Ibex.
      5: The OTBN hardware block could also run as part of a different system and interact with a different main processor, but this page will focus on the OpenTitan context.

25: - If OTBN encounters an error, it will lock itself, meaning that Ibex can't read back any data from the program when OTBN is finished (only an error code from a special register).
     26: 
     27: All together, this mode of interaction keeps OTBN separate enough from Ibex to act as a security boundary.
     28: 
>    29: ## Security features
     30: 
     31: Because OTBN exclusively runs cryptographic algorithms, it is built with extra security features to protect secrets during and after execution.
     32: See the [technical specification](../README.md#security-features) for a full description, but at a high level these features include:
     33: - **no branch prediction or speculative execution**: OTBN stalls for one cycle after jump and branch instructions rather than attempt to predict the next PC, as a mitigation against Spectre-style attacks.

>    50: ### Multiplying big numbers
     51: 
     52: OTBN's multiplication instructions are `bn.mulqacc`, `bn.mulqacc.so`, and `bn.mulqacc.wo`.

94: For example, 66% of instructions executed on OTBN during an ECDSA-P256 signature generation are some form of `bn.mulqacc`.
     95: The proportion is similarly high across other ECC and RSA computations.
     96: See the [performance](#performance) section for exact benchmarks.

>    98: ### Add/subtract modulo
     99: 
    100: OTBN has a special `MOD` register that holds a modulus (up to 256 bits).
    101: The instructions `bn.addm` and `bn.subm` perform addition and subtraction over that modulus.
    102: This is especially useful for elliptic-curve cryptography such as ECDSA-P256 and Ed25519, where `bn.addm` replaces a common "add and then conditionally subtract the modulus in constant-time if the sum is greater" pattern.

>    57: ### Passing of data between the host CPU and OTBN
     58: 
     59: Passing data between the host CPU and OTBN is done through the first 2kiB of data memory (DMEM).
     60: No standard or required calling convention exists, every application is free to pass data in and out of OTBN in whatever format it finds convenient.
     61: All data passing must be done when OTBN [is idle](./theory_of_operation.md#operational-states); otherwise both the instruction and the data memory are inaccessible from the host CPU.

>    81: #### Loop nesting
     82: 
     83: OTBN permits loop nesting and branches and jumps inside loops.
     84: However, it doesn't have support for early termination of loops: there's no way to pop an entry from the loop stack without executing the last instruction of the loop the correct number of times.
     85: It can also only pop one level of the loop stack per instruction.

>    30: ## Description
     31: 
     32: The pattern generator HWIP transmits short (maximum 64 bits) time-dependent data patterns on two clock-parallel channels.
     33: Each channel consists of one clock (`pcl`) and one data (`pda`) line.
     34: The output channels may be activated and operated independently, or they can be started at the same time to effectively create a 4-output pattern.

>    36: ## Channels
     37: 
     38: The current `pattgen` implementation is designed to support two channels.
     39: Each channel can run independently, started with the [`CTRL`](doc/registers.md#ctrl) register.
     40: Because the "enable" fields for the different channels are both in the same register, two channels may be started synchronously.

>    42: ## Patterns
     43: 
     44: Each channel can send a pattern of up to 64 bits.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: The pattern can be started (or halted) on either channel by setting the corresponding [`CTRL.ENABLE`](registers.md#ctrl) bit to 1 (or 0) for the desired channel.
      4: Once disabled, either channel can be configured independently.
      5: The channel parameters (i.e. clock divider ratio, clock polarity, pattern length, pattern data, and repetition count) can all be programmed on a per-channel basis.

sections.label: Block Diagram
sections.snippet:
8: Please note that writes to a channel's configuration registers have no effect while the channel is enabled.
      9: For operational simplicity, the configuration registers are only transferred into the internal finite state machines while a channel is disabled.
     10: Changes to the configuration registers only take effect once the channel has been disabled and re-enabled.
     11: 
>    12: ## Block Diagram
     13: 
     14: ![](../doc/pattgen_block_diagram.svg)
     15:

sections.label: Design Details
sections.snippet:
12: ## Block Diagram
     13: 
     14: ![](../doc/pattgen_block_diagram.svg)
     15: 
>    16: ## Design Details
     17: 
     18: The design consists of two identical and independent finite state machines, each an instance of module `pattgen_fsm`.
     19: Each FSM is essentially three nested counters, with one counter to control the clock division, another to count out the sequence bits, and a third to keep count of the number of repetitions.
     20:

sections.label: Interrupts
sections.snippet:
52: All counters halt, the `pda` data line returns to its inactive state as specified by `inactive_level_pda`, the `pcl` clock line similarly assumes `inactive_level_pcl` and an interrupt event is sent out to signal completion.
     53: 
     54: The entire sequence can be restarted either by resetting or disabling and re-enabling the FSM.
     55: 
>    56: ### Interrupts
     57: 
     58: The pattern generator HWIP provides two interrupt pins, `done_ch0` and `done_ch1`, which indicate the completion of pattern generation on the output channels.
     59: These interrupts can be enabled/disabled by setting/un-setting the corresponding bits of the [`INTR_ENABLE`](registers.md#intr_enable) register.
     60: To clear the interrupts, a value of `1` must be written to the corresponding bits of the [`INTR_STATE`](registers.md#intr_state) register.

>    50: ## Primitive Implementations & Libraries
     51: 
     52: Primitives in OpenTitan exist at a low level of RTL abstraction where it may be desirable under different circumstances to swap-out implementations to obtain better optimized hardware.
     53: For this reason, our definition of a primitive is "*a module with a fixed name and set of ports*".
     54: This minimizes the changes required for different implementations of a primitive to be substituted for each other.

sections.label: Virtual Primitives
sections.snippet:
69: While primatives are defined primarily by their interface, SystemVerilog does not allow a module interface to be defined without an implementation.
     70: This is unlike constructs in other languages such as Abstract Methods and Interfaces in Java or Traits in Rust.
     71: To determine the interface for a primitive (the module ports and parameters), the generic module implementation should be consulted.
     72: 
>    73: ### Virtual Primitives
     74: 
     75: OpenTitan utilizes the *[Fusesoc][]* build system and package manager to manage RTL at a fileset level.
     76: To allow hardware blocks to be generic across implementations of technology-dependent primitives, a feature of FuseSoC called *[Virtual Cores][]* is used.
     77: Virtual Cores allow FuseSoC to swap in a chosen implementation of a module without changing the RTL instantiation itself.

sections.label: Resolution of Concrete Implementations
sections.snippet:
107: The following section further describes the resolution process.
    108: 
    109: It is still possible and valid for a Core to depend only on a specific implementation of a technology-dependent primitive, however the implementation cannot be substituted at build time in this case, and it functions as a normal FuseSoC Core.
    110: 
>   111: ### Resolution of Concrete Implementations
    112: 
    113: When invoking FuseSoC, a 'target' in a Core file is selected to choose the flow we wish to run.
    114: Targets can depend on one or more 'filesets' defined within the Core, and each fileset can optionally depend on other Cores.
    115: Therefore, when FuseSoC is run a dependency graph comprised of Cores and filesets is constructed.

sections.label: Mappings
sections.snippet:
139: To reduce the hassle of pulling in implementations for all virtual cores in a Technology Libraries into a dependency tree, the library will provide an `:all` core, e.g. `lowrisc:prim_generic:all` or `lowrisc:prim_xilinx_ultrascale:all`.
    140: For example, the core `hw/top_earlgrey/chip_earlgrey_cw310.core` targeting a synthesis for a specific Xilinx FPGA depends on `lowrisc:prim_xilinx:all` to select a Xilinx Technology Library for primitives.
    141: 
    142: 
>   143: ### Mappings
    144: 
    145: 
    146: Fusesoc .core files may contain a 'mapping' key, which can define injective/one-to-one *[mappings][]* from virtual cores to a implementation of that virtual core.
    147: Passing `--mapping=<VLNV>` via the CLI will cause any 'mapping' keys in the core to be used to resolve virtual cores to concrete implementations.

153: An example set of mappings for the Xilinx Technology Library can be found in the following .core file.
    154: Notice that there are not Xilinx specific implementations for all primitives, so we fallback to the generic implementation in those cases.
    155: 
    156: ```yaml
>   157: # hw/ip/prim_xilinx/prim_xilinx.core
    158: name: "lowrisc:prim_xilinx:all:0.1"
    159: description: "Xilinx 7-series prim library"
    160: 
    161: mapping:

165:   "lowrisc:prim:clock_div"    : lowrisc:prim_generic:clock_div
    166:   "lowrisc:prim:clock_gating" : lowrisc:prim_xilinx:clock_gating
    167:   "lowrisc:prim:clock_inv"    : lowrisc:prim_generic:clock_inv
    168:   "lowrisc:prim:clock_mux2"   : lowrisc:prim_xilinx:clock_mux2
>   169:   # ...
    170: ```
    171: 
    172: One specific use of mappings is the lints for each block, such as the lint target for the OpenTitan UART in `hw/ip/uart/uart.core`.
    173: At the HWIP level, the UART is generic across technology-dependent primitives, and hence its dependencies do not contain any concrete primitive implementations.

1: # Primitive Component: SRAM Scrambler
      2: 
>     3: # Overview
      4: 
      5: The scrambling primitive `prim_ram_1p_scr` employs a reduced-round (5 or 7 instead of 11) PRINCE block cipher in CTR mode to scramble the data.
      6: The PRINCE lightweight block cipher has been selected due to its low latency and low area characteristics, see also [prim_prince](./prim_prince.md) for more information on PRINCE.
      7: In the default configuration, the number of rounds is reduced to 7 in order to ease timing pressure and ensure single cycle operation (the number of rounds can always be increased via the `NumPrinceRoundsHalf` parameter if it turns out that there is enough timing slack).

sections.snippet:
8: This IP has been taped out in Earl Grey 1.0.0. The corresponding documentation and regression results can be found [here](https://opentitan.org/earlgrey_1.0.0/book/hw/ip/rom_ctrl/index.html).
      9:

     11: 
>    12: # Overview
     13: 
     14: The ROM controller (`rom_ctrl`) is the connection between the chip and its ROM.
     15: It has three main tasks:
     16: - Pass read requests to the ROM and respond with the memory contents.

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
33: There is also a dedicated connection to the power manager (to allow the third item).
     34: A basic check that the contents look reasonable is performed by storing the expected value of the hash in the top 8 words of the ROM.
     35: The ROM controller checks that this matches the hash that was computed, and passes this information to the power manager (which can stop the startup if the SHA doesn't match).
     36: 
>    37: ## Features
     38: 
     39: - Logic for memory and address descrambling
     40: - Post-boot ROM integrity check
     41: - Alert trigger and status CSRs for ROM integrity errors or FSM glitches.

>    16: ## ROM access when chip is in operation

sections.label: The startup ROM check
sections.snippet:
49: 
     50: The `prim_prince` primitive and the two substitution-permutation networks are all parameterised by "keys".
     51: For `rom_ctrl`, these keys are global randomised netlist constants: they are assumed to be difficult to recover, but aren't considered secret data.
     52: 
>    53: ## The startup ROM check
     54: 
     55: The ROM checker runs immediately after reset.
     56: Until it is done, it controls ROM address requests (through the green multiplexer).
     57: The select signal for this multiplexer has a redundant encoding to protect it against fault injection attacks.

sections.label: What does the ROM check do?
sections.snippet: 80: ![ROM checker FSM Diagram](../doc/rom_check_fsm.svg) 81: 82: 83: > 84: ## What does the ROM check do? 85: 86: One of the possible physical attacks on a system like OpenTitan is to subvert the ROM. 87: The regular structure of a ROM is useful because it makes metal fixes easy, but (for the same reasons) it makes the ROM quite an easy target for an attacker. 88: See \[SKO-05\][^SKO-05], section 2.1.1, for a description of ROMs and attacks on them.

sections.label: Fault-injection hardening
sections.snippet:
109: `CreatorRootKey` forms the first key in the chain described in [Identities and Root Keys](../../../../doc/security/specs/identities_and_root_keys/README.md).
    110: An attacker who modifies the ROM will perturb `CreatorRootKey` (to avoid doing so would require a preimage attack on the ROM checksum calculation or the `KM_DERIVE` function).
    111: The result is that, while the chip will function, it will have the "wrong" root key and the chain of trust used for attestation will be broken.
    112: 
>   113: ## Fault-injection hardening
    114: 
    115: The core integrity check, flowing from the ROM data to `CreatorRootKey`, should be infeasible to subvert.
    116: However, `rom_ctrl` also controls bus access to ROM data and interacts with other blocks.
    117: To avoid attacks propagating into the rest of the system, we take the following extra hardening steps:

     23: - TileLink Uncached Light (TL-UL) bus interfaces
     24: - Late debug enable mechanism in DEV life cycle state
     25: 
>    26: ## Description
     27: 
     28: This module provides a RISC-V Debug Specification-compliant debug system with TileLink Uncached Light bus interfaces.
     29: The main functionality is provided by the [PULP RISC-V Debug System](https://github.com/pulp-platform/riscv-dbg), which is instantiated by this module.
     30: All bus interfaces are converted into TL-UL.

>    66: ## Life Cycle Control
     67: 
     68: Debug system functionality is controlled by the [HW_DEBUG_EN](../../lc_ctrl/README.md#hw_debug_en) function of the life cycle controller.
     69: Note that in order to support the non-debug module (NDM) reset functionality, the debug module needs to use a latched version of debug enable signal during the NDM reset.
     70: There are two HW_DEBUG_EN signal inputs in the `rv_dm` module:

sections.label: JTAG
sections.snippet:
78: When using a dedicated JTAG TAP in the debug module, e.g., in Earlgrey, the second signal is a latched version coming from the [strap sampling and TAP selection logic inside the pinmux](../../../top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/pinmux/doc/theory_of_operation.md#strap-sampling-and-tap-isolation).
     79: When using the debug module with the DMI interface, e.g., in Darjeeling, the debug module itself latches the debug enable signal while the NDM reset is taking place.
     80: When NDM reset is triggered the life cycle controller is reset, but the debug module is not, so the latched variant of the signal keeps the JTAG side and its gating of the debug module operational.
     81: 
>    82: ## JTAG
     83: 
     84: The debug system provides a standard JTAG (IEEE Std 1149.1-2013) port for external debug access.
     85: All JTAG logic is clocked with an externally supplied test clock (`tck`).
     86: The protocol used for this JTAG port is specified in the RISC-V Debug Specification as JTAG Debug Transport Module (DTM).

>    21: ## Late Debug Enable Mechanism
     22: 
     23: The RV_DM is gated by life cycle so that it is only usable during TEST_UNLOCKED*, DEV and RMA life cycle states where the LC_HW_DEBUG_EN signal is asserted.
     24: In the DEV life cycle state, this gating mechanism supports "late enablement" via firmware in order to implement a debug policy where ROM or ROM_EXT first secures and locks critical regions, assets and mechanisms in the device before ungating the RV_DM completely.

>    93: ## Interrupt Handling
     94: 
     95: If `mtime` is greater than or equal to the value of `mtimecmp`, the interrupt is generated from the RV_TIMER module.
     96: If the core enables the timer interrupt in `MIE` CSR, it jumps into the timer interrupt service routine.

>    15: ### Tick Generator
     16: 
     17: The tick module inside the timer IP is used to generate a fixed period of pulse
     18: signal. This allows creation of a call-clock timer tick such as 1us or 10us
     19: regardless of the system clock period. It is useful if the system has more than

sections.label: Configurable number of timers and harts

25: value of **47** for 48MHz and **199** for 200MHz will generate a 1us tick.
     26: In this version, the timer only supports a single fixed clock, so the firmware
     27: should change [`CFG0.prescaler`](registers.md#cfg0) appropriately.
     28: 
>    29: ### Configurable number of timers and harts
     30: 
     31: The timer IP supports more than one HART and/or more than one timer per hart.
     32: Each hart has a set of tick generator and counter. It means the timer IP has the
     33: same number of prescalers, steps, and `mtime` registers as the number of harts.

35: The debug policy - CAT2_UNLOCKED and/or CAT3_UNLOCKED and/or CAT4_UNLOCKED gets broadcast to all TAPs/DebugModules in the system, which must use this debug policy to accept/reject debug commands.
     36: For most debug modules CAT4_UNLOCKED opens up the same debug capabilities as CAT3_UNLOCKED.
     37: Units that need to distinguish between a pre-production and post-production part can differentiate debug actions for CAT4_UNLOCKED and CAT3_UNLOCKED.
     38: 
>    39: ## Debug Authorization Window
     40: 
     41: The debug authorization protocol and interfaces are defined in Integrated OpenTitan: Design for Test and Debug Support.
     42: 
     43: Before the owner and creator root keys are finalized, the ROM obtains an indication from the debugger if there is an intent to debug.

sections.label: Relock
sections.snippet:
53: During this flow, the ROT firmware drives all status bits related to the debug control.
     54: Integrated OpenTitan: Design for Test and Debug Support defines various status bits such as debug_auth_window/open etc.
     55: These status bits are mirrored to the debugger accessible JTAG interface, allowing debuggers to read the debug authorization status of the system.
     56: 
>    57: ## Relock
     58: 
     59: Following a successful debug authorization, the debugger may wish to relock the debug interface.
     60: In order to relock the debug interface, the debugger specifies a password which the debugger can use to re-unlock the part later by providing the password.
     61: When relocking the device, the RELOCKED field in DEBUG_POLICY_RELOCKED shall be set to `Mubi4::True`.

>    48: ## Description
     49: 
     50: The SPI device module consists of three functions, SPI Flash mode, SPI passthrough mode, and TPM over SPI mode.

sections.label: TPM over SPI
sections.snippet:
22: This separation of flows allows the memory to be implemented by two SRAM instances that each have one read-only and one write-only port (the "1r1w" SRAM macro).
     23: In addition, regardless of whether the memory is implemented using a single instance with two read-write ports or the two 1r1w instances, the access controls are the same.
     24: Software can only write to the egress memory, and it can only read from the ingress memory.
     25: 
>    26: ## TPM over SPI
     27: 
     28: ### Initialization
     29: 
     30: The SW should enable the TPM submodule by writing 1 to the TPM_CFG.en CSR field.

sections.label: TPM mode: FIFO and CRB
sections.snippet:
33: Update TPM_ACCESS_0, TPM_ACCESS_1 CSRs.
     34: The TPM submodule uses TPM_ACCESS_x.activeLocality to determine if the TPM_STS is returned to the host system.
     35: The SW may configure TPM_CFG.hw_reg_dis and/or TPM_CFG.invalid_locality to fully control the TPM transactions.
     36: 
>    37: ### TPM mode: FIFO and CRB
     38: 
     39: The TPM protocol supports two protocol interfaces: FIFO and CRB (Command Response Buffer).
     40: In terms of hardware design, these two interfaces differ in how return-by-HW registers are handled.
     41:

sections.label: Return-by-HW register update
sections.snippet:
42: In FIFO mode, when [`TPM_CFG.tpm_mode`](registers.md#tpm_cfg) is set to 0, HW registers reads must be returned after a maximum of 1 wait state.
     43: In CRB mode, when [`TPM_CFG.tpm_mode`](registers.md#tpm_cfg) is set to 1, there are no such restrictions.
     44: The logic always uploads both the command and address to the SW and waits for the return data in CRB mode.
     45: 
>    46: ### Return-by-HW register update
     47: 
     48: The SW manages the return-by-HW registers.
     49: The contents are placed inside the SPI_DEVICE CSRs.
     50: The SW must maintain the other TPM registers outside of the SPI_DEVICE HWIP and use write/read FIFOs to receive the content from/ send the register value to the host system.

sections.label: TPM Read
sections.snippet:
51: 
     52: When the SW updates the return-by-HW registers, the SW is recommended to read back the register to confirm the value is written.
     53: Due to the CDC issue, the SW is only permitted to update the registers when the TPM CS# is de-asserted.

     16: 
>    17: ## Features
     18: 
     19: - Hardware control for remote devices using the Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI)
     20: - Primarily designed for serial NOR flash devices such as the [Winbond W25Q01JV](https://www.winbond.com/resource-files/W25Q01JV%20SPI%20RevB%2011132019.pdf)
     21: - Number of chip select lines controlled by `NumCS` parameter

sections.label: Description

38: - Automatic control of chip select lines
     39: - Condensed interrupt footprint: Two lines for two distinct interrupt classes: "error" and "spi_event"
     40:    - Fine-grain interrupt masking supplied by secondary enable registers
     41: 
>    42: ## Description
     43: 
     44: The Serial Peripheral Interface (SPI) is a synchronous serial interface, commonly used for NOR flash devices and off-chip peripherals such as ADCs, DACs, or temperature sensors.
     45: 
     46: The interface is a *de facto* standard (not a formal one), so there is no definitive reference or established compliance criteria.

     50: 
>    51: ## Issuing Transactions
     52: 
     53: As mentioned above, each command is typically specified in three phases: loading the TX data, specifying the command segments/format, and reading the RX data.
     54: In principle, the first two steps can be performed in either order.
     55: If the SPI_HOST does not find any data to transmit it will simply stall until data is inserted.

sections.label: Loading TX data
sections.snippet:
58: For longer transactions, with data larger than the capacity of the FIFOs, the command sequence may become more complex.
     59: For instance, to send 1024 bytes of data in a single transaction, the TX data may need to be loaded several times if using a 256-byte FIFO.
     60: In this instance, the programming sequence will consist of at least four iterations of entering TX data and waiting for the TX FIFO to drain.
     61: 
>    62: ### Loading TX data
     63: 
     64: SPI transactions expect each command to start with some command sequence from the host, and so usually data will be transmitted at least in the first command segment.
     65: The [`TXDATA`](registers.md#txdata) window provides a simple interface to the TX FIFO.
     66: Data can be written to the window using 8-, 16- or 32-bit instructions.

sections.label: Byte-ordering Conventions
sections.snippet:
66: Data can be written to the window using 8-, 16- or 32-bit instructions.
     67: 
     68: Some attention, however, should be paid to byte-ordering and segmenting conventions.
     69: 
>    70: #### Byte-ordering Conventions
     71: 
     72: For SPI flash applications, it is generally assumed that most of the *payload* data will be directly copied from embedded SRAM to the flash device.
     73: 
     74: If this data is to copied to the [`TXDATA`](registers.md#txdata) window using 32-bit instructions, the SPI_HOST should be parameterized such that the `ByteOrder` parameter matches the byte order of the embedded CPU (i.e., for Ibex, `ByteOrder` should be left set to `1` to indicate a Little-Endian CPU).

sections.label: Segmenting Considerations
sections.snippet:
120: - Flash transactions with 3-byte addressing require some care, as there are no 24-bit I/O instructions, though there are a several options:
    121:     - After the 8-bit command code is sent, the address can either be sent in several I/O operations (e.g., the MSB is sent as an 8-bit command, and the remaining 16-bits can be sent after swapping)
    122:     - If bandwidth efficiency is a priority, the address, `A[23:0]`, and command code, `C[7:0]`, can all be packed together into a single 4-byte quantity `W[31:0] = {A[7:0], A[15:8], A[23:16], C[7:0]}`, which when loaded into [`TXDATA`](registers.md#txdata) will ensure that the command code is sent first, followed by the address in MSB-first order.
    123: 
>   124: #### Segmenting Considerations
    125: 
    126: Data words are *not* shared across segments.
    127: If at the end of each TX (or bidirectional) segment there is a partially transmitted data word then any unsent bytes will be discarded as the SPI_HOST IP closes the segment.
    128: For the next TX segment, the transmitted data will start with the following *word* from the TX FIFO.

sections.label: Refilling the TX FIFO
sections.snippet:
126: Data words are *not* shared across segments.
    127: If at the end of each TX (or bidirectional) segment there is a partially transmitted data word then any unsent bytes will be discarded as the SPI_HOST IP closes the segment.
    128: For the next TX segment, the transmitted data will start with the following *word* from the TX FIFO.
    129: 
>   130: #### Refilling the TX FIFO
    131: 
    132: For extremely long transactions, the TX FIFO may not have enough capacity to hold all the data being transmitted.
    133: In this case software can either poll the [`STATUS.TXQD`](registers.md#status) register to determine the number of elements in the TX FIFO, or enable the SPI_HOST IP to send an interrupt when the FIFO drains to a certain level.
    134: If [`INTR_ENABLE.spi_event`](registers.md#intr_enable) and [`EVENT_ENABLE.TXWM`](registers.md#event_enable) are both asserted, the IP will send an interrupt whenever the number of elements in the TX FIFO falls below [`CONTROL.TX_WATERMARK`](registers.md#control).

>    10: # SPI Protocol Basics
     11: 
     12: SPI is a source-synchronous serial interface, consisting of data lines (`SD[x]`), a clock (`SCK`), and an active-low chip select (`CS#`) per target device.
     13: The host is responsible for generating the serial clock, and typically each side asserts outgoing data on one edge of the clock (e.g. on the rising edge) and samples data in the next edge (e.g. on the falling edge).
     14: The SPI bus can be connected to many target devices, but each device on the bus must get its own chip select, and so this signal designates a particular device for each command.

sections.label: API Details
sections.snippet:
45: For even faster transfer rates, some flash chips support double transfer rate (DTR) variations to the SPI protocol wherein the device receives and transmits fresh data on *both* the leading and trailing edge.
     46: This IP only supports single transfer rate (STR), *not* DTR.
     47: A preliminary investigation of DTR transfer mode suggests that proper support for setup and hold times in this mode may require a level of sub-cycle timing control which is not currently planned for this IP.
     48: 
>    49: # API Details
     50: 
     51: Broadly speaking, the SPI_HOST IP accepts commands from the TL-UL interface, and based on these commands, serially transmits and receives data on the external SPI interface pins.
     52: The timing and data-line formatting of the command sequence depend on the external peripheral device and the nature of the specific command issued.
     53:

>    54: ## Command Interface

     56: The SPI_HOST command interface defines a **segment** as a compounding bus operation where the IP performs a simpler, repetitive action over a fixed number of bytes.
     57: This allows software to specify any number of command *segments* to build larger, more complex transactions.

    200: 
    201: The [`CSID`](registers.md#csid) register is used to identify the target device for the next command segment.
    202: Whenever a command segment descriptor is written to [`COMMAND`](registers.md#command), [`CSID`](registers.md#csid) is passed into the FSM along with the command segment descriptor and the corresponding configurations options (taken from the CSID'th element of the `CONFIGOPTS` multi-register).
    203:

sections.label: Configuration Options
sections.snippet:
209: The previous `CSB` line is held low for *at least* `CSNTRAIL` cycles (as defined by the previous value of [`CONFIGOPTS.CSNTRAIL`](registers.md#configopts)) and then brought high.
    210: All `CSB` lines are held high for `CSNIDLE` cycles (using the new value of [`CONFIGOPTS.CSNIDLE`](registers.md#configopts)).
    211: The new `CSB` line is asserted low, and `SCK` begins toggling after the usual `CSNLEAD` cycle delay.
    212: 
>   213: ### Configuration Options
    214: 
    215: Before starting a command, some common configuration for the target device must be setup.
    216: Each target device attached to a chip-select can have an independent set of configuration parameters to match it's specific needs.
    217: When starting a command, the value of [`CSID`](registers.md#csid) is used to select the correct set of configuration parameters.

sections.label: Clock rate selection
sections.snippet:
222: The following sections give details on how the SPI_HOST IP can be used to control a specific peripheral.
    223: For simplicity, this section describes how to interact one device, attached to `CSB[0]`, and as such references are made to the multi-registers [`CONFIGOPTS`](registers.md#configopts) and [`COMMAND`](registers.md#command).
    224: To configure timing and send commands to devices on other `CSB` lines, instead use the `CONFIGOPTS` multi-register corresponding to desired `CSB` line.
    225: 
>   226: #### Clock rate selection
    227: 
    228: The SPI clock rate for each peripheral is set by two factors:
    229: - The SPI_HOST input clock
    230: - A 16-bit clock divider ([`CONFIGOPTS.CLKDIV`](#configopts--clkdiv))

sections.label: Chip-select Timing Control
sections.snippet:
236: This is configured per-peripheral by setting the field [`CONFIGOPTS.CLKDIV`](#configopts--clkdiv).
    237: 
    238: $$T_{\textrm{SCK},0}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{T_\textrm{clk}}{\textrm{CONFIGOPTS.CLKDIV}+1}$$
    239: 
>   240: #### Chip-select Timing Control
    241: 
    242: Typically the `CSB` line is automatically deasserted after the last edge of `SCK`.
    243: However, by asserting [`COMMAND.CSAAT`](registers.md#command) when issuing a particular command, one can instruct the core to hold `CSB` low indefinitely after the last clock edge.
    244: This is useful for merging two adjacent command segments together, to create more complex commands, such as flash Quad read commands which require a mix of segments with different speeds and directions.

>    12: # Overview
     13: 
     14: This document specifies the functionality of the SRAM memory controller.
     15: The SRAM controller is a module that is a peripheral on the chip interconnect bus, and thus follows the [Comportability Specification](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md).
     16:

sections.label: Features
sections.snippet:
16: 
     17: 
     18: The SRAM controller contains the SRAM data and address scrambling device and provides CSRs for requesting the scrambling keys and triggering the hardware initialization feature.
     19: 
>    20: ## Features
     21: 
     22: - [Lightweight scrambling mechanism](../prim/doc/prim_ram_1p_scr.md#custom-substitution-permutation-network) based on the PRINCE cipher.
     23: - Key request logic for the lightweight memory and address scrambling device.
     24: - Alert sender and checking logic for detecting bus integrity failures.

sections.label: Interfaces to OTP and the SRAM Scrambling Primitive
sections.snippet:
85: `sram_otp_key_i`           | `input`          | `otp_ctrl_pkg::sram_otp_key_rsp_t` | Ephemeral scrambling key coming back from the key derivation interface of the OTP controller.
     86: `otp_en_sram_ifetch_i`     | `input`          | `otp_ctrl_pkg::mubi8_t`            | Multibit value coming from the OTP HW_CFG partition EN_SRAM_IFETCH, set to kMuBi8True in order to enable the [`EXEC`](../data/sram_ctrl.hjson#exec) CSR. For example, see earlgrey's [OTP Field Descriptions](../../../top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/otp_ctrl/doc/programmers_guide.md#otp-field-descriptions))
     87: `cfg_i`                    | `input`          | `logic [CfgWidth-1:0]`             | Attributes for physical memory macro.
     88: 
>    89: ### Interfaces to OTP and the SRAM Scrambling Primitive
     90: 
     91: The interface to the key derivation interface inside the OTP controller follows a simple req / ack protocol, where the SRAM controller first requests an updated ephemeral key by asserting the `sram_otp_key_i.req`.
     92: The OTP controller then fetches entropy from CSRNG and derives an ephemeral key using the SRAM_DATA_KEY_SEED and the PRESENT scrambling data path as described in the earlgrey's [OTP controller spec](../../../top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/otp_ctrl/README.md#scrambling-datapath) for example.
     93: Finally, the OTP controller returns a fresh ephemeral key via the response channels (`sram_otp_key_o[*]`, `otbn_otp_key_o`), which complete the req / ack handshake.

sections.label: Global and Local Escalation
sections.snippet:
122: Note that the key and nonce output signals on the OTP controller side are guaranteed to remain stable for at least 62 OTP clock cycles after the `ack` signal is pulsed high, because the derivation of a 64bit half-key takes at least two passes through the 31-cycle PRESENT primitive.
    123: Hence, if the SRAM controller clock `clk_i` is faster or in the same order of magnitude as `clk_otp_i`, the data can be directly sampled upon assertion of `src_ack_o`.
    124: If the SRAM controller runs on a significantly slower clock than OTP, an additional register (as indicated with dashed grey lines in the figure) has to be added.
    125: 
>   126: ### Global and Local Escalation
    127: 
    128: If `lc_escalate_en_i` is set to any different value than `lc_ctrl_pkg::Off`, the current scrambling keys are discarded and reset to `RndCnstSramKey` and `RndCnstSramNonce` in the subsequent cycle.
    129: Any subsequent memory request to `prim_ram_1p_scr` will then be blocked as well.
    130: This mechanism is part of the [life cycle](../../lc_ctrl/README.md) state scrapping and secret wiping countermeasure triggered by the alert handler (global escalation).

1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
>     3: ## Block Diagram
      4: 
      5: ![SRAM Controller Block Diagram](../doc/sram_ctrl_blockdiag.svg)
      6: 
      7: As shown in the block diagram above, the SRAM controller contains a TL-UL adapter, an initialization LFSR, the CSR node, key request logic and an instance of `prim_ram_1p_scr` that implements the actual scrambling mechanism.

sections.label: Scrambling Primitive
sections.snippet:
22: Note that TL-UL accesses to the memory that occur while a key request or hardware initialization is pending will be blocked until the request has completed.
     23: 
     24: The individual mechanisms are explained in more detail in the subsections below.
     25: 
>    26: ## Scrambling Primitive
     27: 
     28: As explained in [`prim_ram_1p_scr`](../../prim/doc/prim_ram_1p_scr.md) the scrambling mechanism employs a reduced-round PRINCE block cipher in CTR mode to scramble the data.
     29: 
     30: In order to break the linear address space, the CTR mode is augmented with an S&P network to non-linearly remap the SRAM address as shown in the block diagram above. The S&P network employed is similar to the one employed in PRESENT and is explained in more detail [here](../../prim/doc/prim_ram_1p_scr.md#custom-substitution-permutation-network).

sections.label: Integrity Error Handling
sections.snippet:
28: As explained in [`prim_ram_1p_scr`](../../prim/doc/prim_ram_1p_scr.md) the scrambling mechanism employs a reduced-round PRINCE block cipher in CTR mode to scramble the data.
     29: 
     30: In order to break the linear address space, the CTR mode is augmented with an S&P network to non-linearly remap the SRAM address as shown in the block diagram above. The S&P network employed is similar to the one employed in PRESENT and is explained in more detail [here](../../prim/doc/prim_ram_1p_scr.md#custom-substitution-permutation-network).
     31: 
>    32: ### Integrity Error Handling
     33: 
     34: When an integrity error is encountered, the `sram_ctrl` will latch the integrity error and send out a `fatal_bus_integ_error` until the next reset (the generation of the integrity error is determined by system integration).
     35: In addition, the latched error condition is fed into the `prim_ram_1p_scr` primitive via a dedicated input, causing the scrambling primitive to do the following:
     36: *  Reverse the nonce used during the address and CTR scrambling.

sections.label: LFSR Initialization Feature
sections.snippet:
37: *  Disallow any transaction (read or write) on the actual memory macro.
     38: 
     39: This behavior, combined with other top level defenses, forms a multi-layered defense when integrity errors are seen in the system.
     40: 
>    41: ### LFSR Initialization Feature
     42: 
     43: Since the scrambling device uses a block cipher in CTR mode, it is undesirable from a security perspective to initialize the memory with all zeros.
     44: Doing so would reveal the XOR keystream.
     45: To avoid this, the `sram_ctrl` contains an LFSR-based initialization mechanism that overwrites the entire memory with pseudorandom data.

sections.label: Code Execution from SRAM
sections.snippet:
53: 
     54: There is no limit on how often the initialization feature can be called, and hence it can also be used as a cheap SRAM wiping mechanism at runtime.
     55: Note however that the PRNG sequence does not have strong security guarantees, since it is produced using an LFSR.
     56: 
>    57: ### Code Execution from SRAM
     58: 
     59: The SRAM controller contains an access control mechanism for filtering instruction fetches from the processor.
     60: As illustrated below, an OTP switch EN_SRAM_IFETCH (for example, see earlgrey's [OTP memory map](../../../top_earlgrey/ip_autogen/otp_ctrl/README.md#direct-access-memory-map)) allows to either tie code execution from SRAM to the life cycle state via the HW_DEBUG_EN function (see [life cycle docs](../../lc_ctrl/README.md#hw_debug_en)), or it can be enabled / disabled via the [`EXEC`](registers.md#exec) CSR.
     61:

sections.label: Read and Write Sequencing
sections.snippet:
75: If the feature is turned off via the `InstrExec` parameter, the execute from SRAM feature is permanently disabled, and the status of the OTP switch, the life cycle state and the value of the EXEC register are irrelevant.
     76: 
     77: As an example, the `top_earlgrey` design only enables this feature on the main SRAM, and permanently disables it on the retention SRAM.
     78: 
>    79: ### Read and Write Sequencing
     80: 
     81: For timing reasons, the scrambling primitive instantiates a register halfway in the PRINCE block cipher.
     82: This means that the keystream block becomes available in the second request cycle, which naturally aligns with read operations since the SRAM memory latency is 1 clock cycle.

sections.label: ECC Error Handling and Correction
sections.snippet:
99: 
    100: Note that this has been implemented in this way to not overly complicate the design, and since it is assumed that sub-word write operations happen relatively infrequently.
    101: For full write throughput, a more elaborate write buffering scheme would be required.
    102: 
>   103: ### ECC Error Handling and Correction
    104: 
    105: This memory utilizes a SECDED ECC code stored alongside the data in the underlying memory primitive to enhance data integrity.
    106: Error correction for single-bit errors can be enabled by setting the top-level parameter `EccCorrection` to 1.
    107: When enabled and a correctable single-bit error is detected, the memory automatically corrects the data before providing it.

sections.label: Important Considerations
sections.snippet:
111: Regardless of whether an error is correctable or not, the `sram_rerror_o` output port signals its detection.
    112: This output also indicates whether the error was corrected (if correction is enabled) and provides the memory location where the error occurred.
    113: This information is valuable for system-level Reliability, Availability, and Serviceability (RAS) monitoring and management.
    114: 
>   115: #### Important Considerations
    116: 
    117: * Activating the single-bit correction mechanism slightly reduces the overall probability of detecting multi-bit errors compared to detection-only mode.
    118: * The correction process involves internal decoding and re-encoding steps, during which unencoded, non-redundant data exists temporarily on internal wires.
    119: * Dedicated DV support for this specific correction feature is not yet available.

>    11: # Overview
     12: 
     13: This document specifies the functionality of the System Reset Controller (`sysrst_ctrl`) that provides programmable hardware-level responses to trusted IOs and basic board-level reset sequencing capabilities.
     14: These capabilities include keyboard and button combination-triggered actions, reset stretching for system-level reset signals, and internal reset / wakeup requests that go to the OpenTitan reset and power manager blocks.
     15: This module conforms to the [Comportable guideline for peripheral functionality](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md).

>    74: ## Auto-block key outputs
     75: 
     76: Software can program the `sysrst_ctrl` block to override the output value of specific passthrough signals, depending on whether certain input signals are asserted or not.

     78: When `pwrb_in_i` is asserted, `key1_out_o` (row) should be overridden so that `sysrst_ctrl` can detect if `key0_in_i` (column) is Refresh.

>   150: ## EC and Power-on-reset
    151: 
    152: OpenTitan and EC will be reset together during power-on.
    153: When OpenTitan is in reset, `ec_rst_l_o` will be asserted (active low).
    154: The power-on-reset value of [`PIN_ALLOWED_CTL.EC_RST_L_1`](registers.md#pin_allowed_ctl) and [`PIN_OUT_CTL.EC_RST_L`](registers.md#pin_out_ctl) will guarantee that `ec_rst_l_o` remains asserted after OpenTitan reset is released.

>    20: ## Features
     21: 
     22: - 2-pin full duplex external interface
     23: - 8-bit data word, optional even or odd parity bit per byte
     24: - 1 stop bit

sections.label: Description
sections.snippet:
27: - Programmable baud rate
     28: - Interrupt for transmit empty, receive overflow, frame error, parity error, break error, receive
     29:   timeout
     30: 
>    31: ## Description
     32: 
     33: The UART module is a serial-to-parallel receive (RX) and parallel-to-serial
     34: (TX) full duplex design intended to communicate to an outside device, typically
     35: for basic terminal-style communication. It is programmed to run at a particular

sections.label: Compatibility
sections.snippet:
36: baud rate and contains only a transmit and receive signal to the outside world,
     37: i.e. no synchronizing clock. The programmable baud rate guarantees to be met up
     38: to 1Mbps.
     39: 
>    40: ## Compatibility
     41: 
     42: The OpenTitan UART is feature compatible to a specific implementation in [Chromium EC](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromiumos/platform/ec/+/refs/heads/cr50_stab/chip/g/uart.c).
     43: Additional features such as parity have been added.

sections.label: tx watermark / tx empty / rx watermark
sections.snippet:
164: 
    165: UART module has a few interrupts including general data flow interrupts
    166: and unexpected event interrupts.
    167: 
>   168: #### tx_watermark / tx_empty / rx_watermark
    169: If the TX FIFO level becomes smaller than the TX water mark level (configurable via [`FIFO_CTRL.TXILVL`](registers.md#fifo_ctrl--txilvl)), the `tx_watermark` interrupt is raised to inform SW.
    170: If the TX FIFO is empty, the `tx_empty` interrupt is raised to inform SW.
    171: If the RX FIFO level becomes greater than or equal to RX water mark level (configurable via [`FIFO_CTRL.RXILVL`](registers.md#fifo_ctrl--rxilvl)), the `rx_watermark` interrupt is raised to inform SW.
    172:

sections.label: tx done
sections.snippet:
173: Note that the watermark interrupts and the empty interrupt are level-based status interrupts.
    174: They will stay asserted for as long as the FIFO levels are in violation of the configured level and cannot be cleared by writing to the status register.
    175: This also means that `tx_watermark` and `tx_empty` start off in an asserted state (reset high).
    176: 
>   177: #### tx_done
    178: If TX FIFO becomes empty as part of transmit, the interrupt `tx_done` is asserted once the final byte has been transmitted.
    179: The transmitted contents may be garbage at this point as old FIFO contents will likely be transmitted.

>    11: # Overview
     12: 
     13: This document specifies the USB device hardware IP functionality.
     14: This IP block implements a Full-Speed device according to the [USB 2.0 specification.](https://www.usb.org/document-library/usb-20-specification)
     15: It is attached to the chip interconnect bus as a peripheral module and conforms to the [Comportable guideline for peripheral functionality.](../../../doc/contributing/hw/comportability/README.md)

32: Isochronous transfers larger than 64 bytes are currently not supported.

>    36: ## Description
     37: 
     38: The USB device module is a simple software-driven generic USB device interface for Full-Speed USB 2.0 operation.
     39: The IP includes the physical layer interface, the low level USB protocol and a packet buffer interface to the software.
     40: The physical layer interface features multiple transmit and receive paths to allow interfacing with a variety of USB PHYs or regular 3.3V IO pads for FPGA prototyping.

sections.label: Programmer's Guide
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
      3: ## Initialization
      4: 
      5: The basic hardware initialization is to (in any order) configure the physical interface for the implementation via the [`phy_config`](registers.md#phy_config) register, fill the Available Buffer FIFO, enable IN and OUT endpoints with ID 0 (this is the control endpoint that the host will use to configure the interface), enable reception of SETUP and OUT packets on OUT Endpoint 0, and enable any required interrupts.

sections.label: Initialization
sections.snippet:
1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
>     3: ## Initialization
      4: 
      5: The basic hardware initialization is to (in any order) configure the physical interface for the implementation via the [`phy_config`](registers.md#phy_config) register, fill the Available Buffer FIFO, enable IN and OUT endpoints with ID 0 (this is the control endpoint that the host will use to configure the interface), enable reception of SETUP and OUT packets on OUT Endpoint 0, and enable any required interrupts.
      6: Finally, the interface is enabled by setting the enable bit in the [`usbctrl`](registers.md#usbctrl) register.
      7: Setting this bit causes the USB device to assert the pullup on the D+ line, which is used by the host to detect the device.

sections.label: Buffers
sections.snippet:
16: In response to the Set Configuration request, software should set up the rest of the endpoints for that configuration, including configuring the flow control behavior for OUT endpoints via the [`set_nak_out`](registers.md#set_nak_out) register, configuring the endpoint type via the [`rxenable_setup`](registers.md#rxenable_setup) register (for a control endpoint) and the [`out_iso`](registers.md#out_iso) and [`in_iso`](registers.md#in_iso) registers (for isochronous OUT and IN endpoints, respectively).
     17: Finally, software should enable the configured endpoints via the [`ep_out_enable`](registers.md#ep_out_enable) and [`ep_in_enable`](registers.md#ep_in_enable) registers.
     18: The status stage of the Set Configuration request should not be allowed to complete until all endpoints are set up.
     19: 
>    20: ## Buffers
     21: 
     22: Software needs to manage the buffers in the packet buffer (2 kB SRAM).
     23: Each buffer can hold the maximum length packet for a Full-Speed interface (64 bytes).
     24: Other than for data movement, the management is most likely done based on their buffer ID which is a small integer between zero and (SRAM size in bytes)/(max packet size in bytes).

sections.label: Reception
sections.snippet:
36: Flow control (using NAKs) may be done on a per-endpoint basis using the [`rxenable_out`](registers.md#rxenable_out) register.
     37: If this does not indicate OUT packet reception is enabled, then any OUT packet will receive a NAK to request a retry later.
     38: This should only be done for short durations or the host may timeout the transaction.
     39: 
>    40: ## Reception
     41: 
     42: The host will send OUT or SETUP transactions when it wants to transfer data to the device.
     43: The data packets are directed to a particular endpoint, and the maximum packet size is set per-endpoint in its Endpoint Descriptor (this must be the same or smaller than the maximum packet size supported by the device).
     44: A pkt_received interrupt is raised whenever there are one or more packets in the Received Buffer FIFO.

sections.label: Transmission
sections.snippet:
53: It is important for software to collect received packets promptly so that there is always space available for the receipt of subsequent SETUP packets.
     54: The USB protocol specification does not provide a mechanism for signaling that the device is busy, so when a SETUP packet cannot be received it must be dropped.
     55: This can lead to the host faulting a Control Transfer in as little as 30us by retrying it twice in rapid succession.
     56: 
>    57: ## Transmission
     58: 
     59: Data is transferred to the host based on the host requesting a transfer with an IN transaction.
     60: The host will only generate IN requests if the endpoint is declared as an IN endpoint in its Endpoint Descriptor (note that two descriptors are needed if the same endpoint is used for both IN and OUT transfers).
     61: The Endpoint Descriptor also includes a description of the frequency the endpoint should be polled (for isochronous and interrupt endpoints).

sections.label: Stalling
sections.snippet:
69: Note that the [`configin`](registers.md#configin) for an endpoint is a single register, so no new data packet should be queued until the previous packet has been ACKed.
     70: If a SETUP transaction is received on a control endpoint that has a transmission pending, the hardware will **clear the rdy bit** and **set the pend bit** in the [`configin`](registers.md#configin) register of that endpoint.
     71: Software must remember the pending transmission and, after the Control transaction is complete, write it back to the [`configin`](registers.md#configin) register with the rdy bit set.
     72: 
>    73: ## Stalling
     74: 
     75: The [`out_stall`](registers.md#out_stall) and [`in_stall`](registers.md#in_stall) registers are used for endpoint stalling.
     76: There is one dedicated register per endpoint.
     77: Stalling is used to signal that the host should not retry a particular transmission or to signal certain error conditions (functional stall).

sections.label: Notification Interrupts
sections.snippet:
84: The hardware will then send a STALL response to all IN/OUT transactions until the next SETUP is received for this endpoint.
     85: Receiving the **SETUP token clears the [`in_stall`](registers.md#in_stall) and [`out_stall`](registers.md#out_stall) registers** for that endpoint.
     86: If either a control endpoint's [`set_nak_out`](registers.md#set_nak_out) bit is set or software has cleared the [`rxenable_out`](registers.md#rxenable_out) bit before this transfer began, the hardware will send NAKs to any IN/OUT requests until the software has decided what action to take for the new SETUP request.
     87: 
>    88: ## Notification Interrupts
     89: 
     90: The following usbdev interrupts should be regarded as notifications of events occurring on the USB and not as indications of failures.
     91: In accordance with the USB 2.0 protocol specification, usbdev performs error reporting, retrying and recovery automatically in the event of data corruptions and signal integrity issues.
     92:

sections.label: Performance and Diagnostic Event Counters
sections.snippet:
105: - link_out_err
    106: 
    107: Each of these interrupts may be useful during development but consideration should be given to whether the raising and handling of these interrupts is beneficial in production software, given that the usbdev hardware handles these events automatically.
    108: 
>   109: ## Performance and Diagnostic Event Counters
    110: 
    111: The usbdev IP block is required to perform a number of operations automatically in hardware without software intervention, because these actions are part of the error recovery and guaranteed delivery mechanisms of the USB. In particular, packets that suffer transmission issues are retried in a manner that would not necessarily be visible to software via the CSR interface. Such events may therefore be monitored through the use of these counters.
    112: 
    113: The counters may also be used to monitor whether software is meeting performance expectations by presenting IN side packets in a timely fashion for collection by the USB host. The four counters [`count_out`](registers.md#count_out), [`count_in`](registers.md#count_in), [`count_nodata_in`](registers.md#count_nodata_in) and [`count_errors`](registers.md#count_errors) all operate in the same manner, incrementing whenever one of the enabled events occurs on one of the enabled endpoints.

sections.label: Device Interface Functions DIFs
sections.snippet:
115: Software may issue a reset of any of these counters at any time and, because the counters have limited width, they should be monitored and reset at regular intervals when it is important to gather statistics over a longer time period, eg. when monitoring performance. The `frame` interrupt from the USB device itself, indicating the passing of bus frames, may be used for this purpose if desired. Since a new event may occur within the brief time interval between reading a counter and the action of resetting the counter, it is worth avoiding the reset if the counter reads as zero, particularly if the counter is being used to detect the presence of any unanticipated or infrequent event such as a decoding error.
    116: 
    117: Lastly, the counters have been designed to permit the set of enables to be changed at any instant, so by varying the per-endpoint enables and/or the per-event enables within the register over time, the four counters may be multiplexed to gather average statistics over a much larger number of data pipes and endpoints.
    118:

>    10: ## Clocking
     11: 
     12: The USB Full-Speed interface runs at a data rate of 12 Mbit/s.
     13: The interface runs at four times this bit rate and must be clocked from an accurate 48 MHz clock source.
     14: The USB specification for a Full-Speed device requires the average bit rate is 12 Mbps +/- 0.25%, so the clock needs to support maximum error of 2,500 ppm.

sections.label: USB Interface Pins
sections.snippet:
41: Any bus-related clock domain crossings must happen outside the core, except for the transition between the 48 MHz clock and the wake detection module's clock.
     42: The 48 MHz clock must be enabled to reach the registers in `usbdev`.
     43: 
     44: 
>    45: ## USB Interface Pins
     46: 
     47: Full-Speed USB uses a bidirectional serial interface as shown in Figure 7-24 of the [USB 2.0 Full-Speed specification](https://www.usb.org/document-library/usb-20-specification).
     48: For reasons of flexibility, this IP block features multiple transmit and receive paths for interfacing with various transceivers.

sections.label: Data Transmit
sections.snippet:
49: 
     50: The following sections describe how the various input/output signals relate to the USB interface pins for the different receive and transmit configurations.
     51: 
     52: 
>    53: ### Data Transmit
     54: 
     55: The IP block supports two different encodings, driving out on separate TX interfaces.
     56: The default encoding looks like the USB bus, with D+ and D- values driven on usb_dp_o and usb_dn_o pins.
     57: The alternate encoding uses usb_se0_o to indicate a single-ended zero (SE0), and usb_d_o encodes K/J (when usb_se0_o is low).

70: For TX data, these separate signals `cio_usb_dp_en_o` and `cio_usb_dn_en_o` all correspond to the same TX or output enable signal (`OE` in the USB spec).
     71: The other signals listed are of the "intersignal" variety, and they do not go directly to pads or have dedicated output enable signals.
     72: 
     73: 
>    74: ### Data Receive
     75: 
     76: The IP block supports recovery of the differential K and J symbols from the output of an external differential receiver or directly from the D+/D- pair.
     77: The RX mode can be selected to use a differential receiver's output by setting the `use_diff_rcvr` bit in [`phy_config`](registers.md#phy_config).
     78: The D+/D- pair is always used to detect the single-ended zero (SE0) state.

sections.label: USB Link State
sections.snippet:
112: To control the pullup on the D- line, this USB device features `usb_dn_pullup_o` signal.
    113: Of the two pullup signals `usb_dp_pullup_o` and `usb_dn_pullup_o`, only one can be enabled at any time.
    114: As this is a Full-Speed device, `usb_dp_pullup_o`, i.e., the pullup on D+ is used by default (`pinflip` equals zero).
    115: 
>   116: ## USB Link State
    117: 
    118: The USB link has a number of states.
    119: These are detected and reported in [`usbstat.link_state`](registers.md#usbstat) and state changes are reported using interrupts.
    120: The FSM implements a subset of the USB device state diagram shown in Figure 9-1 of the [USB 2.0 specification.](https://www.usb.org/document-library/usb-20-specification)

sections.label: USB Protocol Engine
sections.snippet:
137: |Link Resume| The link has been driven to a non-J state after being in Suspend. For the case of resuming to active link states, the end of resume signaling has occurred.|
    138: |Host Lost| Signaled using an interrupt if the link is active but a start of frame (SOF) packet has not been received from the host in 4 frames. The host is required to send a SOF packet every 1 ms. This is not an expected condition.|
    139: 
    140: 
>   141: ## USB Protocol Engine
    142: 
    143: The USB 2.0 Full-Speed Protocol Engine is provided by the common USB interface code and is, strictly speaking, not part of this USB device module.
    144: 
    145: At the lowest level of the USB stack the transmit bitstream is serialized, converted to non-return-to-zero inverted (NRZI) encoding with bit-stuffing and sent to the transmitter.

sections.label: Buffer Interface
sections.snippet:
151: This means the USB device module must accept or provide data when requested.
    152: The protocol engine may cancel a transaction because of a bad cyclic redundancy check (CRC) or request a retry if an acknowledgment (ACK) was not received.
    153: 
    154: 
>   155: ## Buffer Interface
    156: 
    157: A 2 kB SRAM is used as a packet buffer to hold data between the system and the USB interface.
    158: This is divided up into 32 buffers each containing 64 bytes.
    159: This is an asynchronous dual-port SRAM with software accessing from the bus clock domain and the USB interface accessing from the USB 48 MHz clock domain.

sections.label: Reception

158: This is divided up into 32 buffers each containing 64 bytes.
    159: This is an asynchronous dual-port SRAM with software accessing from the bus clock domain and the USB interface accessing from the USB 48 MHz clock domain.
    160: 
    161: 
>   162: ### Reception
    163: 
    164: Software provides buffers for packet reception through an 8-entry Available OUT Buffer FIFO and a 4-entry Available SETUP Buffer FIFO.
    165: The [`rxenable_out`](registers.md#rxenable_out) and [`rxenable_setup`](registers.md#rxenable_setup) registers is used to indicate which endpoints will accept data from the host using OUT or SETUP transactions, respectively.
    166: When a packet is transferred from the host to the device (using an OUT or SETUP transaction) and reception of that type of transaction is enabled for the requested endpoint, the next buffer ID is pulled from the appropriate Available Buffer FIFO.

>   113: ## Fast-track Alerts
    114: 
    115: Note that it is possible to program a certain class to provide a fast-track response for critical alerts by setting its accumulation trigger value to 1, and configuring the escalation protocol such that the appropriate escalation measure is triggered within escalation phase 0.
    116: This results in a minimal escalation latency of 4 clock cycles from alert sender input to escalation receiver output in the case where all involved signaling modules are completely synchronous with the alert handler.
    117: In case the alert sender is asynchronous w.r.t. to the alert handler, the actual latency depends on the clock periods involved.

>     6: ## Transactional Clock Hints
      7: 
      8: To enable a transactional clock, set the corresponding hint in [`CLK_HINTS`](registers.md#clk_hints) to `1`.
      9: To disable a transactional clock, set the corresponding hint in [`CLK_HINTS`](registers.md#clk_hints) to `0`.
     10: Note, a `0` does not indicate clock is actually disabled, software can thus check [`CLK_HINTS_STATUS`](registers.md#clk_hints_status) for the actual state of the clock.

15: In this situation, the read FIFO will fill up (or hit programmable fill value), pause the flash read and trigger an interrupt to software.
     16: Once there is space inside the FIFO, the controller will resume reading until the appropriate number of words have been read.
     17: Once the total count has been reached, the flash controller will post OP_DONE in the [`OP_STATUS`](registers.md#op_status) register.
     18: 
>    19: ## Issuing a Controller Program
     20: 
     21: To program flash, the same procedure as read is followed.
     22: However, instead of setting the [`CONTROL`](registers.md#control) register for read operation, a program operation is selected instead.
     23: Software will then fill the program FIFO and wait for the controller to consume this data.

sections.label: Debugging a Read Error

23: Software will then fill the program FIFO and wait for the controller to consume this data.
     24: Similar to the read case, the controller will automatically stall when there is insufficient data in the FIFO.
     25: When all desired words have been programmed, the controller will post OP_DONE in the [`OP_STATUS`](registers.md#op_status) register.
     26: 
>    27: ## Debugging a Read Error
     28: Since flash has multiple access modes, debugging read errors can be complicated.
