sections.label: Simple Address Translation
sections.snippet:
1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
>     3: ## Simple Address Translation
      4: 
      5: The wrapper supports a simple address translation scheme.
      6: The goal of the scheme is to provide hardware support for A/B software copies.
      7:

sections.label: Translation and Instruction Caching
sections.snippet:
22: If a transaction matches multiple regions, the lowest indexed region has priority.
     23: 
     24: For details on how to program the related registers, please see [`IBUS_ADDR_MATCHING_0`](registers.md#ibus_addr_matching) and [`IBUS_REMAP_ADDR_0`](registers.md#ibus_remap_addr).
     25: 
>    26: ### Translation and Instruction Caching
     27: 
     28: The simple address translation scheme used in this design is not aware of the processor context, specifically, any instruction caching done in the core.
     29: This means if the address translation scheme were to change, instructions that are already cached may not reflect the updated address setting.
     30:

sections.label: Random Number Generation
sections.snippet:
30: 
     31: In order to correctly utilize simple address translation along with instruction caching, it is recommended that after the address is updated a `FENCE.I` instruction is issued.
     32: The `FENCE.I` instruction forces the instruction cache to flush, and this aligns the core to the new address setting.
     33: 
>    34: ## Random Number Generation
     35: 
     36: The wrapper has a connection to the [Entropy Distribution Network (EDN)](../../../../ip/edn/README.md) with a register based interface.
     37: The [`RND_DATA`](registers.md#rnd_data) register provides 32-bits directly from the EDN.
     38: [`RND_STATUS.RND_DATA_VALID`](registers.md#rnd_status) indicates if the data in [`RND_DATA`](registers.md#rnd_data) is valid or not.

sections.label: Crash Dump Collection
sections.snippet:
47: Software should take care not to enable the EDN until the entropy complex configuration is as desired.
     48: When the entropy complex configuration is changed reading [`RND_DATA`](registers.md#rnd_data) when it is valid will suffice to flush any old random data to trigger a new request under the new configuration.
     49: If a EDN request is pending when the entropy complex configuration is changed ([`RND_STATUS.RND_DATA_VALID`](registers.md#rnd_status) is clear), it is advisable to wait until it is complete and then flush out the data to ensure the fresh value was produced under the new configuration.
     50: 
>    51: ## Crash Dump Collection
     52: 
     53: In general, when the CPU encounters an error, it is software's responsibility to collect error status and supply it for debug.
     54: 
     55: However, there are situations where it may not be possible for software to collect any error logging.

sections.label: Hung Transaction
sections.snippet:
80: This allows the software to see both fault locations and debug accordingly.
     81: 
     82: In terms of how the crash state information can be used, the following are a few examples.
     83: 
>    84: ### Hung Transaction
     85: 
     86: Assuming the system has a watchdog counter setup, when a CPU transaction hangs the bus (accessing a device whose clock is not turned on or is under reset), the PC and bus access freeze in place until the watchdog resets the system.
     87: Upon reset release, software can check the last PC and data access address to get an idea of what transaction might have caused the bus to hang.
     88:

>    89: ### Double Exception
     90: 
     91: If the software has some kind of error and encounters two exceptions in a row, the previous exception PC and address show the location of the first exception, while the current exception address and PC show the location of the most recent exception.

>    94: ## Fetch Enable
     95: 
     96: Ibex has a top-level fetch enable input (``fetch_enable_i``), which uses the same multi-bit encoding used by the lifecycle controller.
     97: When Ibex fetch is disabled it will cease to execute, but will complete instructions currently in the pipeline.
     98: Ibex fetch is enabled when all of the following conditions are met:

sections.label: Local Escalation Path
sections.snippet:
99:   - The lifecycle controller has enabled it
    100:   - The power manager has enabled it
    101:   - A ``fatal_hw_err`` alert hasn't been raised
    102: 
>   103: ### Local Escalation Path
    104: 
    105: When the ``fatal_hw_err`` alert is raised Ibex fetch is disabled and will remain disabled until ``rv_core_ibex`` is reset.

35: #### RV_PLIC assertions
     36: The file `rv_plic_bind.sv` binds the `rv_plic_assert` under `rv_plic_assert.sv`.
     37: The assertion file ensures RV_PLIC's outputs (`irq_o` and `irq_id_o`) and important signals (`ip`) are being asserted.
     38: 
>    39: ##### Symbolic variables
     40: Due to there are large number of input interrupt sources, the symbolic variable
     41: is used to reduce the number of repeated assertions code. In RV_PLIC, we
     42: declared two symbolic variables `src_sel` and `tgt_sel` to represent the index for
     43: interrupt source and interrupt target.

>    48: #### AST Clocking and Reset Relationship
     49: 
     50: While the ast supplies clocks and resets to the `top_earlgrey`, it also contains additional functions that interact with the design.
     51: These include the `RNG`, `ADC`, jittery clock controls and an assortment of other sensors.

>    76: ### System Reset Handling and Flash
     77: 
     78: Since `top_earlgrey` contains flash, it is important to examine the memory's relationship with resets.
     79: 
     80: For flash, resets that occur during a stateful operation (program or erase) must be carefully handled to ensure the flash memory is not damaged.

sections.label: Reset due to External Supply
sections.snippet:

>    87: #### Reset due to External Supply
     88: 
     89: Device resets due to supply dropping below a specific threshold are commonly known as "brown-out".
     90: When this occurs, the flash memory must go through specialized sequencing to ensure the cells are not damaged.
     91: This process is handled exclusively between ast and the flash.

sections.label: Reset due to Internal Request

90: When this occurs, the flash memory must go through specialized sequencing to ensure the cells are not damaged.
     91: This process is handled exclusively between ast and the flash.
     92: Please see the [relevant section](../../ip/ast/README.md#main-vcc-power-detection-and-flash-protection) for more details.
     93: 
>    94: #### Reset due to Internal Request
     95: 
     96: When the device receives an internal request to reset (for example [aon_timer](../../../ip/aon_timer/README.md#aon-watchdog-timer)), device power is kept on and the flash is directly reset.
     97: It is assumed that the flash device, when powered, will be able to correctly handle such a sequence and properly protect itself.

>   104: ### Main processor (`core_ibex`)
    105: 
    106: The main processor (`core_ibex`) is a small and efficient, 32-bit, in-order RISC-V core with a 2-stage pipeline that implements the RV32IMC instruction set architecture.
    107: It was initially developed as part of the [PULP platform](https://www.pulp-platform.org) under the name "Zero-riscy" [\[1\]](https://doi.org/10.1109/PATMOS.2017.8106976), and has been contributed to [lowRISC](https://www.lowrisc.org) who maintains it and develops it further.
    108: See the [core_ibex specification](https://ibex-core.readthedocs.io/en/latest/) for more details of the core.

      2: 
      3: Each available alert has a corresponding fatality configuration.

      5: Fatal events are not acknowledged, and continuously send alert events in the system until some kind of escalation is seen.

sections.label: Recoverable and Fatal Alerts
sections.snippet:
3: ## Block Diagram
      4: 
      5: The diagram below shows how `sensor control` helps `analog sensor top` integration into the overall design.
      6: 
>     7: ## Recoverable and Fatal Alerts
      8: 
      9: The `analog sensor top` sends alert requests in independent, differential form to the `sensor control`.
     10: Each alert request consists of a pair of signals, one active high and one active low.
     11: The active polarity of each signal is independent, due to the imprecise sensor timing that drives the alert.

sections.label: Wakeup Requests
sections.snippet:
22: 
     23: If set to fatal, an alert will be registered in [`FATAL_ALERT`](registers.md#fatal_alert) but the original `analog sensor top` event will not be acknowledged.
     24: This causes the alert to constantly send until the system escalates in some form.
     25: 
>    26: ## Wakeup Requests
     27: 
     28: In addition to forwarding events to the `alert handler`, incoming events can also be aggregated into a wakeup request to the system.
     29: The `sensor control` does not make assumptions about its power domains and thus it is up to the integrating system to decide which power modes allow alert event wakeups.
     30:

>   113: ## Fast-track Alerts
    114: 
    115: Note that it is possible to program a certain class to provide a fast-track response for critical alerts by setting its accumulation trigger value to 1, and configuring the escalation protocol such that the appropriate escalation measure is triggered within escalation phase 0.
    116: This results in a minimal escalation latency of 4 clock cycles from alert sender input to escalation receiver output in the case where all involved signaling modules are completely synchronous with the alert handler.
    117: In case the alert sender is asynchronous w.r.t. to the alert handler, the actual latency depends on the clock periods involved.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: Clock management in OpenTitan is divided into groups.
      4: Each group has specific attributes and controls whether software is allowed to influence individual clocks during the active power state.
      5: For low power states, please see [power manager](../../pwrmgr/README.md).

sections.label: Power-up Clock Group
sections.snippet:
28: * 1 - Transactional clock group's software control is only a software hint.
     29: * 2 - Transactional clock group's wait-for-interrupt control is only a hint.
     30: * 3 - May require additional complexity to handle multi-host (non-wait-for-interrupt) scenarios
     31: 
>    32: ## Power-up Clock Group
     33: 
     34: The group refers to modules responsible for power up, such as power, reset and clock managers.
     35: Large portions of these modules operate to release clocks and resets for the rest of the design, thus cannot operate on gated versions of the clocks themselves.
     36: They are the only group running clocks directly from the source.

sections.label: Transactional Clock Group
sections.snippet:
36: They are the only group running clocks directly from the source.
     37: All follow groups are derived after root clock gating.
     38: See [block diagram](#block-diagram) for more details.
     39: 
>    40: ## Transactional Clock Group
     41: 
     42: This group refers to the collection of modules that are transactional by nature (example: `Hmac` / `Aes` / `Kmac`).
     43: This means these modules perform specific tasks (for example encrypt, decrypt or hashing).
     44: While performing these tasks, it is unsafe to manipulate or change the clocks.

sections.label: Infrastructure Clock Group
sections.snippet:
57: 
     58: For modules in this group, each module can be individually influenced, and thus each has its own dedicated clock gating logic.
     59: The added benefit of allowing software control in this group is to save power, as some transactional modules can be both power and area hungry.
     60: 
>    61: ## Infrastructure Clock Group
     62: 
     63: This group refers to the collection of modules that support infrastructure functions.
     64: 
     65: If the clocks to these modules are turned off, there may not be a way to turn them back on and could thus result in system deadlock.

sections.label: Security Clock Group
sections.snippet:
70: For this group, there is no reason to allow software control over the clocks, as it could be used to create a system deadlock where after disabling infrastructure clocks there is no way to turn them back on.
     71: Wait-for-interrupt controls however can be used, as long as there is a way to break the processor out of wait-for-interrupt and handle other bus hosts, while also separating the functional portions from bus access.
     72: See Wait-for-interrupt clock gating for more details.
     73: 
>    74: ## Security Clock Group
     75: 
     76: The security clock group is made up of security modules that either have background functions (entropy, alert manager, sensors) or perform critical security functions where disabling clocks could have unexpected side effects (life cycle, otp, pinmux, plic).
     77: 
     78: For this group, no software influence over the clock state is allowed during the active state.

sections.label: Timer Clock Group
sections.snippet:
80: 
     81: This group is not functionally identical to the power-up group.
     82: The power-up group is run on clocks directly from the clock source, while the security group is derived after root clock gating.
     83: 
>    84: ## Timer Clock Group
     85: 
     86: The timer clock group is composed of modules that track time for various purposes.
     87: As influencing time can change the perspective of software and potentially reveal security vulnerabilities, the clock state for these modules cannot be directly or indirectly influenced by software.
     88:

sections.label: Peripheral Clock Group
sections.snippet:
87: As influencing time can change the perspective of software and potentially reveal security vulnerabilities, the clock state for these modules cannot be directly or indirectly influenced by software.
     88: 
     89: Functionally, this group is identical to the security group.
     90: 
>    91: ## Peripheral Clock Group
     92: 
     93: The peripheral clock group is composed of I/O peripherals modules.
     94: By their nature, I/O peripherals are both transactional and most of the time not security critical - so long as proper care is taken to sandbox peripherals from the system.
     95:

sections.label: Wait-for-Interrupt wfi Gating
sections.snippet:
95: 
     96: These modules can be both directly and indirectly controlled by software.
     97: The controls can also be individual to each peripheral.
     98: 
>    99: ## Wait-for-Interrupt (wfi) Gating
    100: 
    101: Wait-for-interrupt clock gating refers to the mechanism of using a processor's sleep indication to actively gate off module clocks.
    102: Of the groups enumerated, only transactional, infrastructural and peripheral groups can be influenced by `wfi`.
    103:

sections.label: Infrastructural Clock Group
sections.snippet:
118: In this scenario, it is important to ensure the functional clocks are responsible for creating interrupts and not the bus clocks, as the latter may not be available during `wfi`.
    119: 
    120: This division may only be beneficial for peripherals where register and local fabric size is large relative to the functional component.
    121: 
>   122: ### Infrastructural Clock Group
    123: 
    124: This clock group matches `wfi` functionality well.
    125: Most infrastructural components such as fabric, gaskets and memories, have no need to be clocked when the processor is idle.
    126: Some components such as flash controller however would also need to be split into bus and functional halves to support long, background activities while the processor is idle.

sections.label: Block Diagram

132: The bus requests themselves thus become dynamic clock request signals to help enable components in its path.
    133: 
    134: There is thus a moderate design and high verification cost to supporting `wfi` gating for the infrastructural group.

>    19: ## Issuing a Controller Program
     20: 
     21: To program flash, the same procedure as read is followed.
     22: However, instead of setting the [`CONTROL`](registers.md#control) register for read operation, a program operation is selected instead.
     23: Software will then fill the program FIFO and wait for the controller to consume this data.

     28: Since flash has multiple access modes, debugging read errors can be complicated.
     29: The following lays out the expected cases.

>    31: ### Error Encountered by Software Direct Read
     32: If software reads the flash directly, it may encounter a variety of errors (read data integrity / ECC failures, both reliability and integrity).
     33: ECC failures create in-band error responses and should be recognized as a bus exception.
     34: Read data integrity failures also create exceptions directly inside the processor as part of end-to-end transmission integrity.
     35:

sections.label: Error Encountered by Software Initiated Controller Operations
sections.snippet:
35: 
     36: From these exceptions, software should be able to determine the error address through processor specific means.
     37: Once the address is discovered, further steps can be taken to triage the issue.
     38: 
>    39: ### Error Encountered by Software Initiated Controller Operations
     40: A controller operation can encounter a much greater variety of errors, see [`ERR_CODE`](registers.md#err_code).
     41: When such an error is encountered, as reflected by [`OP_STATUS`](registers.md#op_status) when the operation is complete, software can examine the [`ERR_ADDR`](registers.md#err_addr) to determine the error location.
     42: Once the address is discovered, further steps can be taken to triage the issue.

sections.label: Hardware Initiated Reads
sections.snippet:
40: A controller operation can encounter a much greater variety of errors, see [`ERR_CODE`](registers.md#err_code).
     41: When such an error is encountered, as reflected by [`OP_STATUS`](registers.md#op_status) when the operation is complete, software can examine the [`ERR_ADDR`](registers.md#err_addr) to determine the error location.
     42: Once the address is discovered, further steps can be taken to triage the issue.
     43: 
>    44: ### Hardware Initiated Reads
     45: 
     46: If the root secrets have been provisioned and the life cycle state is in either DEV, PROD* or RMA, the special info pages holding the creator and owner seeds will be read out automatically by the flash controller and sent to the keymanager upon flash initialization.
     47: Hence, it is important that these pages are initialized with valid data, since otherwise the hardware will likely encounter ECC errors during the automatic readout.
     48:

sections.label: Correctable ECC Errors
sections.snippet:
49: Note that by default, hardware assumes that scrambling and ECC is enabled on these special info pages.
     50: If software decides to not use scrambling or ECC on these partitions at the time of provisioning, software should disable these features in the [`HW_INFO_CFG_OVERRIDE`](registers.md#hw_info_cfg_override) register accordingly when initializing the flash controller.
     51: Otherwise, a configuration mismatch between hardware interface and the software side will lead to corrupted seed values and ECC errors upon automatic readout.
     52: 
>    53: ### Correctable ECC Errors
     54: Correctable ECC errors are by nature not fatal errors and do not stop operation.
     55: Instead, if the error is correctable, the flash controller fixes the issue and registers the last address where a single bit error was seen.
     56: See [`ECC_SINGLE_ERR_CNT`](registers.md#ecc_single_err_cnt) and [`ECC_SINGLE_ERR_ADDR`](registers.md#ecc_single_err_addr)
     57:

sections.label: Errors during Multi-Word Controller Reads
sections.snippet:
54: Correctable ECC errors are by nature not fatal errors and do not stop operation.

     57: 
>    58: ### Errors during Multi-Word Controller Reads
     59: 
     60: Note that upon experiencing the first error during any multi-word read operation, the flash controller aborts the internal read operation but still returns the requested amount of data.
     61: For the word where the read error has been observed, the actual flash data is returned.
     62: For subsequent words, the flash controller may return:

sections.label: Granularity of Scrambling and Reliability ECC
sections.snippet:
64: - An all-zero word in case of a flash read error (e.g. reliability ECC and ICV errors) and if the flash read pipeline remains idle.
     65: - The data belonging to other read operations in case of a flash read error and if the flash read pipeline continues doing, e.g., host initiated read operations.
     66:   In this case, the data returned for the subsequent words may contain further ECC and ICV errors.
     67: 
>    68: ## Granularity of Scrambling and Reliability ECC
     69: 
     70: While the minimum granularity for host and controller interface accesses is 32 bits, the scrambling as well as reliability ECC operate on full Flash words (64 bits).
     71: Whenever reliability ECC and/or scrambling are enabled, read, program and erase operations should thus be based on 64-bit aligned addresses.

>     7: ### Flash Protocol Controller
      8: 
      9: The Flash Protocol Controller sits between the host software interface, other hardware components and the flash physical controller.
     10: Its primary functions are two fold
     11: *  Translate software program, erase and read requests into a high level protocol for the actual flash physical controller

sections.label: RMA Entry Handling
sections.snippet:
23: 
     24: Once the seed phase is complete, the flash controller switches to the software interface.
     25: Software can then read / program / erase the flash as needed.
     26: 
>    27: #### RMA Entry Handling
     28: 
     29: When an RMA entry request is received from the life cycle manager, the flash controller waits for any pending flash transaction to complete, then switches priority to the hardware interface.
     30: The flash controller then initiates RMA entry process and notifies the life cycle controller when it is complete.
     31: The RMA entry process wipes out all data, creator, owner and isolated partitions.

sections.label: Initialization
sections.snippet:
35: However, flash memory access are not allowed, either directly by the host or indirectly through flash protocol controller initiated transactions.
     36: It is expected that after an RMA transition, the entire system will be rebooted.
     37: 
     38: 
>    39: #### Initialization
     40: 
     41: The flash protocol controller is initialized through [`INIT`](registers.md#init).
     42: When initialization is invoked, the flash controller requests the address and data scrambling keys from an external source, for example the otp controller.
     43:

sections.label: RMA Entry
sections.snippet:
43: 
     44: After the scrambling keys are requested, the flash protocol controller reads the root seeds out of the [secret partitions](#secret-information-partitions) and sends them to the key manager.
     45: Once the above steps are completed, the read buffers in the flash physical controller are enabled for operation.
     46: 
>    47: #### RMA Entry
     48: During RMA entry, the flash controller "wipes" the contents of the following:
     49: - Creator partition
     50: - Owner partition
     51: - Isolated partition

sections.label: Memory Protection
sections.snippet:
54: This process ensures that after RMA there is no sensitive information left that can be made use on the tester.
     55: As stated previously, once RMA entry completes, the flash memory can no longer be accessed, either directly or indirectly.
     56: The flash controller registers however, remain accessible for status reads and so forth, although new operations cannot be issued.
     57: 
>    58: #### Memory Protection
     59: 
     60: Flash memory protection is handled differently depending on what type of partition is accessed.
     61: 
     62: For data partitions, software can configure a number of memory protection regions such as [`MP_REGION_CFG_0`](registers.md#mp_region_cfg).

sections.label: Bank Erase Protection
sections.snippet:
71: Each page can be configured with access privileges.
     72: As a result, software does not need to define a start and end page for information partitions.
     73: See [`BANK0_INFO0_PAGE_CFG_0`](registers.md#bank0_info0_page_cfg) as an example.
     74: 
>    75: #### Bank Erase Protection
     76: 
     77: Unlike read, program and page erase operations, the bank erase command is the only one that can be issued at a bank level.
     78: Because of this, bank erase commands are not guarded by the typical [memory protection mechanisms](#memory-protection).
     79:

sections.label: Memory Protection for Key Manager and Life Cycle
sections.snippet:

     83: The specific behavior of what is erased when bank erase is issued is flash memory dependent and thus can vary by vendor and technology.
     84: [This section](#flash-bank-erase-behavior) describes the general behavior and how open source modeling is done.
     85: 
>    86: #### Memory Protection for Key Manager and Life Cycle
     87: 
     88: While memory protection is largely under software control, certain behavior is hardwired to support key manager secret partitions and life cycle functions.
     89:

sections.label: Program Resolution
sections.snippet:
96: 
     97: During life cycle RMA transition, the software configured memory protection for both data and information partitions is ignored.
     98: Instead, the flash controller assumes a default accessibility setting that allows it to secure the chip and transition to RMA.
     99: 
>   100: #### Program Resolution
    101: 
    102: Certain flash memories place restrictions on the program window.
    103: This means the flash accepts program beats only if all beats belong to the same address window.
    104: Typically, this boundary is nicely aligned (for example, 16 words, 32 words) and is related to how the flash memory amortizes the program operation over nearby words.

     10:   It supports up to 32 GPIO ports and each of these ports can be written as peripheral outputs in two modes: either with direct access to each GPIO value using direct write, allowing software to control all GPIO ports simultaneously, or with masked writes to half of the bits at a time, allowing software to affect the output value of a subset of the bits without requiring a read-modify-write.
     11:   In the input direction, software can read the contents of any of the GPIO peripheral inputs, and it can request the detection of an interrupt event for any of the 32 bits in a configurable manner for detecting rising edge, falling edge, or active low/high input.
     12:   A noise filter is available through configuration for any of the inputs.

     73: if the noise filter is enabled).
     74: 
>    75: #### GPIO Inputs as HW Straps
     76: 
     77: The GPIO controller provides an optional feature to sample GPIO input values as hardware configuration straps.
     78: After each reset, on the first cycle when the `strap_en_i` signal is asserted, the GPIO detects its transition from low to high.
     79: One clock cycle later, it samples the GPIO input values and stores them in the `HW_STRAPS_DATA_IN` register.

sections.label: EDN Interface
sections.snippet:
113: <!-- END CMDGEN -->
    114: 
    115: The OTP controller contains various interfaces that connect to other comportable IPs within OpenTitan, and these are briefly explained further below.
    116: 
>   117: ### EDN Interface
    118: 
    119: The entropy request interface that talks to EDN in order to fetch fresh entropy for ephemeral SRAM scrambling key derivation and the LFSR counters for background checks.
    120: It is comprised of the `otp_edn_o` and `otp_edn_i` signals and follows a req / ack protocol.
    121:

sections.label: Power Manager Interface
sections.snippet:
120: It is comprised of the `otp_edn_o` and `otp_edn_i` signals and follows a req / ack protocol.
    121: 
    122: See also [EDN documentation](../../../../ip/edn/README.md).
    123: 
>   124: ### Power Manager Interface
    125: 
    126: The power manager interface is comprised of three signals overall: an initialization request (`pwr_otp_i.otp_init`), an initialization done response (`pwr_otp_o.otp_done`) and an idle indicator (`pwr_otp_o.otp_idle`).
    127: 
    128: The power manager asserts `pwr_otp_i.otp_init` in order to signal to the OTP controller that it can start initialization, and the OTP controller signals completion of the initialization sequence by asserting `pwr_otp_o.otp_done` (the signal will remain high until reset).

sections.label: Life Cycle Interfaces
sections.snippet:
133: The power manager is responsible for synchronizing the `pwr_otp_o.otp_done` and `pwr_otp_o.otp_idle` signals.
    134: 
    135: See also [power manager documentation](../../pwrmgr/README.md).
    136: 
>   137: ### Life Cycle Interfaces
    138: 
    139: The interface to the life cycle controller can be split into three functional sub-interfaces (vendor test, state output, state transitions), and these are explained in more detail below.
    140: Note that the OTP and life cycle controllers are supposed to be in the same clock domain, hence no additional signal synchronization is required.
    141: See also [life cycle controller documentation](../../../../ip/lc_ctrl/README.md) for more details.

sections.label: Vendor Test Signals
sections.snippet:
139: The interface to the life cycle controller can be split into three functional sub-interfaces (vendor test, state output, state transitions), and these are explained in more detail below.
    140: Note that the OTP and life cycle controllers are supposed to be in the same clock domain, hence no additional signal synchronization is required.
    141: See also [life cycle controller documentation](../../../../ip/lc_ctrl/README.md) for more details.
    142: 
>   143: #### Vendor Test Signals
    144: 
    145: The `lc_otp_vendor_test_i` and `lc_otp_vendor_test_o` signals are connected to a 32bit control and a 32bit status register in the life cycle TAP, respectively, and are directly routed to the `prim_otp` wrapper.
    146: These control and status signals may be used by the silicon creator to exercise the OTP programming smoke checks on the VENDOR_TEST partition.
    147: The signals are gated with the life cycle state inside the life cycle controller such that they do not have any effect in production life cycle states.

sections.label: Programmer's Guide
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
      3: During provisioning and manufacturing, SW interacts with the OTP controller mostly through the Direct Access Interface (DAI), which is described below.
      4: Afterwards during production, SW is expected to perform only read accesses via the exposed CSRs and CSR windows, since all write access to the partitions has been locked down.
      5:

sections.label: General Guidance
sections.snippet:
5: 
      6: The following sections provide some general guidance, followed by an explanation of the DAI and a detailed OTP memory map.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: Conceptually speaking, the OTP functionality is at a high level split into "front-end" and "back-end".
      4: The "front-end" contains the logical partitions that feed the hardware and software consumer interfaces of the system.
      5: The "back-end" represents the programming interface used by hardware and software components to stage the upcoming values.

sections.label: Calibration and Test
sections.snippet:
51: Generally speaking, the production life cycle of a device is split into 5 stages "Manufacturing" -> "Calibration and Testing" -> "Provisioning" -> "Mission" -> "RMA".
     52: OTP values are usually programmed during "Calibration and Testing", "Provisioning" and "RMA" stages, as explained below.
     53: A detailed listing of all the items and the corresponding memory map can be found in the [Programmer's Guide](programmers_guide.md).
     54: 
>    55: ### Calibration and Test
     56: 
     57: During this stage, the device is tested for functionality and calibrated to ensure uniformity.
     58: The calibration can focus on a number of things, but usually is centered around adjusting clock, voltage and timing sources to remove process variation.
     59: These calibration values are programmed into the CREATOR_SW_CFG partition, as they are non-secret values meant to be read out by software and programmed into respective peripherals.

sections.label: Provisioning
sections.snippet:
59: These calibration values are programmed into the CREATOR_SW_CFG partition, as they are non-secret values meant to be read out by software and programmed into respective peripherals.
     60: 
     61: Early on during this stage, the various tokens are also programmed into the secret partitions and harvested by the silicon creator.
     62: 
>    63: ### Provisioning
     64: 
     65: During this stage, the device is provisioned with the final firmware and a "unique" seed or identity.
     66: The secret partitions are populated with root secrets and keys that are critical to establishing the device identity.
     67:

sections.label: Life Cycle Partition
sections.snippet:
66: The secret partitions are populated with root secrets and keys that are critical to establishing the device identity.
     67: 
     68: As part of injecting the final firmware, the stock-keeping-unit-specific hardware and software configurations are also programmed.
     69: 
>    70: ### Life Cycle Partition
     71: 
     72: The life cycle partition is active throughout all stages and hence it is the **ONLY** partition that cannot be locked.
     73: After the device finishes provisioning and goes into production, it must retain the ability to transition back to RMA in case of unexpected failures.
     74:

sections.label: Locking a Partition
sections.snippet:
73: After the device finishes provisioning and goes into production, it must retain the ability to transition back to RMA in case of unexpected failures.
     74: 
     75: In order to support this transition, the [life cycle state](../../../../ip/lc_ctrl/README.md) and counters must always be update-able.
     76: 
>    77: ## Locking a Partition
     78: 
     79: Write access to a partition can be permanently locked when software determines it will no longer make any updates to that partition.
     80: To lock, an integrity constant is calculated and programmed alongside the other data of that partition.
     81: The size of that integrity constant depends on the partition size granule, and is either 32bit or 64bit.

sections.label: Vendor Test Partition
sections.snippet:
89: This gives software an opportunity to confirm that the locking operation has proceeded correctly, and if not, scrap the part immediately.
     90: 
     91: Calculation of the integrity digest depends on whether the partition requires periodic background verification.
     92: 
>    93: ### Vendor Test Partition
     94: 
     95: The vendor test partition is intended to be used for OTP programming smoke checks during the manufacturing flow.
     96: The silicon creator may implement these checks inside the proprietary version of the `otp_macro` wrapper.
     97: This partition behaves like any other SW partition, with the exception that ECC uncorrectable errors will not lead to fatal errors / alerts as they do in all other partitions.

sections.label: Software Configuration Partitions
sections.snippet:
96: The silicon creator may implement these checks inside the proprietary version of the `otp_macro` wrapper.
     97: This partition behaves like any other SW partition, with the exception that ECC uncorrectable errors will not lead to fatal errors / alerts as they do in all other partitions.
     98: This is due to the nature of the OTP programming smoke checks, which may leave certain OTP words in a state inconsistent with the ECC polynomial employed upon OTP readout.
     99: 
>   100: ### Software Configuration Partitions
    101: 
    102: The software configuration partitions are used as non-volatile storage for flags, configuration and calibration data.
    103: As such, the contents of this partition are usually consumed once as part of code execution, or moved to another storage compartment somewhere in the design.
    104: For example, the clock calibration values and the LDO calibration values are programmed to the analog sensor top (AST) at startup.

sections.label: Pad Attributes
sections.snippet:
1: # Programmer's Guide
      2: 
>     3: ## Pad Attributes
      4: 
      5: Software should determine and program the pad attributes at startup, or reprogram the attributes when the functionality requirements change at runtime.
      6: 
      7: This can be achieved by writing to the [`MIO_PAD_ATTR_0`](registers.md#mio_pad_attr) and [`DIO_PAD_ATTR_0`](registers.md#dio_pad_attr) registers.

sections.label: Pinmux Configuration
sections.snippet:
28: This behavior is also referred to as "writes-any-reads-legal" or "WARL" in the RISC-V world.
     29: For example, certain pads may only support two drive-strength bits, instead of four.
     30: The unsupported drive-strength bits in the corresponding CSRs would then always read as zero, even if SW attempts to set them to 1.
     31: 
>    32: ## Pinmux Configuration
     33: 
     34: Upon POR, the `pinmux` state is such that all MIO outputs are high-Z, and all MIO peripheral inputs are tied off to 0.
     35: Software should determine and program the `pinmux` mapping at startup, or reprogram it when the functionality requirements change at runtime.
     36: This can be achieved by writing the following values to the [`PERIPH_INSEL_0`](registers.md#periph_insel_0) and [`MIO_OUTSEL_0`](registers.md#mio_outsel) registers.

sections.label: Sleep Features
sections.snippet:
55: Note that the `pinmux` configuration should be sequenced after any IO attribute-specific configuration in the [`MIO_PAD_ATTR_0`](registers.md#mio_pad_attr) and [`DIO_PAD_ATTR_0`](registers.md#dio_pad_attr) registers to avoid any unwanted electric behavior and/or contention.
     56: If needed, each select signal can be individually locked down via [`MIO_PERIPH_INSEL_REGWEN_0`](registers.md#mio_periph_insel_regwen) or [`MIO_OUTSEL_REGWEN_0`](registers.md#mio_outsel_regwen).
     57: The configuration can then not be altered anymore until the next system reset.
     58: 
>    59: ## Sleep Features
     60: 
     61: The sleep behavior of each individual MIO or DIO can be defined via the (registers.md#mio_pad_sleep_en), [`DIO_PAD_SLEEP_EN_0`](registers.md#dio_pad_sleep_en), [`MIO_PAD_SLEEP_MODE_0`](registers.md#mio_pad_sleep_mode) and [`DIO_PAD_SLEEP_MODE_0`](registers.md#dio_pad_sleep_mode)) registers.
     62: Available sleep behaviors are:
     63:

sections.label: Wakeup Features
sections.snippet:
80: When exiting sleep, the task of disabling the sleep behavior is however up to SW.
     81: I.e., it must clear the per-pad sleep status bits in registers [`MIO_PAD_SLEEP_STATUS_0`](registers.md#mio_pad_sleep_status) and [`DIO_PAD_SLEEP_STATUS_0`](registers.md#dio_pad_sleep_status) that have been set upon sleep entry.
     82: The rationale for this is that it may not be desirable to disable sleep behavior on all pads at once due to some additional book keeping / re-initialization that needs to be performed while exiting sleep.
     83: 
>    84: ## Wakeup Features
     85: 
     86: The `pinmux` contains eight wakeup detectors.
     87: These detectors can be individually enabled and disabled regardless of the sleep state.
     88: This ensures that SW can set them up before and disable them after sleep in order to ensure that no events are missed during sleep entry and exit.

sections.label: Pinout and Pinmux Mapping
sections.snippet:
105: 6. SW should in any case disable the wakeup detectors and clear the [`WKUP_CAUSE`](registers.md#wkup_cause) registers once it is safe to do so (in order to not miss any events).
    106:    Note that the [`WKUP_CAUSE`](registers.md#wkup_cause) registers reside in the slow AON clock domain, and hence clearing them takes a few uS to take effect.
    107:    If needed, a SW readback can be performed to ensure that the clear operation has completed successfully.
    108:

sections.label: Block Diagram and Overview
sections.snippet:
1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
>     3: ## Block Diagram and Overview
      4: 
      5: The `pinmux` peripheral is a programmable module designed to wire arbitrary peripheral inputs and outputs to arbitrary multiplexable chip bidirectional pins.
      6: It gives much flexibility at the top level of the device, allowing most data pins to be flexibly wired and controlled by many peripherals.
      7: Even though the `pinmux` is referred to as one IP, it is logically split into two modules that are instantiated on the top-level and the chip-level, respectively, as can be seen in the block diagram below.

sections.label: MIO and DIO Signal Categories
sections.snippet:
9: The chip-level module `padring` instantiates the bidirectional pads and connects the physical pad attributes.
     10: 
     11: ![Pinmux Block Diagram](../doc/pinmux_overview_block_diagram.svg)
     12: 
>    13: ### MIO and DIO Signal Categories
     14: 
     15: The `pinmux` supports two different IO signal categories:
     16: Muxed IO (MIO) signals that are routed through the `pinmux` matrix, and dedicated IO (DIO) signals that bypass the `pinmux` matrix.
     17: This distinction is useful for accommodating IO signals that are timing critical or that must have a fixed IO mapping for another reason.

sections.label: Retention and Wakeup Features
sections.snippet:
27: In addition to wiring programmability, each muxed peripheral input can be set constantly to 0 or 1, and each muxed chip output can be set constantly to 0, 1 or high-Z.
     28: 
     29: See the [muxing matrix](#muxing-matrix) section for more details about the mux implementation.
     30: 
>    31: ### Retention and Wakeup Features
     32: 
     33: The retention logic allows SW to specify a certain behavior during sleep for each muxed and dedicated output.
     34: Legal behaviors are tie low, tie high, high-Z, keeping the previous state, or driving the current value (useful for peripherals that are always on).
     35:

sections.label: USB Wakeup Detection Module
sections.snippet:
40: However, only the wakeup detector logic will be actively clocked during sleep in order to save power.
     41: 
     42: See the [retention logic](#retention-logic) and [wakeup detectors](#wakeup-detectors) sections for more details about the mux implementation.
     43: 
>    44: ### USB Wakeup Detection Module
     45: 
     46: The USB device in the Earlgrey top-level is not in the AON power domain and hence the associated wakeup detection module is placed inside the pinmux IP in that top-level.
     47: The USB wakeup module is not connected to any pinmux infrastructure or CSRs except for the `usb_wkup_req` signal going to the power manager.
     48: See [USB device documentation](../../../../ip/usbdev/README.md) for more information on the USB wakeup mechanism.

>    55: ### Pad Attributes
     56: 
     57: Additional pad-specific features such as inversion, pull-up, pull-down, virtual open-drain, drive-strength and input/output inversion etc. can be exercise via the pad attribute CSRs.
     58: The `pinmux` module supports a comprehensive set of such pad attributes, but it is permissible that some of them may not be supported by the underlying pad implementation.
     59: For example, certain ASIC libraries may not provide open-drain outputs, and FPGAs typically do not allow all of these attributes to be programmed dynamically at runtime.

59: For example, certain ASIC libraries may not provide open-drain outputs, and FPGAs typically do not allow all of these attributes to be programmed dynamically at runtime.
     60: See the [generic pad wrapper](#generic-pad-wrapper) section below for more details.
     61: Note that static pad attributes for FPGAs are currently not covered in this specification.
     62: 
>    63: ## Muxing Matrix
     64: 
     65: The diagram below shows connectivity between four arbitrary chip pins, named `MIO0` .. `MIO3`, and several muxed peripheral inputs and outputs.
     66: This shows the connectivity available in all directions, as well as the control registers described later in this document.
     67: Two example peripherals (`uart` and `spidev`) are attached to the `pinmux` in this example, one with one input and one output, the other with three inputs and one output.

sections.label: Retention Logic
sections.snippet:
72: Note that apart from selecting a specific input pad, the `periph_insel[*]` signals can also be used to tie the peripheral input to 0 or 1.
     73: Likewise, the output select signals `mio_outsel[*]` can also be used to constantly drive an output pin to 0/1 or to put it into high-Z state (default).
     74: The output enable and the associated data signal (i.e. `periph_to_mio` and `periph_to_mio_oe`) are indexed with the same select signal to allow the peripheral hardware to determine the pad direction instead of demoting that control to SW.
     75: 
>    76: ## Retention Logic
     77: 
     78: As illustrated in the picture above, all muxing matrix and DIO outputs are routed through the retention logic, which essentially consists of a set of multiplexors and two retention registers per output (one register is for the output data and one for the output enable).
     79: This multiplexor can be configured to be automatically activated upon sleep entry in order to either drive the output low, high, high-Z or to the last seen value (keep).
     80: If no sleep behavior is specified, the retention logic will continue to drive out the value coming from the peripheral side, which can be useful for peripherals that reside in the AON domain.

sections.label: Wakeup Detectors
sections.snippet:
82: The sleep behavior of all outputs is activated in parallel via a trigger signal asserted by the power manager.
     83: Once activated, it is the task of SW to disable the sleep behavior for each individual pin when waking up from sleep.
     84: This ensures that the output values remain stable until the system and its peripherals have been re-initialized.
     85:

     88: The `pinmux` contains eight programmable wakeup detector modules that can listen on any of the MIO or DIO pins.

sections.label: Hardware-Controlled Blink Features
sections.snippet:
142: 
    143: There is a register `pwm_out` at the output pin, which adds an additional delay cycle before the output pin.
    144: Thus, in addition to delay of the clock domain crossing, there is in total a minimum two clock delay between the assertion of [`CFG.CNTR_EN`](registers.md#cfg) and the rising edge of the first output pulse.
    145: 
>   146: ### Hardware-Controlled Blink Features
    147: 
    148: By default, the duty cycle of each channel is directly controlled by firmware, by writing the desired PWM duty cycle to the [`DUTY_CYCLE_0.A_0`](registers.md#duty_cycle) register.
    149: 
    150: There are two other modes which allow for programmably-timed duty cycle modulations, under hardware control.

sections.label: Standard Blink Mode
sections.snippet:
158: Both of the blink modes make use of a 16-bit internal blink counter (one per channel).
    159: This counter is reset whenever [`PWM_PARAM_0.BLINK_EN_0`](registers.md#pwm_param) is cleared.
    160: In other words, changing the blink behavior requires first halting the blink pattern, and the pattern starts from the beginning whenever the blink enable bit is reasserted.
    161: 
>   162: #### Standard Blink Mode
    163: 
    164: To enter standard blink mode, assert [`PWM_PARAM_0.BLINK_EN_0`](registers.md#pwm_param), while leaving [`PWM_PARAM_0.HTBT_EN_0`](registers.md#pwm_param) deasserted.
    165: 
    166: In standard blink mode, the duty cycle abruptly alternates between two values: [`DUTY_CYCLE_0.A_0`](registers.md#duty_cycle) and [`DUTY_CYCLE_0.B_0`](registers.md#duty_cycle).

sections.label: Heartbeat Mode
sections.snippet:
169: Typically multiple channels need to be configured to blink synchronously, for example in the tri-color LED case.
    170: This can be achieved by first disabling the desired PWM outputs using the [`PWM_EN`](registers.md#pwm_en) multi-register.
    171: Once the blink parameters have been configured for these channels, they can be simultaneously re-enabled using a single write to [`PWM_EN`](registers.md#pwm_en).
    172: 
>   173: #### Heartbeat Mode
    174: 
    175: To enter heartbeat mode, assert both [`PWM_PARAM_0.BLINK_EN_0`](registers.md#pwm_param) and [`PWM_PARAM_0.HTBT_EN_0`](registers.md#pwm_param).
    176: 
    177: In heartbeat mode the duty cycle gradually transitions from [`DUTY_CYCLE_0.A_0`](registers.md#duty_cycle) to [`DUTY_CYCLE_0.B_0`](registers.md#duty_cycle) and back in a series of small steps.

      2: 
      3: The process in which the power manager is used is highly dependent on the system's topology.
      4: The following proposes one method for how this can be done.

sections.label: Programmer Sequence for Entering Low Power
sections.snippet:
4: The following proposes one method for how this can be done.
      5: 
      6: Assume first the system has the power states described [above](theory_of_operation.md#supported-low-power-modes).
      7: 
>     8: ## Programmer Sequence for Entering Low Power
      9: 
     10: 1. Disable interrupt handling.
     11: 2. Mask all interrupt sources that should not prevent low power entry.
     12:    - Note that merely *disabling* interrupt handling with the `mie` global interrupt-enable bit on the processing host is insufficient.

21: 
     22: Note that entering low power mode requires that pwrmgr's `pwr_cpu_i.core_sleeping` input be at logic high long enough to be sampled.
     23: A wait-for-interrupt instruction does not guarantee entry into low power, since the CPU could immediately resume execution in some cases.
     24: 
>    25: ### Possible Exits
     26: 
     27: Once low power is initiated, the system may exit due to several reasons.
     28: 1. Graceful low power exit - This exit occurs when some source in the system gracefully wakes up the power manager.
     29: 2. System reset request - This exit occurs when either software or a peripheral requests the pwrmgr to reset the system.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: The power manager performs the following functions:
      4: - Turn on/off power domain(s).
      5: - Control root resets with the reset manager.

sections.label: Block Diagram
sections.snippet:
6: - Control root clock enables with AST and clock manager.
      7: - Sequence various power up activities such as OTP sensing, life cycle initiation and releasing software to execute.
      8: 
      9: 
>    10: ## Block Diagram
     11: 
     12: See the below high level block diagram that illustrates the connections between the power manager and various system components.
     13: Blocks outlined with a solid magenta line are always on; while blocks outlined with a dashed magenta line are a mix of components that are and those that are not.
     14:

sections.label: Overall Sequencing
sections.snippet:
13: Blocks outlined with a solid magenta line are always on; while blocks outlined with a dashed magenta line are a mix of components that are and those that are not.
     14: 
     15: ![Power Manager Connectivity Diagram](../doc/pwrmgr_connectivity.svg)
     16: 
>    17: ## Overall Sequencing
     18: 
     19: The power manager contains two state machines.
     20: One operates on the always-on slow clock (this clock is always running and usually measured in KHz) and is responsible for turning faster clocks on and off and managing the power domains.
     21: The other operates on a normal fixed clock (usually measured in MHz) and is responsible for everything else in the power sequence.

sections.label: Slow Clock Domain FSM
sections.snippet:
36: 
     37: The slow FSM `Low Power` and fast FSM `Active` states specifically are concepts useful when examining [reset handling](#reset-request-handling).
     38: 
     39: 
>    40: ## Slow Clock Domain FSM
     41: 
     42: The slow clock domain FSM (referred to as the slow FSM from here on) resets to the Reset state.
     43: This state is released by `por_rst_n`, which is supplied from the reset controller.
     44: The `por_rst_n` signal is released when the reset controller detects the root power domains (`vcaon_pok` from AST) of the system are ready.

sections.label: Sparse FSM
sections.snippet:
52: When a power down request is received, the slow FSM turns off AST clocks and power as directed by software configuration.
     53: This means the clocks and power are not always turned off, but are rather controlled by software configurations in [`CONTROL`](registers.md#control) prior to low power entry .
     54: Once these steps are complete, the slow FSM transitions to a low power state and awaits a wake request, which can come either as an actual wakeup, or a reset event (for example always on watchdog expiration).
     55: 
>    56: #### Sparse FSM
     57: 
     58: Since the slow FSM is sparsely encoded, it is possible for the FSM to end up in an undefined state if attacked.
     59: When this occurs, the slow FSM sends an `invalid` indication to the fast FSM and forcibly powers off and clamps everything.
     60:

sections.label: Fast Clock Domain FSM
sections.snippet:
63: 
     64: Unlike [escalation resets](#escalation-reset-request), the system does not self reset.
     65: Instead the system goes into a terminal non-responsive state where a user or host must directly intervene by toggling the power or asserting an external reset input.
     66: 
>    67: ## Fast Clock Domain FSM
     68: 
     69: The fast clock domain FSM (referred to as fast FSM from here on) resets to `Low Power` state and waits for a power-up request from the slow FSM.
     70: 
     71: Once received, the fast FSM sequences the initialization of various units before the system is put in active state.

sections.label: ROM Integrity Checks
sections.snippet:
103: 
    104: The fast FSM does not recover from this state until the system is reset by POR.
    105: 
    106: 
>   107: ### ROM Integrity Checks
    108: 
    109: The power manager coordinates the [start up ROM check](../../../../ip/rom_ctrl/README.md#the-startup-rom-check) with `rom_ctrl`.
    110: 
    111: After every reset, the power manager sends an indication to the `rom_ctrl` to begin performing integrity checks.

sections.label: Fall Through Handling
sections.snippet:
116: If the device is not in one of the test states, the `good` signal is used to determine ROM execution.
    117: If `good` is true, ROM execution is allowed.
    118: If `good` is false, ROM execution is disallowed.
    119: 
>   120: ### Fall Through Handling
    121: 
    122: A low power entry fall through occurs when some condition occurs that immediately de-assert the entry conditions right after the software requests it.
    123: 
    124: This can happen if right after software asserts WFI, an interrupt is shown to the processor, thus breaking it out of its currently stopped state.

sections.label: Abort Handling
sections.snippet:
127: 
    128: For a normal low power entry, the fast FSM first checks that the low power entry conditions are still true.
    129: If the entry conditions are no longer true, the fast FSM "falls through" the entry handling and returns the system to active state, thus terminating the entry process.
    130: 
>   131: ### Abort Handling
    132: 
    133: If the entry conditions are still true, the fast FSM then checks there are no ongoing non-volatile activities from `otp_ctrl`, `lc_ctrl` and `flash_ctrl` (if they re part of the system).
    134: If any module is active, the fast FSM "aborts" entry handling and returns the system to active state, thus terminating the entry process.
    135:

sections.label: Reset Request Handling
sections.snippet:
132: 
    133: If the entry conditions are still true, the fast FSM then checks there are no ongoing non-volatile activities from `otp_ctrl`, `lc_ctrl` and `flash_ctrl` (if they re part of the system).
    134: If any module is active, the fast FSM "aborts" entry handling and returns the system to active state, thus terminating the entry process.
    135: 
>   136: ## Reset Request Handling
    137: 
    138: There are 4 reset requests in the system
    139: - peripheral requested reset such as watchdog.
    140: - reset manager's software requested reset, which is functionally very similar to a peripheral requested reset.

     14:   Reset Manager controls the on-chip reset.
     15:   It receives one root power-on reset signal for each power domain from AST and feeds one reset signal for each on-chip reset domain to the OpenTitan hardware blocks.
     16:   Resets can be requested by Power Manager, which internally arbitrates peripheral resets, e.g., from AON Timer and Alert Handler, RISC-V Debug Module, and to a limited extent by software.
     17:   Through always-on registers, software can get information on the reset cause, as well as alert and CPU status prior to a triggered reset (crash dump).

>   107: ### Shadow Resets
    108: 
    109: OpenTitan supports the shadow configuration registers.
    110: These are registers stored in two constantly checking copies to ensure the values are not maliciously or accidentally disturbed.
    111: For these components, the reset manager outputs a shadow reset dedicated to resetting only the shadow storage.

sections.label: Reset Consistency Checks

110: These are registers stored in two constantly checking copies to ensure the values are not maliciously or accidentally disturbed.
    111: For these components, the reset manager outputs a shadow reset dedicated to resetting only the shadow storage.
    112: This reset separation ensures that a targetted attack on the reset line cannot easily defeat shadow registers.
    113: 
>   114: ### Reset Consistency Checks
    115: 
    116: The reset manager implements reset consistency checks to ensure that triggered resets are supposed to happen and not due to some fault in the system.
    117: Every leaf reset in the system has an associated consistency checker.

    138: 
    139: The alert handler needs to know the status of the various reset domains in the system to avoid false alert indications due to the ping mechanism.
    140: To that end, the reset manager outputs a 4bit MuBi signal for each reset domain that indicates whether its reset is active.
    141: For more information on this mechanism, see [alert handler documentation](../../alert_handler/doc/theory_of_operation.md#low-power-management-of-alert-channels).

>   143: ## Design Details
    144: 
    145: The reset manager generates the resets required by the system by synchronizing reset tree components to appropriate output clocks.
    146: As a result, a particular reset tree (for example `rst_lc_n`) may have multiple outputs depending on the clock domains of its consumers.

sections.label: POR Reset Tree
sections.snippet:
146: As a result, a particular reset tree (for example `rst_lc_n`) may have multiple outputs depending on the clock domains of its consumers.
    147: 
    148: Each reset tree is discussed in detail below.
    149: 
>   150: ## POR Reset Tree
    151: 
    152: The POR reset tree, `rst_por_n`, is the root reset of the entire device.
    153: If this reset ever asserts, everything in the design is reset.
    154:

sections.label: Life Cycle Reset Tree
sections.snippet:
162:     *   If any stage at any point becomes '0', the reset counter returns to 0 and downstream logic is driven to reset again.
    163: *   Both functions are expected to operate on slow, always available KHz clocks.
    164: 
    165: 
>   166: ## Life Cycle Reset Tree
    167: 
    168: Life cycle reset, `rst_lc_n` asserts under the following conditions:
    169: *  Whenever `rst_por_n` asserts.
    170: *  Whenever a peripheral reset request (always on timer watchdog, rbox reset request, alert handler escalation, direct software request) is received.

sections.label: System Reset Tree

171: 
    172: The `rst_lc_n` tree contains both always-on and non-always-on versions.
    173: How many non-always-on versions is dependent on how many power domains are supported by the system.
    174: 
>   175: ## System Reset Tree
    176: 
    177: System reset, `rst_sys_n` , assertion depends on life cycle state.
    178: 
    179: When in PROD and PROD_END states, `rst_sys_n` is identical to `rst_lc_n`.

>    11: ## Scope

sections.label: Overview
sections.snippet:
12: 
     13: This document covers the boot mechanism for Integrated OpenTitan.
     14: This includes the execution of the OpenTitan ROM, associated patch support in efuses / OTP for survivability and the code fetch from external flash.
     15: 
>    16: ## Overview
     17: 
     18: The integrated Open Titan is a root of trust for measurement, integrated within the SoC.
     19: It provides the framework necessary to bootstrap the SoC computing elements in a secure and trusted fashion.
     20: This document covers the changes necessary for the OpenTitan to boot first while also allowing an SoC with integrated OpenTitan to add small customizations to the boot path configuration that fit with the SoC topology.

39: Note that patch structure for both deployment models is the same.
     40: An infield patch can be viewed as a new revision of the OTP patch.
     41: The patch in eFuses will be signed using an appropriate PK signing algorithm
     42: 
>    43: ### Programming method:
     44: 
     45: - If prior to the PROD lifecycle stage: Using the manufacturing efuse programming interface.
     46: - In PROD lifecycle stage: Secure, verified patch update programming managed by secure application running on OpenTitan Ibex core (e.g., update patch revision in factory after provisioning, backup in-field patching mechanism).
     47:

sections.label: Simple Address Translation
sections.snippet:
1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
>     3: ## Simple Address Translation
      4: 
      5: The wrapper supports a simple address translation scheme.
      6: The goal of the scheme is to provide hardware support for A/B software copies.
      7:

sections.label: Translation and Instruction Caching
sections.snippet:
22: If a transaction matches multiple regions, the lowest indexed region has priority.
     23: 
     24: For details on how to program the related registers, please see [`IBUS_ADDR_MATCHING_0`](registers.md#ibus_addr_matching) and [`IBUS_REMAP_ADDR_0`](registers.md#ibus_remap_addr).
     25: 
>    26: ### Translation and Instruction Caching
     27: 
     28: The simple address translation scheme used in this design is not aware of the processor context, specifically, any instruction caching done in the core.
     29: This means if the address translation scheme were to change, instructions that are already cached may not reflect the updated address setting.
     30:

sections.label: Random Number Generation
sections.snippet:
30: 
     31: In order to correctly utilize simple address translation along with instruction caching, it is recommended that after the address is updated a `FENCE.I` instruction is issued.
     32: The `FENCE.I` instruction forces the instruction cache to flush, and this aligns the core to the new address setting.
     33: 
>    34: ## Random Number Generation
     35: 
     36: The wrapper has a connection to the [Entropy Distribution Network (EDN)](../../../../ip/edn/README.md) with a register based interface.
     37: The [`RND_DATA`](registers.md#rnd_data) register provides 32-bits directly from the EDN.
     38: [`RND_STATUS.RND_DATA_VALID`](registers.md#rnd_status) indicates if the data in [`RND_DATA`](registers.md#rnd_data) is valid or not.

sections.label: Crash Dump Collection
sections.snippet:
47: Software should take care not to enable the EDN until the entropy complex configuration is as desired.
     48: When the entropy complex configuration is changed reading [`RND_DATA`](registers.md#rnd_data) when it is valid will suffice to flush any old random data to trigger a new request under the new configuration.
     49: If a EDN request is pending when the entropy complex configuration is changed ([`RND_STATUS.RND_DATA_VALID`](registers.md#rnd_status) is clear), it is advisable to wait until it is complete and then flush out the data to ensure the fresh value was produced under the new configuration.
     50: 
>    51: ## Crash Dump Collection
     52: 
     53: In general, when the CPU encounters an error, it is software's responsibility to collect error status and supply it for debug.
     54: 
     55: However, there are situations where it may not be possible for software to collect any error logging.

sections.label: Hung Transaction
sections.snippet:
80: This allows the software to see both fault locations and debug accordingly.
     81: 
     82: In terms of how the crash state information can be used, the following are a few examples.
     83: 
>    84: ### Hung Transaction
     85: 
     86: Assuming the system has a watchdog counter setup, when a CPU transaction hangs the bus (accessing a device whose clock is not turned on or is under reset), the PC and bus access freeze in place until the watchdog resets the system.
     87: Upon reset release, software can check the last PC and data access address to get an idea of what transaction might have caused the bus to hang.
     88:

85:

     88: 
>    89: ### Double Exception
     90: 
     91: If the software has some kind of error and encounters two exceptions in a row, the previous exception PC and address show the location of the first exception, while the current exception address and PC show the location of the most recent exception.

>    94: ## Fetch Enable
     95: 
     96: Ibex has a top-level fetch enable input (``fetch_enable_i``), which uses the same multi-bit encoding used by the lifecycle controller.
     97: When Ibex fetch is disabled it will cease to execute, but will complete instructions currently in the pipeline.
     98: Ibex fetch is enabled when all of the following conditions are met:

sections.label: Local Escalation Path
sections.snippet:
99:   - The lifecycle controller has enabled it
    100:   - The power manager has enabled it
    101:   - A ``fatal_hw_err`` alert hasn't been raised
    102: 
>   103: ### Local Escalation Path
    104: 
    105: When the ``fatal_hw_err`` alert is raised Ibex fetch is disabled and will remain disabled until ``rv_core_ibex`` is reset.

sections.label: Theory of Operation
sections.snippet:
>     1: # Theory of Operation
      2: 
      3: Clock management in OpenTitan is divided into groups.
      4: Each group has specific attributes and controls whether software is allowed to influence individual clocks during the active power state.
      5: For low power states, please see [power manager](../../pwrmgr/README.md).

sections.label: Power-up Clock Group
sections.snippet:
28: * 1 - Transactional clock group's software control is only a software hint.
     29: * 2 - Transactional clock group's wait-for-interrupt control is only a hint.
     30: * 3 - May require additional complexity to handle multi-host (non-wait-for-interrupt) scenarios
     31: 
>    32: ## Power-up Clock Group
     33: 
     34: The group refers to modules responsible for power up, such as power, reset and clock managers.
     35: Large portions of these modules operate to release clocks and resets for the rest of the design, thus cannot operate on gated versions of the clocks themselves.
     36: They are the only group running clocks directly from the source.

sections.label: Transactional Clock Group
sections.snippet:
36: They are the only group running clocks directly from the source.
     37: All follow groups are derived after root clock gating.
     38: See [block diagram](#block-diagram) for more details.
     39: 
>    40: ## Transactional Clock Group
     41: 
     42: This group refers to the collection of modules that are transactional by nature (example: `Hmac` / `Aes` / `Kmac`).
     43: This means these modules perform specific tasks (for example encrypt, decrypt or hashing).
     44: While performing these tasks, it is unsafe to manipulate or change the clocks.

sections.label: Infrastructure Clock Group
sections.snippet:
57: 
     58: For modules in this group, each module can be individually influenced, and thus each has its own dedicated clock gating logic.
     59: The added benefit of allowing software control in this group is to save power, as some transactional modules can be both power and area hungry.
     60: 
>    61: ## Infrastructure Clock Group
     62: 
     63: This group refers to the collection of modules that support infrastructure functions.
     64: 
     65: If the clocks to these modules are turned off, there may not be a way to turn them back on and could thus result in system deadlock.

sections.label: Security Clock Group
sections.snippet:
70: For this group, there is no reason to allow software control over the clocks, as it could be used to create a system deadlock where after disabling infrastructure clocks there is no way to turn them back on.
     71: Wait-for-interrupt controls however can be used, as long as there is a way to break the processor out of wait-for-interrupt and handle other bus hosts, while also separating the functional portions from bus access.
     72: See Wait-for-interrupt clock gating for more details.
     73: 
>    74: ## Security Clock Group
     75: 
     76: The security clock group is made up of security modules that either have background functions (entropy, alert manager, sensors) or perform critical security functions where disabling clocks could have unexpected side effects (life cycle, otp, pinmux, plic).
     77: 
     78: For this group, no software influence over the clock state is allowed during the active state.

sections.label: Timer Clock Group
sections.snippet:
80: 
     81: This group is not functionally identical to the power-up group.
     82: The power-up group is run on clocks directly from the clock source, while the security group is derived after root clock gating.
     83: 
>    84: ## Timer Clock Group
     85: 
     86: The timer clock group is composed of modules that track time for various purposes.
     87: As influencing time can change the perspective of software and potentially reveal security vulnerabilities, the clock state for these modules cannot be directly or indirectly influenced by software.
     88:

sections.label: Peripheral Clock Group
sections.snippet:
87: As influencing time can change the perspective of software and potentially reveal security vulnerabilities, the clock state for these modules cannot be directly or indirectly influenced by software.
     88: 
     89: Functionally, this group is identical to the security group.
     90: 
>    91: ## Peripheral Clock Group
     92: 
     93: The peripheral clock group is composed of I/O peripherals modules.
     94: By their nature, I/O peripherals are both transactional and most of the time not security critical - so long as proper care is taken to sandbox peripherals from the system.
     95:

sections.label: Wait-for-Interrupt wfi Gating
sections.snippet:
95: 
     96: These modules can be both directly and indirectly controlled by software.
     97: The controls can also be individual to each peripheral.
     98: 
>    99: ## Wait-for-Interrupt (wfi) Gating
    100: 
    101: Wait-for-interrupt clock gating refers to the mechanism of using a processor's sleep indication to actively gate off module clocks.
    102: Of the groups enumerated, only transactional, infrastructural and peripheral groups can be influenced by `wfi`.
    103:

sections.label: Infrastructural Clock Group
sections.snippet:
118: In this scenario, it is important to ensure the functional clocks are responsible for creating interrupts and not the bus clocks, as the latter may not be available during `wfi`.
    119: 
    120: This division may only be beneficial for peripherals where register and local fabric size is large relative to the functional component.
    121: 
>   122: ### Infrastructural Clock Group
    123: 
    124: This clock group matches `wfi` functionality well.
    125: Most infrastructural components such as fabric, gaskets and memories, have no need to be clocked when the processor is idle.
    126: Some components such as flash controller however would also need to be split into bus and functional halves to support long, background activities while the processor is idle.

sections.label: Block Diagram

132: The bus requests themselves thus become dynamic clock request signals to help enable components in its path.
    133: 
    134: There is thus a moderate design and high verification cost to supporting `wfi` gating for the infrastructural group.

sections.label: Issuing a Controller Program
